noticias.titulo: Community care: Former Jewish school becomes Iraq's first Jewish museum
noticias.resumen: Iraq has opened its first Jewish museum in Baghdad, dedicated to preserving the heritage of the country's Jewish community. Housed in a former school dating back to 1928, it displays historical photographs, religious objects and documents. Organisers hope it will highlight Iraq's diversity.
noticias.texto:
Iraq has opened its first Jewish museum in Baghdad, dedicated to preserving the heritage of the country's Jewish community. Housed in a former school dating back to 1928, it displays historical photographs, religious objects and documents. Organisers hope it will highlight Iraq's diversity.
In Iraq, the country's first Jewish museum has opened its doors in Baghdad, offering visitors a glimpse into the history and heritage of its once-thriving Jewish community.
The Shamash Jewish Museum is housed in a former Jewish school on Al-Rashid Street, founded in 1928 by wealthy Iraqi Jew Yaakov Shlomo Shamash. Its collection includes historic photographs, religious objects, Hebrew books and documents tracing Jewish life in Iraq.
Iraq's once-thriving Jewish community, which numbered around 130,000 people in the 1940s, has dwindled to just a handful of residents today.
Ammar Al-Tamimi, a member of the committee managing Iraqi Jews' assets, explains that political upheaval led to the school's closure in 1975. The building was later used for other educational purposes before being returned to the Jewish community in 1992 following a court ruling.
The museum is intended not only to preserve this heritage but also to send a wider message about religious diversity in Iraq. "It conveys a message that the state cares for its minorities, a message to other nations that Iraq is a diverse, non-sectarian country, one that brings together all ethnicities and minority groups. It is a highly significant message, both for the world at large and for those within and outside of Iraq", Al-Tamimi explained.
For visitors, the museum is also an opportunity to remember a community that once played an important role in the country's history. Ramzi Al-Saadi, a 74-year-old visitor, says looking back at Iraqi Jewish heritage reminds him of its members as kind, peaceful and humble people who meant no harm to anyone.

noticias.titulo: Can Europe fix its chronic medicine shortage and supply chain disruptions?
noticias.resumen: The European Parliament just approved new legislation to strengthen the production of essential treatments and cut risks linked to limited suppliers. But will it be enough?
noticias.texto:
The European Parliament just approved new legislation to strengthen the production of essential treatments and cut risks linked to limited suppliers. But will it be enough?
Approved today by the European Parliament, the Critical Medicines Act aims to boost supply, industry innovation, and combat antimicrobial resistance.
Initially proposed by the EU Commission in March 2025, the legislation focuses in particular on essential drugs, whose shortage might cause serious harm to patients, including antibiotics, insulin and treatments for chronic diseases.
Why is Europe's drug supply under threat?
One of the main reasons is the continent's dependence on a limited number of suppliers, particularly outside the EU, for essential medicines and their active ingredients.
Even if some medicines are manufactured in Europe, they still depend on substances produced, for example, in India or in China, tells Euronews Jorge Batista, pharmacist and senior advisor at The Pharmaceutical Group of the European Union (PGEU).
He adds that about three-quarters of production sites for chemically active pharmaceutical ingredients are actually outside the EU.
When a manufacturer faces production problems, or demand suddenly increases, the entire supply chain can be disrupted. And as countries often compete to buy the same medicines, smaller markets can struggle to secure supplies.
How will the Act strengthen the EU's pharmaceutical industry?
Factories producing critical medicines or their active ingredients could receive financial support and faster administrative procedures to expand their production.
Second, governments will have to consider supply reliability when purchasing medicines, rather than focusing mainly on the lowest price.
Europe is heavily dependent on a small number of non-EU suppliers, and public buyers will generally have to favour European manufacturing. The Act also makes it easier for countries to buy medicines together, pooling their purchasing power to improve access, particularly in smaller markets.
“Small countries may need too few packs to attract several suppliers on their own", says Batista. "We see already that the demand is quite low. So, by pulling orders, by bringing together different countries, for example, small countries can increase the number of orders, and they can offer manufacturers, let's say, a larger, more predictable market."
Which drugs are currently running short?
Medicines currently facing supply shortages are Vaxigrip, a seasonal flu vaccine; Azactam, an antibiotic for serious bacterial infections; ifosfamide, used in chemotherapy; extended-release quetiapine, prescribed for schizophrenia and bipolar disorder; and Creon, which helps people with pancreatic enzyme insufficiency digest food.
But the Critical Medicines Act is not an emergency measure that will immediately restock pharmacies.
Building new factories, diversifying suppliers and changing public procurement practices will take time, and the law cannot guarantee that every medicine will always be available, or that prices for patients will fall.
Its success will depend on whether governments will actually use these new tools, whether manufacturers will invest in additional production, and whether countries will cooperate when supplies are limited.
Is Europe on the road to extinction?
Also in today's episode, we take a look at the demographic crisis affecting the continent.
Europe is running out of babies, and the clock is ticking. It’s more than a demographic shift. It’s a challenge that could reshape Europe’s economy, workforce and future.
“This is extremely difficult for the balance of public budgets of the governments, which have to allocate more and more funding for elderly care for healthcare, but also for keeping basic infrastructure running.", Tomas Sobotka, Deputy Director, Vienna Institute of Demography, tells Euronews.
"It will squeeze the amount of money available for investments. It will also squeeze the amount of money available for younger people, for supporting families and for allocating money to other generations and other needs than the needs of the elderly.
Where are some of the worst birth rates in Europe?
In some cases, birth rates are dropping to wartime levels.
Deaths outnumbered births in France last year, with the lowest level of newborns since 1942: 645,000. It doesn't go much better in Germany, with only 654,000 babies in 2026, the lowest number on record since data collection began in 1946.
And then there’s Italy, where births have fallen for 17 straight years, dropping 38% since 2008, to 356,000 in 2025.
Spain saw a similar decline (- 24% between 2015 and 2025), and last year’s tiny 1% growth won’t make up for it.
What are governments doing?
Parental leave is great, but it doesn’t pay for prams. That’s why some countries are going straight for people’s wallets.
In Hungary, mothers with at least three children are exempt from employment income tax for life, even after their children have grown up. Poland is taking a similar approach. Families receive about €2,200 a year for each child under 18. And in Malta, families with a combined annual income below €30,000 can receive up to €1,400 per child annually, plus an annual supplement of around €900.
But according to Anna Matysiak, President of the European Association for Population Studies, these measures are not likely to be a silver bullet.
“Researchers consistently say that these policies are rather unlikely to bring fertility back to the levels of around two children per woman, the level we ideally would like to have."
"I still think Scandinavian countries are doing a good job, with public childcare combined with parental leave. They also have universal financial support for families. These countries are still a model which many countries in Europe are trying to follow.”
Watch Euronews Verify
Join Euronews Verify live on TV, Euronews' website, and on digital platforms (YouTube, Facebook, X, and Instagram) every weekday at 6:40 pm Brussels time. In just under 11 minutes, our new format goes beyond the headlines to make sense of what's happening, fact-checking and untangling the day's most pressing issues to explain why they matter to you.

noticias.titulo: ESA releases first images showing 'complete chaos' on asteroid smashed by NASA probe
noticias.resumen: The European Space Agency's first images of the asteroid deliberately smashed by NASA's Dart mission show a huge impact zone with hundreds of rocks drifting near the surface. Is this how we should defend our planet?
noticias.texto:
The European Space Agency's first images of the asteroid deliberately smashed by NASA's Dart mission show a huge impact zone with hundreds of rocks drifting near the surface. Is this how we should defend our planet?
The images taken by the Hera mission show that the 151 metre diameter object, called Dimorphos, has one side that has been transformed by the impact of the American probe named DART.
Dimorphos orbits around a larger asteroid called Didymos, which is clearly visible in the foreground of the pictures, and the pair were chosen for investigation because they pose no threat to our planet.
The new images, with a resolution of 2.7 metres per pixel, show a massive impact zone that's unlike anything scientists have seen up close before.
Patrick Michel, Principal Investigator on the European Space Agency (ESA) mission tells Euronews, "It's a huge crater, yet it didn't destroy the object, and there are things in the middle of it that we still don't understand."
Surprisingly, hundreds of lumps of debris of up to a metre in size are now floating around the asteroid, too. "It's complete chaos," Hera Project Manager Ian Carnelli tells Euronews. "It's completely different from what our brain would tell us rationally that these rocks should look like and behave."
This is the first time that a spacecraft made by humans has actually impacted an interplanetary body with the direct intention of altering its course.
Right now, Dimorphos appears to be reeling chaotically like a boxer after a powerful punch.
"Its rotation around its own axis is very chaotic and very unstable. It doesn't rotate around a single axis, sometimes, the crater on the side facing the direction of rotation is visible, and sometimes it shifts to the other side. So there has also been a significant destabilisation of its rotation," Michel says.
The next step will be to release two tiny cubesats from the Hera spacecraft, which itself will fly much closer than its current 30 kilometre distance, in order to study the asteroid's surface, density and interior structure.
Scientists are keen to understand why it didn't smash apart, and are wary of drawing rapid conclusions given how unearthly and strange these asteroids can be.
"We have six months of investigation ahead of us, with risky operations almost every month. So, it's a bit like an Indiana Jones adventure, full of suspense," says Michel, his voice buzzing with excitement.
It's a sentiment echoed by Margherita Cardi: "It's a nightmare, there's a mix of excitement and panic," she laughs. She is managing the Milani CubeSat, which will now need to navigate its way through and around the boulders drifting above the asteroid, aiming to image and map the surface, and characterise the dust around it.
Why are space agencies deliberately smashing satellites into asteroids?
The images are the latest step in a long-running effort by the European, American and Japanese space agencies to understand how to deviate an asteroid from its path.
With the fate of the dinosaurs in mind, killed off when an asteroid struck 65 million years ago, they believe that humans need to master the skill of knocking space rocks off track, in order to be ready should a dangerous body be spotted on a collision course with planet Earth.
And it looks like we're learning how to do so very quickly. When NASA's DART probe hit Dimorphos back in 2022 it successfully shortened its orbit around Didymos by about 33 minutes.
Carnelli, who fought hard to secure funding for the mission for the past decade or more, says it's gratifying to see the progress they have made.
"I'm really proud to say that for once, space agencies, but also politicians and taxpayers, are taking a natural hazard very seriously. And we're doing something about it, for the good of humanity," he tells Euronews.
Hera is part of ESA's Space Safety Programme, and it will be followed by a new mission called Ramses, which will rendez-vous with an asteroid called Apophis as it passes by Earth in 2029.
In the meantime, Carnelli is preparing to request funding for a mission extension for Hera, given that the European probe still has plenty of propellant on board.
"The idea being that we leave in September and we go on a two year journey around the solar system. We visit two more asteroids - flybys - and then we come back to Didymos." he explains.
Returning to check on the battered space rock makes a great deal of sense scientifically, as the ESA team can observe if its orbit and rotation have changed over the years, and whether the structures on the surface have shifted or eroded since the impact.

noticias.titulo: Unannounced strike by Eurostar staff halts Paris-London trains
noticias.resumen: The rail operator has advised customers to postpone their journeys and has warned that more disruption on other routes is possible.
noticias.texto:
The rail operator has advised customers to postpone their journeys and has warned that more disruption on other routes is possible.
Several Eurostar trains due to travel between Paris and London have been cancelled because of strike action by Paris-based staff.
The operator said it was informed of the industrial action overnight. Train drivers and managers are among the staff on strike.
A spokesperson for Eurostar said: "Regrettably, Eurostar customers travelling between Paris and London today are being impacted by industrial action which the company was notified of overnight."
The statement continued: "Unfortunately, this is causing some cancellations to services. Other routes are not directly affected but may see some knock-on impact."
At least six trains have been cancelled, including one that originated in Brussels. Another five have been subject to delays.
One passenger travelling from Paris Gare du Nord to London St Pancras International told Euronews that they were initially told their delay was due to an "unexpected number of travellers". This was later corrected in an email informing them of the unannounced strike action.
The email reads: "Due to unannounced strike action by some of our staff, we expect your train to be delayed by about 90 minutes," and advised passengers with onward connections to speak to staff.
The operator has told customers whose trains have been cancelled that they can rebook for another date or receive a full refund.
Eurostar also said discussions with unions were ongoing.

noticias.titulo: Pakistan: Emergency teams search for survivors beneath collapsed building
noticias.resumen: At least one person was killed and 10 others injured when a multi-storey building under construction collapsed in Karachi, on Wednesday 25 November 2026. Emergency teams are searching the rubble for people feared missing.
noticias.texto:
Emergency teams pulled one survivor alive from the ruins of a collapsed six-storey building in Karachi as rescuers raced to reach around 15 workers feared trapped beneath vast piles of concrete and twisted metal. Using heavy machinery and carving three access routes into the wreckage, crews from Pakistan’s main emergency service, Rescue 1122, carried injured victims away on stretchers to Medical Centre, though officials cautioned that the exact number of missing remained unconfirmed.
The unfinished structure gave way while still under construction, leaving at least three people dead and 14 injured, according to Rescue 1122, following initial reports of between 10 and 14 hurt. As authorities investigate the cause of the disaster, the collapse has renewed concerns over lax building standards and weak safety enforcement in Karachi and across Pakistan.

noticias.titulo: Indra unveils Forward2030 plan to more than double revenue to €12bn
noticias.resumen: The company has unveiled its Forward2030 strategic plan at its Investor Day, targeting over €12 billion in revenue and an EBIT margin above 12.5% by 2030, with €1 billion in investment in in-house product development and a stable workforce of about 56,000 employees.
noticias.texto:
The company has unveiled its Forward2030 strategic plan at its Investor Day, targeting over €12 billion in revenue and an EBIT margin above 12.5% by 2030, with €1 billion in investment in in-house product development and a stable workforce of about 56,000 employees.
Indra wants to more than double its size in five years. The company on Wednesday presented its strategic plan Forward2030 at its Investor Day, under which it aims to exceed €12 billion in revenue in 2030, compared with €5.457 billion in 2025, and to achieve EBIT of more than €1.5 billion. The stock market responded positively to the plan, and the share price rose as much as 7% in the first minutes of trading.
The new strategic plan replaces Leading the Future, presented in 2024, which had set a target of €10 billion in revenue for 2030 and an EBIT margin of 12%. The company is now looking ahead to 2035, when it expects to generate €20 billion in revenue, half of it outside Spain.
Before turning to the figures, Indra chairman Ángel Simón devoted much of his speech to the wider context. He noted that there are there are currently 60 armed conflicts of medium and high intensity around the world and that in Spain a cyber incident is handled every four minutes. He referred to security alerts that have disrupted commercial flights in Europe and to cyberattacks that have hit supermarkets and schools. "Our everyday life depends on secure and reliable systems," he said.
Simón argued that defence "is a public good that benefits all citizens" and called for the armed forces and state security forces to have the best technological capabilities. He also warned that the boundary between civil and military technology is disappearing, and that artificial intelligence has opened up the market to companies that are born with it already embedded.
According to the chairman, Forward2030 should help Indra stop being "a mere aggregator of businesses" and become "an integrated, synergistic company". He wants the firm drive the growth of the rest of Spain's defence industry, from SMEs to start-ups and universities, and to spread its production centres across different parts of the country. Europe, he added, has to overcome the fragmentation of its defence markets, and Indra aspires to be Spain's main representative there.
Chief executive Josep Maria Recasens explained why a new strategic plan was needed. He gave two reasons. The boundaries between the civil and military sectors are blurring, and tech giants and newcomers that compete in different ways have entered the playing field. "It is a totally different sport, in which the recipe of the past no longer works," he summed up.
The company has structured the strategic plan around what it calls the three Es: execute, evolve and expand. Recasens stressed that they do not follow one after the other, because a company like the one he wants to build has to manage "two clocks" at the same time, delivering today while preparing for the future.
The most immediate lever is the order book, worth more than €22 billion, of which around 70% should turn into revenue before 2030. Some €12 billion relates to physical deliveries, mainly from Defence Special Modernisation Programmes (PEM), air-traffic control radars for the United States, equipment for London and the European IRIS² satellite programme.
To achieve this, execution will depend on a single team under a new chief operating officer, while the business units retain their client relationships and their profit and loss accounts. Indra will keep control of system architecture, integration and delivery, and will rely on partners and around 2,500 suppliers for the rest.
It will go from six plants in 2025 to 14 in 2027, will add 2,000 engineers to its industrial operations and will quadruple its manufacturing footprint, with an investment of €400 million.The factories will be grouped into three corridors in Spain. The northern corridor will focus on land vehicles, the central one on drones, electronic warfare and simulators, and the southern one on radars and anti-drone systems.
The model Recasens wants to replicate is Córdoba, where the company has multiplied its radar production capacity by seven in less than six months and cut costs by 30%. This year Indra will deliver 70 air-traffic control radars, the highest number in its history.
IndraMind, the cornerstone of the strategic plan
The second E, evolve, translates into investment in product development. Indra will invest €1 billion of its own resources between 2026 and 2030, four times more than in the last five years, to launch more than 200 products. Seventy per cent will have dual use, civil and military, and 90% will have artificial intelligence built in. Recasens pledged to cut to a third the time it takes its products to reach the market.
At the centre is IndraMind, the artificial intelligence unit the company launched in October 2025. It has an order book of €400 million, 15 solutions developed, contracts signed for eight of them and more than 3,000 experts. Recasens described it as an open operating system, "more Android than iOS", to which solutions from the group and from third parties can connect.
He gave an example. Today, coordinating the response to a threat across several systems in different domains takes about 45 minutes. With IndraMind, according to the chief executive, 23 seconds are enough.
In defence, Indra wants to consolidate its position as one of Europe's main prime contractors, with an order book of around €11.4 billion. One of its key projects is Land Next Gen, a modular, hybrid and electric land platform, crewed or uncrewed, in which it will invest nearly €20 million. It wants to have it ready in 2028 or 2029 for under €1 million per unit and to cut to three years a development cycle that in the sector usually runs to around ten.
The space business has expanded significantly following the acquisition of Hispasat and Hisdesat. With IRIS² and the SpainSat NG and PAZ II satellites, the company wants to become a European integrator of complete missions and to move from being a niche player to generating revenue of €1 billion in 2030.
Minsait, "the elephant in the room"
Recasens devoted a separate section to Minsait, the information technology subsidiary. "Let us be honest, it is a bit the elephant in the room," he admitted, referring to those who believe that artificial intelligence is going to sweep away technology services. "We believe in Minsait," he replied. The change, he explained, involves focusing "on value and not on volume".
Minsait will also serve as a talent pool for the rest of the group. According to Recasens, Indra does not need to recruit externally for defence, space or IndraMind, because it can train the people it already has. The plan maintains a stable workforce of around 56,000 employees and sets aside €240 million for retraining programmes. "This company is not going to destroy jobs," he said.
To grow abroad, the group wants to copy the air traffic control business model, which already earns 88% of its revenue overseas, has delivered more than 450 radars and has another 185 under contract in the United States.
Without counting on higher defence spending
Chief financial officer Miguel Forteza argued that the figures are prudent. Revenue will grow at an average annual rate of 17% and EBIT by around 24%. The forecasts also do not assume that Spain will raise its defence spending above 2.1% of GDP, nor that new large European programmes will be launched. Forteza presented them as additional growth opportunities outside the targets.
The company expects to generate more than €3.1 billion in free cash flow between 2026 and 2030, excluding advances from the PEM programmes, and it could take on debt of up to around 1.5 times if a suitable acquisition opportunity arises. Acquisitions will be selective and will focus on aerospace, defence and IndraMind. "We are not going to make acquisitions simply to gain size," the chief financial officer concluded.

noticias.titulo: Tusk government ‘facing armageddon’ as European court resumes cases against Poland
noticias.resumen: The country faces millions of euros in potential compensation payments over its former nationalist government’s judicial overhaul.
noticias.texto: Europe’s top human rights court resumed proceedings against Poland on Wednesday, putting fresh pressure on Prime Minister Donald Tusk to deliver on his promise to restore the independence of the country’s courts. The European Court of Human Rights said it has around 1,600 cases pending over judicial changes introduced by Poland’s former nationalist Law and Justice government. It suspended proceedings in 2023 to give Warsaw time to restore judicial independence. Tusk’s promise to restore the rule of law helped unlock billions in frozen EU funding following his return to power in 2023. But his efforts have been hampered by two successive PiS-backed presidents, most recently Karol Nawrocki. Justice Minister Waldemar Żurek has estimated that compensation payments could exceed €12 million. Speaking by phone Wednesday evening, he said the bill could grow considerably as judges appointed under the disputed system continued to hear cases, creating fresh grounds for compensation claims. “So we’re facing armageddon,” Żurek said. He blamed PiS for undermining Poland’s judicial system and accused Nawrocki of obstructing efforts to repair it. The decision comes amid a wider confrontation between Tusk and Nawrocki over Poland’s courts, including the Constitutional Tribunal . At the heart of the ECHR cases is a 2017 overhaul that gave lawmakers greater control over judicial appointments. Nawrocki vetoed a bill in February aimed at reversing those changes, arguing it would usher in a “new phase of chaos.” Nawrocki’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The ECHR has already sided with applicants ranging from a distributor of sex-enhancing supplements to former Polish President and Nobel Peace Prize winner Lech Wałęsa. Wałęsa had won a defamation case against a former associate who accused him of collaborating with the communist secret police, only to see that victory overturned years later by a newly created chamber of Poland’s Supreme Court. The ECHR awarded him €30,000 in damages in a landmark 2023 ruling that prompted the suspension of similar cases. It twice extended the suspension but let it expire Monday. Another bill addressing the status of thousands of judges appointed under PiS-era rules has been on Nawrocki’s desk since Nov. 9. Żurek said it would address the ECHR’s main concerns but that he feared another politically motivated veto.

noticias.titulo: “Les COP, c’est une blague” : les critiques enflent contre les sommets climatiques après l’échec à Antalya
noticias.resumen: La fin chaotique de la COP31 pousse des pays à remettre en question tout le processus onusien de négociations climatiques.
noticias.texto: Le processus des Nations unies pour coordonner la réponse mondiale au changement climatique se fissure discrètement depuis des années. Aujourd’hui, même ses partisans historiques se rebellent ouvertement et exigent une refonte des négociations internationales. L’élément déclencheur : l’échec retentissant des négociateurs à conclure un accord mondial dimanche. De l’Afrique à l’Europe, les représentants des pays ont exprimé leur méfiance face à un processus qui a permis aux pays riches en pétrole de passer outre les appels à inclure dans le texte final une mention sur la sortie progressive des énergies fossiles — une mesure que les scientifiques réclament depuis des années. Les divisions se sont avérées si profondes lors des pourparlers à Antalya, en Turquie, que les gouvernements n’ont pas pu conclure d’accord de haut niveau pour la première fois depuis 2009. Cela a conduit les ministres, les négociateurs et d’autres responsables à réclamer des changements dans un processus qui, depuis des décennies, nécessite un consensus entre près de 200 pays pour avancer. “Si nous parvenons à donner le meilleur de nous-mêmes, à nous organiser, au cours des douze prochains mois, la COP31 nous paraîtra rétrospectivement comme un moment cathartique de prise de conscience”, a positivé Rachel Kyte, envoyée spéciale du Royaume-Uni pour le climat, lors d’un entretien accordé à POLITICO, ajoutant que les pays devaient corriger le processus qui, ces dernières années, a peiné à produire des résultats. Ceux appelant à une refonte du processus réclament une réforme du format COP, voire sa suppression pure et simple, sans que l’on ait réellement d’idées sur la manière de mettre en œuvre l’une ou l’autre de ces options. Reste que l’échec des organisateurs à négocier un accord final a libéré un flot de critiques. Selon ses détracteurs, le processus actuel, dans lequel les pays pétroliers font obstacle aux initiatives visant à mentionner explicitement les énergies fossiles, n’est plus viable dans un monde qui se dirige à toute vitesse vers une aggravation des conditions climatiques. “Nous avons tous été pris en otage par les producteurs de pétrole, mais aussi par les plus grands consommateurs de pétrole”, a pointé auprès de POLITICO le ministre panaméen du Climat, Juan Carlos Navarro. La faute aux pays pétroliers, mais pas que Ces négociations chaotiques en Turquie interviennent onze ans après que, pour la première fois, tous les pays se sont mis d’accord sur la nécessité de lutter contre le changement climatique en signant l’Accord de Paris. Depuis, des progrès poussifs ont laissé les pays à la traîne par rapport à leurs objectifs. Au point que l’ONU a annoncé le mois dernier qu’il n’y avait plus aucun espoir d’éviter un réchauffement de 1,5 °C. L’échec de ce week-end contraste fortement avec les négociations de l’année dernière au Brésil, où les gouvernements étaient parvenus à un accord malgré les attaques à distance contre le processus du président Donald Trump, et sa décision de retirer les Etats-Unis de l’Accord de Paris. Alors que les négociations entraient en prolongation le week-end dernier, l’Arabie saoudite et un groupe d’autres pays producteurs d’énergies fossiles se sont battus pour empêcher que les négociations ne reprennent les termes convenus il y a trois ans lors de la COP28, qui appelaient à accélérer la sortie des énergies fossiles. “Ce que nous voyons ne doit pas devenir la norme”, insistait le 18 novembre Jiwoh Abdulai, ministre de l’Environnement et du Climat de la Sierra Leone, avant l’échec des négociations. “Il y a un manque de confiance. Je pense que l’essentiel est de trouver un mécanisme permettant de rétablir la confiance.” Certains responsables estiment que les politiques climatiques peuvent être menées par d’autres moyens, par exemple via des accords commerciaux et des partenariats d’approvisionnement en minerais. Une grande partie de ce travail est déjà en cours, consolidant des changements concrets dans l’économie mondiale et dans la lutte contre les gaz à effet de serre. “Les COP, c’est une blague et ce depuis des années. Elles devraient être supprimées”, a tancé mardi sur X Rohan Patel, ancien conseiller à la Maison-Blanche en matière de politique climatique et énergétique sous Barack Obama. “Au mieux, cette conférence apporte un élan moral à un problème qui ne cesse de s’aggraver et auquel nous avons tardé à nous attaquer à bien des égards. Mais en général, c’est un énorme fiasco et tout le monde le sait bien (même ceux qui y participent chaque année).” D’autres pays ont joué un rôle dans cet échec. Les gouvernements des pays riches ont refusé d’accorder des financements aux pays pauvres pour leur permettre de s’adapter au réchauffement climatique. De grandes puissances comme la Chine sont restées en retrait. Plusieurs diplomates ont déploré en privé l’absence des négociateurs américains, qui, historiquement, ont toujours fait pression sur les récalcitrants pour qu’ils fassent des compromis. Des participants de longue date ont estimé que les négociations se sont trop concentrées sur l’élaboration de déclarations de haut niveau, au détriment de progrès concrets pour réduire les émissions de gaz à effet de serre. D’autres ont suggéré que l’échec du week-end dernier pourrait servir à revoir le processus et à le rendre plus efficace dans un monde fragmenté. “Je reçois des appels de partout, me disant : ‘C’est une occasion à ne pas manquer, il faut la saisir’”, a confié Rachel Kyte, l’envoyée britannique. “Donc, tout bien considéré, ça a été une décision difficile [de rejeter l’accord], mais je pense que c’était la bonne.” Des progrès passés inaperçus Par ailleurs, de nombreux diplomates soulignent avoir constaté des progrès discrets à Antalya, mais ils ont été éclipsés par les dernières heures catastrophiques des négociations. L’Allemagne, la France et les Pays-Bas ont publié des feuilles de route détaillées pour abandonner le pétrole, le charbon et le gaz. Le fait que 130 pays, dont l’Union européenne, se soient opposés au texte après le retrait de la mention sur la sortie des énergies fossiles a mis en évidence une large coopération, ont soulevé certains. Plus de 80 pays ont signé un engagement lors de la COP31 visant à électrifier 35% de leur consommation finale d’énergie d’ici 2035, bien que celui-ci n’ait jamais été adopté en raison de l’échec des négociations. En outre, les particuliers achètent de plus en plus de véhicules électriques et les pays développent rapidement leurs capacités de production d’énergies renouvelables. Cette tendance va se poursuivre, a affirmé la semaine dernière l’Agence internationale de l’énergie. Toutefois, celle-ci a également souligné que la demande d’énergie croît, ce qui signifie que la consommation de pétrole, de gaz et de charbon se poursuivra pendant des décennies. “Le sujet, ce n’est pas des feuilles de papier. C’est décarboner réellement l’économie mondiale”, a résumé dans son podcast Christiana Figueres, qui a dirigé les négociations de l’Accord de Paris en 2015. Chris Bowen, le ministre australien du Changement climatique et de l’Energie, qui a coprésidé la COP31 avec la Turquie, a jugé que les négociations de cette année s’étaient déroulées dans un climat particulièrement tendu. La sécurité énergétique constituait une préoccupation majeure, étant donné l’angoisse des populations face aux pénuries d’approvisionnement en carburant et à la flambée des prix due à la fermeture du détroit d’Ormuz. Les guerres au Moyen-Orient et en Europe ont encore davantage mis à rude épreuve la coopération internationale. Les pays économiquement dépendants des énergies fossiles, comme l’Arabie saoudite et la Russie, ont adopté des positions intransigeantes face au désordre mondial. L’Union européenne, le Royaume-Uni et des dizaines d’autres pays ont considéré qu’il valait mieux rejeter un mauvais accord plutôt que de faire marche arrière. “Il est profondément décevant qu’aucun consensus n’ait été trouvé lors de la COP31. Ce moment, après l’été que le monde vient de vivre, appelait à faire preuve d’ambition. Au lieu de cela, on nous a présenté un accord qui constitue un recul en matière de climat, et nous ne pouvions pas le soutenir”, a justifié lundi le Premier ministre britannique Andy Burnham devant la Chambre des communes. Les négociations annuelles constituaient autrefois le mécanisme permettant de parvenir à un accord international sur les moyens de lutter contre le changement climatique. Aujourd’hui, il vaut mieux les utiliser comme une tribune pour faire pression sur les pays afin qu’ils agissent plus rapidement pour réduire leurs émissions, considère Alden Meyer, du think tank E3G. “Je dirais que la coopération pour mener des initiatives de décarbonation sur le terrain dans tous les secteurs de l’économie revêt une importance bien plus grande que l’existence ou non d’un consensus sur une décision-cadre qui se limite au plus petit dénominateur commun”, a-t-il écrit dans un SMS. Cet article a d’abord été publié par POLITICO en anglais, puis a été édité en français par Marie Thirion et Jean-Christophe Catalon.

noticias.titulo: Don’t ‘backslide’ on defense spending, senior US lawmaker tells Europe
noticias.resumen: Brendan Boyle said the EU needs to keep investing in defense amid fraught seven-year budget talks.
noticias.texto: A senior U.S. lawmaker has urged the European Union not to cut defense spending in its next seven-year budget as Europe’s leaders struggle to agree on the almost €2 trillion pot of cash. Brendan Boyle, a Democratic member of the U.S. House of Representatives who will chair its Budget Committee in 2027, warned that Russia was an “enormous threat” to Europe and said the bloc must continue increasing its defense spending. “This is not a time when we can backslide,” Boyle told POLITICO in an interview, pointing to the approaching five-year anniversary of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Earlier this week, Boyle was also elected president of NATO’s parliamentary assembly, which is made up of delegates from the alliance’s 32 member countries. His comments come as EU leaders prepare to discuss the bloc’s next seven-year budget at a summit Thursday and Friday . The latest draft defense budget tabled by European Council President António Costa would see tens of billions cut from the European Commission’s earlier proposal, drawing the ire of some EU countries — though the total is still double the previous seven-year budget. Boyle said he was “heartened” that all NATO allies were now spending more on defense than the alliance’s longstanding 2% of GDP target agreed at the 2014 Wales summit. “I’m glad that that is a floor and no longer considered a ceiling,” he said, while acknowledging that European governments face “similar budget constraints” to the U.S. He said Europe building up its own defense industry after decades of relying on American weapons was a net positive for the NATO alliance, but warned against the bloc breaking that dependence too fast. EU countries are currently only spending about 15% of their defense procurement budgets on European-made equipment, despite calls from the Commission to raise this to at least half by 2030. “Where it would become a negative is if suddenly there was a hard turn away from totally buying U.S. systems,” Boyle said. “That would be a mistake.”

noticias.titulo: With no summit deal expected, it is clear the EU budget falls short on ambition – but does it matter?
noticias.resumen: After months of haggling and negotiation the next seven year EU budget looks devoid of ambition and purpose.
noticias.texto: Of all the EU’s policy battles, nothing causes more ink to be spilled, is given more reverence and yet is unimportant as the EU budget. There – I’ve said it. The income guarantees in the EU budget offer vital financial life-support to millions of European farmers but this week’s budget summit in Brussels, which follows months of painstaking negotiations, will see EU leaders spend two days haggling over the difference of about €30-40bn. And few expect any white smoke to emerge. Read more Less EU money for farmers and regions, but a growing Ukraine bill: Leaders meet to square trillion-euro circles at special summit EU budget negotiations have followed a similar pattern for a generation; the EU commission proposes plans to significantly increase spending; the European Parliament demands more still and member states radically pare down the spending plan. The end result is typically a small increase, close to the rate of inflation, with which nobody is happy. That pattern – or exercise in futility – is set to play out again this week. noticias.titulo: [Exclusive] Details leaked of EU plan to cancel Russian sports in Europe, including Trump Jr.’s boxing pal
noticias.resumen: "Russia increasingly uses the fields of sports and culture as ... avenues for propaganda to legitimise its military aggression," said the draft EU sanctions text.
noticias.texto: Russia is being fully cancelled from European sports, in a cultural counter-offensive that also strikes at the US president’s family, and comes with added financial stings in the tail for Moscow. “Russia increasingly uses the fields of sports and culture as … avenues for propaganda to legitimise its military aggression, exert influence within the Union and undermine European Union democratic values,” said the EU’s draft 22nd sanctions on Russia , an internal document seen by EUobserver on Wednesday (25 November). “In addition, Russia’s war of aggression continues to irreversibly damage the cultural heritage of Ukraine,” added the text. It banned “athletes or sports professionals who compete on behalf of … the Russian Federation to participate at sporting events or competitions on the territory of the Union”. Russian fans in EU stadiums would still be free to wave their flags and sing national songs to cheer on Russian athletes, who could compete “under a neutral status”. But it will be forbidden for “organisers, promoters, or athletes and sports professionals to display or present official symbols of the Russian Federation, including flags, emblems, colours, anthems,” said the draft text. Russian government officials will not be allowed into venues in their formal capacities. Read more Nathan Cofnas is just the latest far-right ‘snowflake’ to pretend he’s being martyred in Europe “It shall be prohibited to allow Russian nationals to hold any posts in the governing bodies of international or … national sports governing bodies established in a member state”, it added. And there will be “restrictions acceptance of financing or other benefits from the Russian State or its proxies by Union sporting and cultural associations or entities,” it also said. Switzerland is home to some 70 international sports federations and normally aligns itself with EU sanctions, but the Swiss foreign ministry did not reply in time when asked if Bern would mirror the sports ban . The International Olympic Committee, in Lausanne, which voted in July to let back Russian athletes into world sports, also did not reply. But, for its part, the EU will also strike a blow against Donald Trump Jr. (the thin-skinned US president’s son) by singling out a Russian billionaire who bankrolled Trump Jr.’s lavish Caribbean wedding in May and went with him to shoot endangered sheep in Mongolia in August – Umar Kremlev. Kremlev, who heads the International Boxing Association (IBA) in Lausanne, Switzerland, and who made his fortune in car dealing and state lotteries in Russia, will go under an EU visa-ban and asset-freeze, as the only internationally known figure out of the 80 new individuals and 81 entities being blacklisted. The EU mentioned the fact Russian president Vladimir Putin personally gave him the Order of Friendship medal this year as one reason to scalp Kremlev, while adding that he was “supporting and implementing actions and policies which undermine or threaten the territorial integrity, sovereignty and independence of Ukraine.” The others were mostly minor names in Russia’s defence and oil industries, except for Alexander Stuglev, the head of Roscongress, which runs the St. Petersburg International Economic Forum, an annual Russian business beauty parade , aimed at wooing Western investors and influencers. Kremlev’s IBA did not reply to EUobserver when asked if he would step down after being blacklisted, but Russia’s former head of the International Chess Federation in Switzerland, Arkady Dvorkovich, did give up his post after being listed by the EU in the 21st round in July. Read more Weird guests and Ukraine drones make ‘Putin’s Davos’ a PR disaster, despite return of US businessmen The final sanctions might still change and Slovakia’s pro-Russian prime minister Robert Fico, as well as Bulgaria’s prime minister Rumen Radev, have, in the past, vetoed EU culture sanctions, for instance against Russian Orthodox Church Patriarch Kirill . But they will both feel under pressure in Brussels on Thursday to agree the Russia measures, when they come to an EU budget summit, in which Germany, for one, has threatened to withhold “cohesion funding” , which poor Bulgarian and Slovak regions need, unless they get behind Ukraine. The 22nd round also comes amid blossoming US-brokered peace talks between Russia and Ukraine, in which Italian foreign minister Antonio Tajani said on 16 November that the EU could use sanctions relief as leverage to force Moscow to listen to its views. The draft 22nd round of Russia sanctions contains nothing on wealthy Russian tourists , who still flock to France, Italy, and Spain in growing numbers.
