noticias.titulo: Anthropic CEO Amodei denies wanting humanity to ‘surrender’ free will to AI
noticias.resumen: Dario Amodei's remarks come amid predictions AI could soon surpass human intelligence.
noticias.texto:
Anthropic CEO Amodei denies wanting humanity to ‘surrender’ free will to AI
Dario Amodei’s remarks come amid predictions AI could soon surpass human intelligence.
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has denied believing that humanity should “surrender” control to artificial intelligence amid predictions that models potentially far exceeding human intelligence are imminent.
In a lengthy post on X on Wednesday, Amodei said he does not support surrendering “human free will” to AI and has long argued that the frontier technology should be subject to “legitimate democratic processes”.
“If I thought any of this was a good idea, I would be advocating for it in public, just as I have not been afraid to advocate for many, many unpopular views over the last few years,” Amodei said, responding to an Axios report about a purported “consensus” inside Anthropic that some decision-making authority should be passed to the technology.
“But I am not advocating for it, because I think turning over governance to AI is a terrible idea.”
Amodei’s remarks come amid a flurry of commentary by top industry executives suggesting that AI will soon match or surpass human intelligence.
The prospect of AI that equals or outperforms the best human minds – referred to as artificial general intelligence (AGI) and artificial super-intelligence (ASI), respectively – has fuelled intense debate in Silicon Valley and beyond about whether such technology can be harnessed for good without exposing humanity to catastrophic harm.
AI safety advocates have raised fears that models being developed by firms such as Anthropic, which made history last week in the biggest initial public offering of all time, could slip out of human control, particularly once systems start improving without human input, a process known as recursive self-improvement.
In his X post, Amodei criticised commentary he said conflated the idea of AI taking over specific tasks with surrendering control in a “grand sense of global governance”.
“This is not AI ‘running the world’, but AI driving a car, designing a cancer drug, or writing software end-to-end,” Amodei said.
“Here, my view is mixed. AI doing more complete or larger tasks is economically valuable and can drive important advances in software, medicine, transportation, energy, etc.”
“It is clearly desirable in many cases and will save a lot of lives,” he added. “But it has downsides as well, and in some areas it may not be worth it.”
Citing unnamed sources, Axios reported on Wednesday that Amodei and other Anthropic executives believe it would be irrational “or even unethical” not to hand over authority to AI for tasks it can do better than humans, such as curing diseases.
‘We’re getting close now’
David Krueger, the founder of Evitable, a nonprofit that advocates for a pause on development of ASI, said Anthropic should pause its work if Amodei is genuinely concerned about humanity losing control of frontier models.
“We don’t have to consciously surrender control to AI to lose it. As AI becomes increasingly capable, there will be mounting pressure to push humans out of decision-making roles across society,” Krueger told Al Jazeera.
“Meanwhile, researchers at Dario’s own company are warning that AI capabilities are advancing faster than our ability to control them. We need an immediate, indefinite, international moratorium on frontier AI development.”
While there is no universally agreed-upon definition of AGI or ASI, key tech industry figures have over the past week suggested that the milestones are near.
Google DeepMind’s chief AGI scientist and cofounder, Shane Legg, said on Wednesday he believes there is a more than 50 percent chance that “minimal” AGI arrives before 2028.
“We’re getting close now,” Legg said on X.
On Sunday, Meta’s chief AI officer, Alexandr Wang, said ASI is “arriving”, pointing to the announcement that an Anthropic employee had used Claude to solve the Riemann hypothesis, one of the most difficult problems in mathematics.
“How humanity acts over the next year will have great consequence on what future world we live in,” Wang said on X.

noticias.titulo: Russia-Ukraine war extends to the Baltic and the Mediterranean
noticias.resumen: By attacking Russian vessels around the world, Kyiv is trying to up the pressure on Moscow and also sending out signals to its Western allies. What is the impact on global maritime trade?
noticias.texto:
Russia-Ukraine war extends to the Baltic Sea and the Mediterranean
November 26, 2026
First there was an attack on a Russian cargo vessel, the Sparta II, off the Finnish coast, then on the Russian corvette Merkury and a dry cargo vessel that was allegedly carrying weapons off the coast of Libya. These spectacular Ukrainian operations in regions far from the Ukrainian capital Kyiv have caused a stir. They came shortly after several suspected Russian missiles crashed in Poland, not far from where an international military exercise was underway.
Intelligence agencies have long warned that Russia was preparing some form of provocation along NATO's eastern flank.
What are the risks of Russia's war in Ukraine escalating further and drawing in other regions?
It is no secret that Russia has long since expanded its operations beyond Ukraine: With military provocation, hybrid operations and acts of sabotage, Moscow has attempted to put pressure on the countries that openly support Ukraine.
And Ukraine has also targeted Russia's military and economy beyond its borders.
Since the summer, attacks by both Russia and Ukraine have increased in the Black Sea. Not only have Russian and Ukrainian cargo ships been targeted, but also vessels from other countries, particularly Turkey.
Furthermore, in the past few years, Ukraine has managed to deal significant blows to Russia, deep within Russian territory, thanks to aerial and maritime drones. It has targeted military airfields and other strategic targets such as oil refineries, including one in Omsk, Siberia, as well as military vessels in the eastern Black Sea.
Ukrainian attacks in Baltic Sea region
Russia has access only to a very narrow strip of the Baltic Sea coast, which is flanked by Finland and Estonia. Even ahead of the attack on the Sparta II, Ukraine had struck in the area multiple times, targeting oil terminals in the region around St. Petersburg, in Ust-Luga and Primorsk.
Russia uses the Baltic Sea to transport supplies to its Kaliningrad exclave and to export oil and other goods to the rest of the world, with the help of its "shadow fleet."
Ukrainian special forces are also said to have carried out operations against Russian military facilities in Syria, well before the fall of the Assad regime in December 2024. They are also reported to have lent support to local Tuareg fighters in Mali who were able to inflict heavy losses on the Malian army and allied Russian mercenaries.
Kyiv is thus attempting to harm Russia's military and economy worldwide, even if in military terms this does not help Ukraine directly.
The Russian corvette that was sunk was part of Russia's Black Sea Fleet but because of Turkey's blockade of the Bosporus and the Dardanelles, it would not have been allowed to return to the Black Sea. Instead, it was escorting Russian cargo ships in the Mediterranean. Primarily, the attacks send a political message: Russian ships can no longer feel safe — anywhere in the world.
Could war become omnipresent?
"We are not speaking about random shadow vessels which simply transport oil above the price cap and as a result bring revenues for the Russian treasury," security expert Elisabeth Braw from the Atlantic Council told DW. Sparta II was suspected of carrying military equipment, which Moscow denies.
"Ukraine is showing that it knows exactly, and secondly that it's able to hit them wherever and whatever waters they are in," Braw continued. "And this is something I don't think Ukraine has been able to do at the beginning of the war."
Officially, Kyiv's goal is to disrupt Russian logistics and supply routes, but military experts and politicians also see the attacks as a clear political signal to Western allies. They suspect that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is sending a clear message of strength with an eye toward possible future peace negotiations.
In an interview on the German news outlet Tagesschau, security expert Joachim Weber from the University of Bonn suggested that Zelenskyy was paying less attention to the US, out of a sense of disappointment. He said that Ukrainian attacks in distant maritime areas were a sign that there was less inhibition and that Ukraine was ready to expand the conflict geographically to increase pressure on Russia, despite the risks.
Weber warned that war could become omnipresent if there was an increase in attacks on civilian vessels or ships that were considered suspicious in international waters. He said that Russia was providing more military escorts for the ships of its shadow fleet. "The likelihood that an accidental exchange of fire between armed forces, coast guards or anyone could occur is rising."
Braw pointed out that violations of the Law of the Sea were not only rising with regard to the Russia-Ukraine war but also in relation to other conflicts and playing out in "the South China Sea, the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea."
She said about 90% of global trade today was conducted via the oceans and she feared that others might conclude it was not "really to their advantage" to follow the rules of international maritime law.
She added that they might find it "beneficial in the short term to violate maritime rules" for short-term gains. "That would make the world's oceans significantly less safe for everybody."
This article was translated from German.

noticias.titulo: FedEx plane overshoots runway at Miami airport on Thanksgiving eve
noticias.resumen: A FedEx plane from Memphis ran past the end of a runway at Miami airport, shutting most runways and causing delays of several hours on the eve of the US holiday.
noticias.texto:
FedEx plane overshoots runway at Miami airport on Thanksgiving eve
November 26, 2026
A FedEx cargo plane went past the end of a runway at Miami International Airport on Wednesday night, shutting most of the airport's runways as the Thanksgiving travel rush began in the United States.
It forced the closure of all but one runway, and by early Thursday the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) was reporting delays of several hours.
The aircraft was a McDonnell Douglas MD-11 arriving from Memphis. The FAA has launched an investigation.
What happened to the plane?
The airport said the plane overran Runway 26R at about 8:40 pm local time.
FedEx said the plane had "an issue upon landing" and that it is working with investigators. "We are grateful that our crew is safe and there are no reported injuries," the company said.
The incident happened amid heavy rain. No injuries were reported.
The airport advised passengers to check with their airlines before traveling.
Overrunning the runway at Miami airport
It is the second runway overrun at Miami in under three months. An Amazon cargo jet overshot a different runway in September, crossing a road and hitting a van and killing five people on the ground.
Three of the airport's runways meet at their western end, so the FedEx plane came to rest near where the Amazon jet went off. A minor collision also occurred between a Copa planand a UPS plane on a taxiway less than two weeks ago.
FedEx only resumed MD-11 flights in May. The type was grounded after a UPS MD-11 crashed in Kentucky last year, killing three pilots and 12 people on the ground.
The incident is the latest in a rough stretch for US aviation, including a nationwide halt to takeoffs on November 13 over air traffic control communication problems.
Up to 80 million people are traveling for Thanksgiving in the country, with a storm expected in the northeastern US.

noticias.titulo: EU leaders seek agreement on long-term budget and Ukraine at summit
noticias.resumen: Leaders of the EU's 27 member states are expected to thrash out the EU's budget for 2028 to 2034. Ukraine and European Central Bank leadership are also up for discussion. DW has more.
noticias.texto:
EU leaders seek agreement on long-term budget and Ukraine at summit
Published November 26, 2026last updated November 26, 2026
What you need to know
- Special European Council meeting for the next two days
- Details of long-term budget, Ukraine's 2027 financial needs and ECB leadership on the agenda
- Euro Summit also taking place with outgoing ECB President Christine Lagarde
You can follow developments from the EU summit taking place on Thursday 26th and Friday 27th November below:
European Council chief urges compromise ahead of summit
European Council President Antonio Costa has called on European leaders to seek compromise on the bloc's long-term budget that's up for discussion over the next two days.
"Today as you know we have several points in our agenda, the most important is the approval and the discussion of the next long-term budget for the European Union," Costa said during his doorstop statement.
He said that the budget needed to be "fit to funding our main priorities."
Costa explained that farmers and regions needed support and that there also needed to be more investment in security and defense.
The price of housing and energy also needed to be addressed, Costa said.
Contributions by member states needed to be kept at a "reasonable level" the European Council chief pointed out.
"My objective is to bring ‌our leaders closer to a deal," Costa told reporters ahead of the ‌summit in Brussels.
WATCH: Europe's coalition trains for a role in postwar Ukraine
With Ukraine support up for discussion at the two-day summit, Europe remains sidelined in Russia-Ukraine peace talks. But a multinational force is training in Poland to help secure Ukraine and NATO's eastern flank following any future ceasefire.
WATCH: Germany's Merz — Russia wants more than Ukraine
Russia wants more than Ukraine, Germany's chancellor warns. But with a majority of Germans now opposed to military aid for Kyiv, can he make the case that defending Ukraine is in their own interest? Terry Martin speaks to DW Chief Political Editor Michaela Küfner.
READ: EU takes aim at tech giants in tax proposal
European Council President Antonio Costa has proposed a smaller EU budget for 2028-2034, including a 3% tax on major digital firms to ease member states' contributions. France has already rejected the plan as inadequate.
European Central Bank leadership also set to be discussed
The Euro Summit will also deal with the process of appointing a new president and two executive board members of the European Central Bank (ECB).
Christine Lagarde has been president since November 2019 but has announced her intention to step down on February 7, 2027.
Eurozone leaders are expected to back Spanish candidate Pablo Hernandez de Cos who is the current head of the Bank for International Settlements.
He's up against Dutch central bank chief Klaas Knot for the presidency, while France's Laurence Boone and Germany's Markus Brunnermeier have been nominated for the ECB's two other top jobs.
EU budget from 2028 to 2034 and Ukraine funding on the agenda
European leaders are meeting for the next two days to thrash out a nearly €1.6 trillion ($1.76 trillion) budget proposal for 2028 to 2034.
The 27 member states are hoping to find common ground for a new budget proposal in the coming weeks and for members to agree on it at a summit on December 17 and 18.
"We, collectively, have the responsibility to find a balanced agreement that will allow the European Union to take on the challenges ahead: boosting our competitiveness, strengthening our security and defence and projecting Europe in the world," said President of the European Council Antonio Costa ahead of the talks.
Costa outlined three key objectives for the next two days:
- to achieve a balanced distribution of funds between the EU's strategic priorities,
- to keep national contributions within reasonable limits
- to include a balanced basket of own resources, including five new sources of EU revenue
Revenue would come from digital services, non-recycled e-waste, tobacco related products, the carbon border adjustment mechanism and the emissions trading system, according to a statement from the European Council.
Ukraine's financing needs for 2027 and beyond will also be dealt with during talks. Currently, €45 billion has been earmarked in additional financial support for Ukraine in 2027, building on the EU's €90 billion Ukraine Support Loan for 2026 and 2027.
It's not expected to be a smooth process with Reuters quoting a diplomat as expecting "leaders to be yelling, complaining, showing they are willing to fight. They need that first. They need a breakdown, blood on the walls, before they can get to an agreement."
Welcome to our coverage
Welcome to DW's coverage of the two-day Special European Council meeting in Brussels, which is expected to focus on the EU’s next long-term budget, support for Ukraine and then the leadership of the European Central Bank (ECB).
Leaders of the bloc's 27 members states will be looking to find common ground over the budget proposal for 2028 to 2034 ahead of an expected deal in December.
Continued support for Ukraine in 2027 and beyond is up for discussion as Russia's invasion drags on towards a fifth year.
The question of who replaces European Central Bank chief Christine Lagarde is also on the agenda.
Follow here for the latest developments from the two-day talks.

noticias.titulo: India news: Resolve tariff concerns in trade talks — India tells US
noticias.resumen: India has denied US claims that New Delhi's policies promote excess manufacturing capacity. Further headlines from India include Constitution Day celebrations. DW has more.
noticias.texto:
India news: Resolve tariff concerns in trade talks — India tells US
Published November 26, 2026last updated November 26, 2026
What you need to know
Here are the latest developments from India on Thursday, November 26:
- New Delhi urges US to work out trade-related within the structures of the ongoing trade deal talks
- India celebrates Constitution Day
- India observes 18th anniversary of deadly 26/11 Mumbai terror attacks
India celebrates Constitution Day
India on Thursday marked 77 years since the formal adoption of its Constitution on November 26, 1949.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi, who officially declared November 26 as Constitution Day or Samvidhan Divas in 2015, hailed the Constitution as "the priceless heritage of Indian democracy."
Before 2015, the date was observed as Law Day.
"Greetings on Constitution Day, a day to pay homage to the makers of our Constitution and an occasion to reaffirm our commitment to strengthening the values enshrined in it," he wrote on X.
Modi also used the observance to attack the opposition.
In an article published on his website, the prime minister wrote that the constitutional democracy had a "clearly defined role for the opposition."
He deemed the opposition as becoming "more of an obstructionist."
Opposition leader Rahul Gandhi called India's Constitution "the foundation" of Indian democracy and the "greatest weapon against injustice."
"It is the shield of every citizen's dignity, the strength of every voice - the guardian of justice, liberty, equality and fraternity." Gandhi said — echoing the four core values enshrined in the Preamble to the Constitution of India.
India's Constituent Assembly adopted the Constitution two years after the country gained independence from British colonial rule.
It came into force two months later on January 26, 1950, establishing India as a Republic.
The most prominent leader of India's Dalit Community, Dr B R Ambedkar — also referred to as Babasaheb — was the chief architect of the Indian Constitution.
CJP to hold protest on Constitution Day
This year, "Constitution" has been the political buzzword in India. Copies of 'The Constitution of India' were a dominant protest prop in a flurry of demonstrations against the Modi government that gripped the country, first over educational reforms and then over alleged voter roll manipulation.
Gandhi too has been seen holding up India's Constitution book several times in protests and press conferences in recent months.
Meanwhile, India's youth-led "Cockroach" movement which has mounted one of the biggest public challenges to Modi in his three terms in power, is planning to hold a "Save Democracy, Save Constitution" rally in the central state of Maharashtra's Nagpur city later in the evening.
In a press conference in Nagpur on Wednesday, the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP's) founder Abhijeet Dipke accused the Modi government of attempting to "dilute" the Indian Constitution.
Dipke went to say that "even 100 dictators like Modi cannot destroy Babasaheb's Constitution and its values."
India seeks 'early conclusion' of trade deal with US
In its statement on planned new US tariffs, India's commerce ministry urged the US to resolve trade disputes and complete negotiations over a new trade deal.
The ministry said that it was "committed to working closely" with the US towards an "early conclusion" of the trade deal.
The US proposed a tariff rate of 25% on goods from India, reduced to 17% if a trade deal is reached.
The state of India-US trade deal negotiations
US President Donald Trump and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi first announced talks for the US-India Bilateral Trade Agreement (BTA) last year.
But negotiations were delayed over strained ties and global conflict, reestablishing headway only this year.
The two nations released the framework for an interim trade agreement in February. As part of that deal, India would "eliminate or reduce tariffs" on all US industrial products and a range of US food and agricultural goods.
However, the negotiations for a final deal were once again stalled after the US Supreme Court invalidated much of Trump's sweeping global tariffs.
In October, India's Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman described the talks as having reached "a plateau, beyond which giving or taking might be very, very difficult."
But US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said a few days later that New Delhi and Washington were "about asclose as you can be without having an executed agreement."
India rejects US charge of excess capacity
Facing a new United States tariff threat, India has stressed that any trade concerns be addressed within the framework of the ongoing trade deal talks between the two countries.
New Delhi's statement comes after Washington on Wednesday unveiled a new wave of tariffs on 14 of its major trade partners, including India, claiming that the economies were promoting excess industrial capacity.
"India and the United States are engaged in negotiations for a Bilateral Trade Agreement. It has been India's position that any trade-related concerns should be addressed within the framework of these negotiations," a statement from New Delhi's Ministry of Commerce and Industry said late Wednesday.
The Office of the US Trade Representative (USTR) announced new import duties of 20% to 40% to counter the alleged excessive manufacturing abroad as it completed a monthslong probe into alleged unfair trade practices involving 16 trading partners.
The new tariffs will be subject to a period of public comment before taking effect.
"Today, after lengthy investigations, Ambassador Greer has determined that the acts, policies, and practices of various economies designed to artificially support manufacturing exports are unreasonable and burden or restrict US commerce and has proposed responsive action," the USTR said on Wednesday.
The USTR said that it will reduce the tariff rate for Indian imports to 17% if a trade deal is sealed between New Delhi and Washington in the long-drawn-out talks trade negotiations between the two sides.
India said that it had "engaged constructively" throughout USTR's investigation and said that it did not have "structural excess capacity in any sector."
Welcome to our coverage
This is Dharvi Vaid Dhulia from DW's bureau in New Delhi, back with our daily India news blog — where we break down all the biggest headlines that have grabbed the attention of the world's most populous democracy.
This Thursday marks 77 years since India officially adopted its Constitution. Prime Minister Narendra Modi has extended his greetings on the occasion and political pressure group Cockroach Janta Party has planned a "Save Democracy, Save Constitution" rally.
After the US proposed raising levies on 14 of its trading partners, including in India, over alleged excess industrial capacity, New Delhi has called for the trade concerns to be addressed through the ongoing talks of a trade deal with Washington. India has also rejected having structural overcapacity in any sector.
Stay tuned as we bring you all this and more.

noticias.titulo: How Chinese companies circumvent chips sanctions in Southeast Asia
noticias.resumen: High-tech AI chips are hard to get in China because of US restrictions. To get around this, Chinese companies often use offshore computing capacity, particularly in Southeast Asia. The US is also trying to stop it.
noticias.texto:
How Chinese companies circumvent chips sanctions in Southeast Asia
November 26, 2026
Some €510 billion ($559 billion) have been invested into AI infrastructure across Malaysia since February 2025. The consulting group Fitch Solutions has opened 125 data centers in Malaysia to serve the global digital economy. The sector is booming in the western Malaysian state of Johor where, according to Malaysia's Digital Ministry, 16 of 27 new data centers are located.
The government in Kuala Lumpur hopes the investment will create numerous new jobs, up to 90% of which are expected to be filled by locals. The advantages of the data center sites include low electricity prices for energy-intensive computing and good links to international submarine cables.
Amazon, Google and Microsoft along Strait of Malacca
Major US technology companies have also set up along the Strait of Malacca. Amazon and Oracle have each invested $6 billion, while Microsoft and Google have invested $2 billion apiece. In early November, Google's parent company, Alphabet, announced additional investments of $15 billion.
"Malaysia's vision is not only to build an economy that uses artificial intelligence, but also one that uses AI creatively,” explained Digital Minister Gobind Singh Deo in a statement that was tellingly published in Chinese, which is not an official language of Malaysia.
Data center growth in Southeast Asia is part of the race for technological supremacy in artificial intelligence. The US has restricted the export of high-performance chips, such as those produced by US tech giant Nvidia, to China. It has also tried to block the sale of the advanced lithography machines used to manufacture microchips that are made by Dutch manufacturer ASML.
Chinese companies rent access to US chips
Since Chinese chips have yet to reach the same technological standards as others, some Chinese companies are testing an alternative model in that they legally purchase or lease capacity in other countries. They can thus rent access to US chips that have been installed in systems in Malaysia, for example, and develop their AI models from abroad.
In October, the Institute for Progress (IFP), an independent think tank in Washington, warned that Southeast Asia was becoming an offshore hub for Chinese AI enclaves. It estimated that by the end of the year about 24% of China's total computing power came from remote access to overseas data centers, three-quarters of which were in Southeast Asia. This was predicted to rise to 31% by the end of 2027.
The IFP said that though "US AI chips hosted in overseas data centers are a significant source of compute for China," they were "difficult to size."
It explained that "Chinese entities can rent GPUs [graphics processing units] as a service from cloud providers or lease data center capacity overseas, directly from developers or through intermediaries. Cloud providers and data center developers rarely name their customers or disclose how much capacity each uses, and Chinese companies disclose little themselves."
Alibaba Cloud sets up shop in Malaysia
The Chinese giant Alibaba Cloud currently operates six data centers in Malaysia — three in Johor and three in the greater Kuala Lumpur region, with the most recent one opening on November 19.
The company has invested $53 billion in data centers in total, including in South Korea, Thailand, the Philippines and Mexico, as well as Malaysia. TikTok's parent company also operates data center capacity in Johor.
In early October, Tencent, another multinational technology conglomerate, which is based in Shenzhen, signed a five-year $7 billion contract with Oracle, allowing it to use computing capacity equivalent to 100,000 modern AI chips for training artificial intelligence. The company was supposed to pay 30% upfront.
The deal fell through a few weeks later, however, and both companies have remained silent about the reasons. According to media reports, there was pressure from the governments in both Beijing and Washington. China wants to develop its own chip industry, whereas high-ranking US officials reportedly raised security concerns with Oracle.
US tariffs on Malaysian imports
In mid-2025, the US threatened to impose an additional 25% tariff on Malaysia imports "to prevent circumvention of export controls on chips," according to the Chinese consulting firm Equal Ocean. "The Malaysian government quickly responded by opposing illegal resale practices and introducing licensing requirements for the transshipment of certain high-end chips."
Washington is now stepping up its efforts. On the same day that US President Donald Trump met with his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping at the APEC meeting in Shenzhen, China last week, the Bureau of Industry and Security, an agency of the US Department of Commerce, issued new rules with regard to remote access to advanced AI chips and servers.
It said that the goal was "to prevent certain foreign actors from leveraging advanced computing power based on US technology to threaten US national security and foreign policy interests." The restrictions pertain to data centers that provide significant computing capacity to companies with ties to countries in "Country Group D:5 or Macau."
According to US export regulations, the D:5 group includes China, Russia, Iran and North Korea and others. In future, companies will have to conduct more thorough checks to identify the ownership and control structures behind their clients.
Washington has also introduced new licensing requirements for advanced semiconductors destined for Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil. Subsidiaries of US companies are exempt.
"The US is not only reviewing which countries will receive AI chips in future but also wants to have a say in where the chips are used, who operates them and which customers they serve," explained Chinese industry expert Xu Sanlang. "This means that data centers, which have been providing remote computing capacity to Chinese clients will have to comply with these restrictions in future."
This article was originally written in German.

noticias.titulo: Can Rassvet, 'Russia's Starlink' change the course of the war in Ukraine?
noticias.resumen: SpaceX's US Starlink satellite system has played a key role in countering the Russian military in Ukraine, but now a Russian counterpart is under development. What could this mean for Ukraine in future?
noticias.texto:
Can Rassvet, 'Russia's Starlink,' change course of the Ukraine war?
November 26, 2026
Both Russian and international media refer to the satellite communications network Rassvet (Dawn) as the "Russian Starlink," a satellite internet service operated by the US company SpaceX.
Rassvet, which was developed by the Russian aerospace company Bureau 1440, operates in low Earth orbit.
Interest in the system surged after the Russian military lost access to Starlink terminals, which until then had ensured communications and internet access in the battle zone in Ukraine.On the front, for example, Starlink helps drone pilots and commanders receive images from drones equipped with cameras. Military personnel also communicate together thanks to Starlink.
Though Russia does not fall within Starlink's area of coverage, the Russian military managed to acquire "illegal" terminals through third countries and was thus using the same system as the Ukrainian army.
In early 2026, SpaceX, in coordination with the Ukrainian Defense Ministry, introduced a "whitelist," which registered all devices on Ukrainian territory authorized to operate on the Starlink network. Any terminals being used by Russian forces were subsequently deactivated, and reports of serious communication problems on the front then began to appear in Russian social media channels.
In May, the US news channel Bloomberg reported that the Ukrainian army had recaptured about 400 square kilometers (ca. 155 square miles) of Ukrainian territory since Russian forces lost access to Starlink.
What is Rassvet?
Two first launches of serial Rassvet satellites took place in March and July 2026.
According to information from Ukraine's military intelligence (HUR) published by the Reuters news agency in early November, Russia has started using Rassvet for military communications over Ukraine and to carry out attacks.
The system is reportedly being used to improve strike accuracy, expand capabilities of reconnaissance drones and to strengthen resilience against electronic warfare.
HUR spokesperson Andriy Yusov also told Reuters that "the constellation is currently insufficient to provide uninterrupted coverage of Ukrainian territory."
Georgiy Trishkin, a rocket analyst and operator of Telegram channel Tekhassky Vestnik (The Texas Herald), told DW that Russia aims to have a functioning "sovereign" alternative to Starlink — consisting of 292 satellites in orbit — running by the end of 2027.
According to Serhii Beskrestnov, aka Flash, an advisor to the Ukrainian president, the main danger posed by the Rassvet system is that it could allow the Russian army to control drones over Ukrainian territory.
He also pointed out on the platform Facebook that the Ukrainian military cannot use Starlink to control drones over Russian territory, since the US service does not work there.
SpaceX remains far superior to Rassvet in tech terms
Inspired by the Starlink model, the Russian military also wants to be able to equip drones with terminals, which will enable connectivity in more remote parts of Ukrainian territory. Bureau 1440 unveiled some initial models last month, but according to Trishkin, the similarities between Rassvet and Starlink stop at the "basic features and concept."
"When it comes to details, these are completely different projects. No one can currently match SpaceX's technological edge — and especially its lead in production technology," he said, pointing out that while the Starlink constellation comprised over 10,000 satellites, Rassvet would not have more than 300 in its first phase.
He added that Bureau 1440 would struggle to make enough of the kits used on the ground. While SpaceX can manufacture about 15,000 per day, this would be a "remarkable achievement even over the course of a year" for the Russian company.
He also said that the terminals produced by Bureau 1440 were much more expensive than those by Starlink as they relied "on foreign components."
"Right now, no one can beat SpaceX in terms of price, volume and quality of service," Trishkin said. "The next step for the company is mobile satellite services, where it's making very rapid progress. Will Bureau 1440 be able to respond? Unlikely for the time being."
SpaceX's Starlink was primarily designed as a civilian service, while Starshield is more for government and military sectors.
According to DW sources, Rassvet was likely designed to support battlefield communications and thus does not currently require as many satellites as Starlink.
Ukrainian military expert Oleh Starikov said that if Rassvet continues to develop as it has then it could fulfil the mission put to it by the Russian military. He added that SpaceX CEO Elon Musk was developing a system that would work around the world, whereas Bureau 1440's satellites sufficed for Russian military purposes.
But he also underlined the massive expansion of Russia's satellite network generally, which — on January 1, 2022, before the full-scale invasion of Ukraine — comprised 102 satellites according to Dmitry Rogozin, who at the time was general director of the Russian space agency Roscosmos.
In September of this year, Rogozin's successor Dmitry Bakanov said that the number almost quadrupled.
Did SpaceX throttle Starlink in Ukraine?
Recent restrictions to Starlink services in Ukraine have brought the issue to the fore again. In mid-November, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that Starshield had been throttled in Ukraine.
"Unfortunately, our units have been recording significant disruptions to Starshield's operations over the territory of Ukraine for several days now — along the entire front line and in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine," he said, adding that the restrictions occurred at speeds of 161 km/h and higher.
Restrictions on the use of Starlink were first put in place on October 14 and then lifted, according to US President Donald Trump, on October 23.
When asked by DW whether the Ukrainian military could gain access to Rassvet, Trishkin said it was "only a matter of time" before terminals fell "into foreign hands and are subsequently examined."
This article was originally published in Russian.

noticias.titulo: US court blocks regulator's early review of ABC's broadcast licenses
noticias.resumen: The FCC chairman had ordered an early review of ABC's licenses a day after President Donald Trump called for the broadcaster to fire Jimmy Kimmel earlier this year. The licenses were not set to expire until 2028.
noticias.texto:
US court blocks regulator's early review of ABC's broadcast licenses
November 26, 2026
A US judge on Wednesday barred the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) ‌from continuing to take steps that threaten ABC's broadcast license.
In April, FCC Chairman Brendan Carr ordered an early license review for eight ABC stations, even though their licenses were not set to expire until 2028.
ABC sued, arguing that the move was retaliation for broadcasting content that angered President Donald Trump.
On Wednesday, US District Judge Loren AliKhan said the FCC chair appeared to have taken "marching orders" from Trump's rhetoric.
"This is not a close case," she wrote in her ruling. "No one doubts that the commission may enforce the law in the manner it sees fit. But in doing so, defendants may not retaliate against or punish plaintiffs and other broadcast license holders for disfavored speech."
Carr's order to review ABC's licenses had come a day after Trump called for ABC to fire late-night host Jimmy Kimmel over a joke he made. His show was taken off the air for six days amid pressure from the White House.
ABC hails 'victory for the First Amendment'
The broadcaster, which is owned by the Walt Disney Company, welcomed the ruling on Wednesday.
"Today's decision is an important victory for the First Amendment," an ABC News spokesperson said in a statement.
Meanwhile, a spokesperson for the FCC said the ruling was "wrong on the facts and wrong on the law — as controlling Supreme Court precedent makes clear."
"We will continue to use our lawful authority to hold broadcasters accountable to their public interest obligations," the spokesperson added.
But one dissenting opinion within the FCC came from its sole Democratic commissioner, Anna Gomez.
She said the ruling brought "badly needed accountability to a commission and an administration that have politicized the machinery of government in a sustained campaign of censorship and control."

noticias.titulo: Kim Jong Un tours nuclear material sites, urges wider use of tactical nuclear weapons
noticias.resumen: North Korea's Kim Jong Un visited sites that produce nuclear material and told his military to focus on tactical weapons, saying his country's nuclear status is irreversible.
noticias.texto:
Kim Jong Un inspects nuclear sites, vows to build more nukes
November 26, 2026
North Korean leader Kim Jong Un toured factories that make nuclear material, along with a research institute, and pressed for the wider use of tactical nuclear weapons, state media reported on Thursday.
The visit took place on Wednesday, but the state news agency KCNA did not provide the location of the sites. Photos showed Kim walking between rows of what appeared to be centrifuges for enriching uranium. Analysts also spotted small, standardized tactical warheads such as the Hwasan-31.
What did Kim say?
Kim said North Korea's production capacity for nuclear material is being steadily expanded. He said tactical weapons should be used in different areas and for different missions, citing the danger from a hostile state on his border, referring to neighbor South Korea.
He also accused the United States of encouraging its allies to seek nuclear-powered submarines and to share nuclear weapons.
"Our possession of nuclear weapons is an absolutely irreversible choice as long as malicious forces exist that use nuclear weapons as a means of achieving hegemony," Kim said, adding that he would treat any attempt to deny North Korea's nuclear status, which was written into its constitution in 2023, as a declaration of war.
Kim said Pyongyang would not seek approval from other countries.
What does it mean for dialogue?
Lim Eul-chul, a professor at South Korea's Kyungnam University, said the visit signals Kim's desire to change the circumstances of any future talks on North Korea's weapons programs.
"This is not so much North Korea permanently closing the door to dialogue with the United States as a strategy of raising the bar: 'denuclearisation talks' are over, and if talks open in future, it will deal only on a 'nuclear state versus nuclear state' basis," he told Reuters news agency.
South Korean news agency Yonhap said this was Kim's fourth visit to a nuclear facility since September 2024. It came about a week after US President Donald Trumpvisited China for the APEC summit, where Kim did not publicly respond to an offer to meet.
Trump told the New York Post that Kim had not ignored it and that the timing was wrong.
Meanwhile, the South Korean Defense Ministry said Pyongyang must stop justifying nuclear development and implement UN Security Council resolutions prohibiting its nuclear weapons and ballistic missile programs.

noticias.titulo: Extreme weather threatens Thanksgiving festivities in US
noticias.resumen: A major storm is forecast to move up the US East Coast and is likely to cause travel delays. Weather warnings were enough to postpone Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade for the first time in its 100 years.
noticias.texto:
Extreme weather threatens Thanksgiving festivities in US
November 26, 2026
New York's iconic Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade has been postponed for the first time in its 100-year history as extreme weather threatens to disrupt the plans of tens of millions of Americans.
The parade has now been pushed back to 8:30 a.m. EST (1330 GMT) Saturday.
"Our team is now working through the complex operational logistics required to bring the Parade to life on Saturday, and we will share additional details as they are finalized," the company said.
New York City Mayor Zohran Mandani said: "I know that this change of plans will cause inconveniences, yet safety has to come first."
"This will be a heavy storm. We are expecting sustained winds between 30 and 40 miles per hour, with gusts as high as 60 to 65 miles per hour possible," he added.
NBC, which broadcasts the parade, said it will instead show a rerun of the 2025 edition on Thursday.
Transport disruptions expected
Despite gale-force winds on the East Coast, coastal flooding in the West and snow in the Midwest, travelers flocked to airports, roads and railways Wednesday for one of America's busiest travel periods of the year.
A major storm developing on the Eastern Seaboard could bring heavy rain, coastal flooding, high winds and power outages to the Carolinas on Wednesday. It is forecast to move to the northern Mid-Atlantic and Northeast on Thanksgiving and is expected to affect air travel at airports in the region.
Already on Wednesday, the security line at New York City's John F. Kennedy International Airport topped one hour.
In the Midwest, winter storm warnings and watches were posted for parts of Missouri and Illinois, with up to 13 inches (33 centimeters) of snow expected in the St. Louis area by Thursday afternoon.
Meanwhile, on the West Coast, king tides were to continue to inundate some coastal areas.

noticias.titulo: FCC says SpaceX can deploy 1 million satellites for data centers in space. Scientists are skeptical
noticias.resumen: The Trump administration gave Elon Musk's SpaceX the green light to deploy 1 million satellites that it said would create data centers in space, a move that has raised skepticism among scientists.
noticias.texto:
FCC says SpaceX can deploy 1 million satellites for data centers in space. Scientists are skeptical
The Trump administration on Wednesday gave SpaceX the green light to deploy 1 million satellites that it said would create data centers in space, a long-lofty goal of Elon Musk's rocket company, in a move that has raised both skepticism and alarm among some scientists.
The U.S. Federal Communications Commission lauded its authorization as a historic first amid the artificial intelligence race. It said that SpaceX's one million "orbital compute modules" (forming a data center constellation called "Starmind") would process massive amounts of data that would be used back on Earth — and bring humans closer to harnessing "the full power of the sun."
"America is leading the world into the era of super intelligence," FCC Chairman Brendan Carr, who was appointed by Republican President Donald Trump, said in a statement. He added that Wednesday's move "opens a bold new frontier."
A lengthier authorization order published by the FCC noted that the company must deploy at least "one authorized space station" by 2033 — and then gradually add more and more through 2040. Musk welcomed the decision over social media.
The world's richest man has long vowed to form vast, solar-powered data centers in space to help run AI tools on Earth. But scientists and industry experts have stressed enormous technical and financial obstacles, as well as a host of environmental concerns.
Adam Becker, an astrophysicist and author, called the prospect of launching a million satellites into space to create data centers "a fantasy."
"It's not going to happen," he said Wednesday.
Proponents of data centers in space argue that capturing the sun's energy would ease pressure on power grids and cut demand for sprawling computing warehouses on Earth (and resources like water needed to cool them). Space seems to offer a solution because it is cold, but it is also a vacuum, trapping heat inside objects much like a thermos. Becker explained that there are "basic physical limits" to otherwise radiating that heat out — and sending lots of smaller satellites could potentially carry the necessary material combined, but it would be expensive and difficult.
He and others also point to additional risks, such as atmospheric pollution through launches and reentries, as well as possible in-orbit collisions that could impact other essential satellites.
"You could end up with a cascading set of space junk collisions," said Becker, noting such crashes could create "a cloud of debris" in the low Earth orbit — where many weather and telecommunication satellites are also found.
In its ruling, the FCC maintained that SpaceX's proposed Starmind constellation operates consistently with its orbital debris rules. It also acknowledged that it had received a "substantial number" of public comments leading up to its authorization Wednesday, including petitions to deny SpaceX's request. But the regulator maintained that deploying the satellites "serves the public interest" — and said that it dismissed topics that it didn't have authority over, such as environmental concerns.
The American Astronomical Society, satellite communication company Viasat and Amazon-owned Kuiper Systems were among those who called on the regulator to deny SpaceX's proposed data centers in space.
In a statement Wednesday, the AAS said it was "disheartened and dismayed" by the FCC's decision. The organization said that SpaceX's proposed position of data centers in low Earth orbit would undermine decades of federal investment in astronomical facilities and "the ability of astronomers and the public to enjoy and study the night sky."
"The proposed constellation involves larger (and therefore brighter) and more numerous objects," AAS said, noting that "these satellites would therefore be visible as extremely bright objects for longer periods in the night sky."
Becker echoed that sentiment. "It also is pollution of the night sky to the naked eye," he said.
Viasat, Amazon, SpaceX and the FCC did not immediately respond to The Associated Press' requests for further comment Wednesday.

noticias.titulo: Andy Taylor, guitarist of new wave icons Duran Duran, dies at 65
noticias.resumen: Taylor revealed his battle with Stage 4 metastatic prostate cancer in 2022. He was the guitarist of the 1980s English band Duran Duran, whose pop hits included "Hungry Like the Wolf" and "Rio".
noticias.texto:
Andy Taylor, guitarist of new wave icons Duran Duran, dies at 65
Andy Taylor, the original guitarist of the 1980s English new wave band Duran Duran, whose huge pop hits included "Hungry Like the Wolf," "The Reflex" and "Rio" and were inextricably linked to the launch of MTV, has died. He was 65.
Taylor's death was confirmed by his family and bandmates in a statement posted on social media and Duran Duran's website.
"From the moment he arrived in Birmingham from the North East with a guitar and an unshakeable belief in what we could become, he brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music. His playing drove the songs that took us around the world, and with a dry wit that was matched only by his wonderfully unsentimental, no-nonsense outlook on life he kept us grounded and gave the band its edge through the extraordinary years that followed," the band said.
On the night he was inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in November 2022, Taylor revealed that he had been battling Stage 4 metastatic prostate cancer for several years and was unable to attend.
"I would like to thank each of my brothers in this great band," he wrote. "You can dream about what happened to us but to experience it, on one's own terms, as mates, was beyond incredible."
The two-time Grammy Award-winners had nine gold records and six platinum ones, with 20 Top 20 singles in the U.K. and 18 in the U.S. They were two-time Ivor Novello Award winners and are MTV Video Visionary Award recipients.
The band's 1981 debut album "Duran Duran" had their first hit single, "Planet Earth," but it was "Rio" that transformed them into trans-Atlantic stars. The Rock Hall explained their appeal this way: "They were new wave outsiders who became music video stars — 'Tiger Beat' fashion pinups who rocked arenas."
How music videos made Duran Duran massively famous
The band's imperial stage occurred with a trio of hit albums between 1981 and 1983, with such dance-floor barnburners as "Girls on Film" and "Union of the Snake" and the moody ballads "The Chauffeur" and "Save a Prayer." Other hits in the coming years included "The Wild Boys," "New Moon on Monday" and "Come Undone." Their popularity was cemented when they recorded the James Bond theme song "A View to a Kill" and earned a slot at Live Aid in 1985.
Mixing fashion, pioneering synthesizers and glam-pop swagger, the telegenic band were all over radio and young people's walls, with bassist John Taylor and singer Simon Le Bon becoming heartthrobs and the band being labeled part of the New Romantics. Princess Diana was known to be a fan, which meant a lot to the band.
"It worked well for us," drummer Roger Taylor told Rolling Stone. "It was genuine. I don't think it was some sort of PR stunt. It was massive for us because she was the No. 1 icon of the early '80s."
The band's success was in large part due to their videos, including their Antigua-set song "Rio," which featured shots of the band in pastel suits sailing confidently on a yacht. For the album "Rio," they shot three music videos in Sri Lanka — including "Save a Prayer," which had John Taylor getting sprayed by an elephant — and two in Antigua, feeding MTV's need to have a stream of visuals, something classic rock didn't have.
"A lot of the success of the album is down to the power of the videos and the way it made the band omnipresent around the globe," Le Bon told The Daily Beast in 2012. Andy Taylor agreed: "I don't think we could have done it without MTV."
John Taylor and keyboardist Nick Rhodes started the band as teenagers in the northern city of Birmingham in 1978, with a name inspired by a character in the Jane Fonda-starring sci-fi movie "Barbarella." Roger Taylor, Le Bon and Andy Taylor joined soon after, with the British press referring to them as the "Fab Five." Andy Taylor answered an ad in Melody Maker music magazine for a "Live-Wire Guitarist." (None of the Taylors were related.)
"We all grew up on the same vinyl records and live gigs, from David Bowie to Roxy Music, The Sex Pistols and, of course, Chic. I could go to all those places as a player and developed a hybrid guitar style that fitted this amazing concept of a band," Andy Taylor wrote in a letter read by the band during their Rock Hall induction.
Behind massive success, Taylor and bandmates were distant
Duran Duran had the unenviable job of following Led Zeppelin at Live Aid in Philadelphia and performed "A View to a Kill," "Union of the Snake," "Save a Prayer" and "The Reflex." In his book, "Wild Child," Andy Taylor revealed the band was, as he put it, "falling apart at the seams."
"Everything should have been perfect, but privately we were screwed and in turmoil. When we came offstage in Philadelphia there were no congratulatory hugs or friendly smiles. It was like we were completely foreign to each other, and it would be the last time we played together for almost two decades."
The various members all had some success with side projects: Le Bon, Rhodes and Roger Taylor recorded an album as Arcadia in 1985; John Taylor and Andy Taylor formed Power Station, a supergroup that included Robert Palmer, in 1984, having hits with "Some Like It Hot" and "Get It On."
In 1986, the band came together to record the hit album "Notorious," produced by Nile Rodgers — with hits including the title single and "Skin Trade" — but Andy Taylor made his second exit from the group after some early recording sessions for the album. He would stay away for such albums as 1997's "Medazzaland" and 2000′s "Pop Trash" — but returned for 2004's "Astronaut."
By 2007, Andy Taylor opted not to participate in the Timbaland-led "Red Carpet Massacre," an attempt to harness a more youthful rhythmic vibe.
"With Andy not turning up, it couldn't be a rock record, so that whole album was an attempt to patch over the cracks with Andy missing," John Taylor told The Atlanta Journal-Constitution in 2011.
Andy Taylor told The Scotsman in 2008: "People have wrongly assumed that I didn't want to be in the band, but the opposite is true. I always wanted to be in a band, but Duran Duran had ceased to function as a band."
At Duran Duran's height, they were as famously destructive as any rock band. Andy Taylor revealed in his memoir that he had a six-year cocaine habit and band members trashed hotel rooms, argued with management about money and had high-end shopping sprees.
Andy Taylor was the first of the Duran boys to get married, tying the knot with Tracey in 1982 and having four children — Andy, Georgie, Bethy and Izzy — and a grandson, Albie. He is survived by all of them, and they credited his devotion to them in a family statement.
"For all the incredible experiences music brought him, family always came first. Nothing made him happier than having us all together, and no matter how far music took him, his heart was always at home," the family statement said.
In 2023, he released the album "Man's a Wolf to Man," his first solo release in over 30 years. On the title track, he sang: "Last night/I dreamt someone loved me/And life was not surreal/Someone's souvenir."
"Andy never took the easy musical route. His overdrive, overdrove us into being the only funk/rock/punk band in the New Romantic movement, with songs that still survive, decades later when his own life is cut so short," Le Bon said in a statement Wednesday.

noticias.titulo: Steelers cut Aaron Rodgers after the QB rips coach Mike McCarthy on TV
noticias.resumen: The move capped a chaotic 18 hours in which the team announced it was benching the 42-year-old future Hall of Famer for backup Mason Rudolph ahead of Friday's visit from Denver.
noticias.texto:
Steelers cut Aaron Rodgers after the QB rips coach Mike McCarthy on TV
PITTSBURGH — Aaron Rodgers came to Pittsburgh in a Chevy.
He left it sitting atop a flamethrower.
The Pittsburgh Steelers cut the four-time MVP on Wednesday, shortly after he torched Steelers coach Mike McCarthy during an appearance on ESPN's "The Pat McAfee Show."
The move capped a chaotic 18 hours in which the team announced it was benching the 42-year-old future Hall of Famer for backup Mason Rudolph ahead of Friday's visit from Denver.
Rodgers responded by taking an excused absence from the club, then used the unexpected time off to go on McAfee's show and repeatedly call out the 62-year-old McCarthy's mental fitness. Rodgers told McAfee he found out about the surprise decision to bench him while on the phone with teammates, including tight end Pat Freiermuth.
McCarthy said later Wednesday, after Rodgers was released, that there were "continuous efforts" to reach the player he's known for two decades dating to their time together in Green Bay.
While McCarthy declined to get into personal conversations, he said things came to a head Tuesday when Rodgers offered an "ultimatum" that McCarthy felt was "clearly out of his job description."
Asked if the decision to cut Rodgers came after he went scorched earth on national television, McCarthy said he couldn't pinpoint the exact timeline because he was in and out of meetings all afternoon.
A Pittsburgh native hired in January to replace Mike Tomlin, McCarthy also brushed off Rodgers' suggestion that the coach had lost the team, saying he had a "very direct, very honest" meeting with the club's players' council after practice Wednesday and believes the Steelers will respond with the proper urgency.
"This is a growth opportunity that I intend to take full advantage of," McCarthy added.
Rodgers says McCarthy fell asleep and blew off meetings
In a blistering offensive, Rodgers painted McCarthy — whom he played under during a long, successful run in Green Bay earlier in their careers — as woefully out of touch.
He described a quarterback meeting last Wednesday where McCarthy arrived late, sat down "and within 10 minutes began snoring," woke up and nodded off again minutes later, then eventually "walks out of the room like nothing happened." Rodgers also said McCarthy missed an offensive meeting Thursday, missed a walkthrough Friday and a morning meeting Saturday, and did not hold a team meeting that night ahead of Sunday's 19-16 loss at Philadelphia.
"And then comes to Sunday, when obviously we struggled and the product wasn't great," Rodgers said, adding that McCarthy broke up the halftime locker room meeting by saying "1-2-3 Packers."
McCarthy didn't deny he misspoke, citing the emotions of the game and the long hours for what he called an "embarrassing moment."
Rodgers said he felt it was the right thing to bring up the issues to McCarthy as a longtime league star instead of putting it on others with fewer years, shaky roster positions or those who "haven't made 400 million dollars in the NFL."
"Me? I don't care, what are you going to do to me?" Rodgers said. "Like I said, you're going to release me? Cool. You're going to deflect this thing and make it that you were trying to bench me and that I'm at home contemplating whether or not I'm going to accept a benching? Couldn't be farther from the truth.
"That word never came up in our meetings. What came up was: sleeping, habits, game plan, understanding what we're doing, being able to call a play, being able to call a game without the game sheet."
The scene played out bizarrely during Rodgers' extended appearance on the show on which he has been an occasional contributor. McCarthy waded through a throng of assembled reporters in the lobby at the Steelers' facility — most of them huddled over their phones listening to Rodgers — after practice ended.
Minutes later, in a subdued locker room, the Steelers tried pick up the pieces declined to get into specifics about Rodgers' accusations but didn't outright dismiss them, either.
Speculation about McCarthy's habits and commitment to his job is nothing new. A former NFL quarterback confirmed that he saw McCarthy asleep during a meeting at an earlier coaching stop. The player spoke to The Associated Press on condition of anonymity because of the delicate nature of the topic.
Asked if he's confident McCarthy can lead the team going forward, Freiermuth responded with a simple "I'm confident" but little else.
Rudolph, who has developed a good friendship with Rodgers over the last 18 months, called him "nothing but the epitome of a first-class teammate."
Wide receiver Marquez Valdes-Scantling, who played alongside Rodgers and under McCarthy as a rookie in Green Bay in 2018, acknowledged there was general frustration about the team's recent performance but allowed, "I didn't think it was this."
Steelers cutting a QB of Rodgers' status is unusual in NFL history
Rodgers has already said this will be his last season. Now it's fair to wonder if he'll reach the end of it on an NFL roster after McCarthy turned to Rudolph, a longtime backup, with the Steelers (6-4) trying to snap out of a two-game funk.
There's little precedent for replacing a future Hall of Famer and Super Bowl winner midseason. Johnny Unitas, playing out his final days in a Chargers uniform, got benched for rookie Dan Fouts after four games in 1973.
Joe Namath never played again after throwing four picks in a loss to Chicago during a late-career cameo for the Los Angeles Rams a month into the 1977 season.
More recently, Denver replaced Peyton Manning with Brock Osweiler midway through 2015 even with the club sitting at 7-2, though Manning's health was a contributing factor in the decision. Manning returned in the season finale and then served as a game manager in the playoffs as the Broncos' dominant defense led the franchise to its third Super Bowl victory.
Manning walked off the field with the Lombardi Trophy in tow in his final game.
This is not that.
While the Steelers are currently in playoff position, their next three games are against AFC West-leading Denver, surging Houston and AFC South leader Jacksonville. While they can probably withstand one loss or maybe two, three would be catastrophic.
Enter Rudolph, who rescued Pittsburgh's season and briefly earned folk hero status in 2023 by coming off the bench in December and leading a surge to a playoff berth.
That didn't stop the Steelers from moving on from him immediately, bringing in Russell Wilson and Justin Fields in 2024 and then Rodgers in 2025, a move designed to help Pittsburgh end a postseason victory drought that's nearing a decade.
"Does it put some of us in an awkward space? Yes," Rudolph said. "But again, it's just another sort of opportunity to overcome adversity."
Rodgers took Steelers to the playoffs before returning to play for McCarthy
Rodgers — who first met with Pittsburgh as a free agent in March 2025 while visiting the facility in a nondescript Chevrolet sedan, wearing a hat and sunglasses to deflect attention — was effective if not spectacular last season, which ended with a blowout loss at home to Houston in the wild-card round of the playoffs. His future seemed uncertain until the Steelers hired McCarthy to replace Tomlin, a job Rodgers played a hand in helping McCarthy land, though how big a hand is up for debate.
Rodgers opted to make one last run at a championship while reuniting with the coach he won a Super Bowl with in early 2011.
Any shot at a storybook ending is gone. For Rodgers and perhaps his now-former team.
Pittsburgh is 2-4 on the road, where it figures to be when the playoffs start if the Steelers can't track down Cincinnati for the AFC North title.
And the team's inconsistent play has offered little evidence that it is a legitimate threat to have an extended postseason stay.
Rodgers' performance was a mixed bag. At times he hardly looked like the league's oldest player, even outdueling Cincinnati star Joe Burrow in a victory over the Bengals in late September. During others, his MVP-winning extended prime looked light years away.
He's struggled to make an impact of late, often checking the ball down to running backs Jaylen Warren and Rico Dowdle or taking sacks behind an inconsistent offensive line when trying to push the ball down the field to a receiving group that has underperformed, particularly two-time Pro Bowler DK Metcalf.
What happens next to a player who has always leaned into doing things on his terms at all times is unclear. Pittsburgh was supposed to be his third and final NFL stop. Whether any quarterback-needy team will be willing to take on the considerable baggage Rodgers brings is anybody's guess.
He seemed content on Tuesday, spending time in the locker room trading jokes with Rudolph and longtime defensive tackle Cam Heyward after addressing reporters.
Barely eight hours later, Rodgers was no longer the starter. Shortly after that, he was no longer a Steeler, the latest and perhaps final twist in a journey that will end with him getting a gold jacket at the Pro Football Hall of Fame, even if this ends up being an inglorious off-ramp for all involved.
