noticias.titulo: Wreckage and burnt vehicles as fuel tanker fire kills 31 on Cairo highway
noticias.resumen: A massive fire from a fuel tanker crash on Giza’s Ring Road in Waraq killed at least 31 and injured 21, highlighting Egypt’s deadly road risks.
noticias.texto:
At least 31 people were killed and 21 others injured when a crash involving a fuel tanker sparked a massive fire on a highway in Giza, Egypt, on Wednesday, 25 November 2026, according to local authorities.
          
          ADVERTISEMENT
        
          
          ADVERTISEMENT
        
Towering flames lit up the night sky as motorists and pedestrians hurried past the blaze. More than two dozen cars and motorcycles were left charred, the Health Ministry said.
The accident occurred in Waraq, a densely populated neighbourhood in Greater Cairo, on the Ring Road, a major highway encircling the capital.
Traffic accidents claim thousands of lives in Egypt every year, with speeding, poor road conditions and inadequate enforcement of traffic laws among the leading causes.

noticias.titulo: Angelina Jolie and Brad Pitt settle long-running legal battle over French winery
noticias.resumen: Ownership of Château Miraval, a prestigious estate in the Var, France, was one of the main points of contention in Brad Pitt and Angelina Jolie’s divorce.
noticias.texto:
Ownership of Château Miraval, a prestigious estate in the Var, France, was one of the main points of contention in Brad Pitt and Angelina Jolie’s divorce.
Brad Pitt and Angelina Jolie have settled a long-running legal battle, a decade after the A-list celebrity couple split.
The actors have settled a dispute over the ownership of a French winery, saying in a joint statement: “We have settled out of court in the best interests of our family and will not be commenting further.”
Pitt, 62, and Jolie, 51, had bought a controlling interest in Château Miraval in 2008 and wed there six years later.
In the lawsuit, Pitt argued that Jolie acted without his permission in selling her share in the winery to Russian oligarch Yuri Sheflzer, stating that he and Jolie had agreed not to sell their stakes without the permission of the other.
Jolie counter-sued, accusing Pitt of drunkenly attacking her and their children on a flight, prompting her to file for divorce in 2016.
Pitt was not charged following an FBI and child services investigation into the incident and he denied the allegations.
They reached a divorce settlement in 2024 after an eight-year legal battle.
All six of the Pitt-Jolie children are now adults, with many of them having dropped their father's surname.

noticias.titulo: Trump thanks Uzbekistan for traditional pavilions gifted to Washington park
noticias.resumen: Crafted from the wood of 200-year-old walnut trees, the structures stand near some of Washington's best-known monuments. The gift commemorates the independence anniversaries of both countries.
noticias.texto:
Crafted from the wood of 200-year-old walnut trees, the structures stand near some of Washington's best-known monuments. The gift commemorates the independence anniversaries of both countries.
US President Donald Trump has thanked his Uzbek counterpart Shavkat Mirziyoyev for two traditional wooden pavilions presented as a gift to mark the 250th anniversary of US independence.
Crafted from the wood of 200-year-old mountain walnut trees, the structures have been installed in Washington's West Potomac Park, near the Tidal Basin, with views of the Jefferson Memorial and the Washington Monument.
Known as aywans, the open-sided gazebos are a traditional feature of Uzbek architecture, with intricately carved columns and roofs decorated with arabesque patterns.
According to the US National Park Service, Trump accepted the gift on behalf of the American people. It also commemorates the 35th anniversary of Uzbekistan's independence.
In a post on his Truth Social platform, Trump said Mirziyoyev was Uzbekistan's “highly respected president” and praised the Uzbek craftsmen who spent several months working on the structures in difficult weather conditions.
“They had real talent,” Trump wrote.
“Rather than keep this gift as ‘private,’ I wanted to donate these beautiful gazebos to the Public,” he added.
The unveiling ceremony last week drew US Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum and Uzbekistan's Ambassador to the United States, Furqat Sidikov. Trump said he had flown over the site aboard Marine One during the ceremony.
He also thanked the Uzbek Embassy in Washington and the US National Park Service for their work alongside the craftsmen.
Trump has invited Mirziyoyev to attend the G20 summit in Miami on 14 and 15 December as a guest, although Uzbekistan is not a member of the group.

noticias.titulo: New images show stadium-sized crater on asteroid NASA crashed into
noticias.resumen: Europe's Hera spacecraft has released its first close-up footage of Dimorphos, four years after NASA deliberately smashed a probe into it.
noticias.texto:
The footage, captured by the European Space Agency's Hera spacecraft, shows Dimorphos circling its larger companion Didymos, with a vast crater clearly visible on its surface.
          
          ADVERTISEMENT
        
          
          ADVERTISEMENT
        
The side struck by NASA's DART probe in September 2022 has been flattened into a crater the size of a sports stadium.
The images also show the small asteroid tumbling as it orbits and briefly passing into Didymos's shadow. The 2022 impact, humanity's first planetary defence test, shortened Dimorphos's orbit by about 33 minutes.

noticias.titulo: Do heat pumps actually work in cold weather? Expert reveals how the technology copes at -20°C
noticias.resumen: Heat pumps are becoming increasingly popular amid spiralling gas prices, but can the green technology survive a freezing winter?
noticias.texto:
Heat pumps are becoming increasingly popular amid spiralling gas prices, but can the green technology survive a freezing winter?
Leaders have been urged to make it easier to install heat pumps in every building across Europe, as the US-led war on Iran continues to send gas prices soaring.
There are currently an estimated 30 million residential heat pumps installed on the continent, with around three million added in 2025. While this may sound like a significant increase, it is a million below the four million target set out by the European Commission.
A new analysis from the European Heat Pump Association (EHPA) found that fitting heat pumps in every building and “compatible industrial process” – powered by renewables like solar and wind – would avoid around 600 million tonnes (Mt) of CO2.
To put that into perspective, this is more than the annual emissions of Germany, the bloc’s biggest economy, or the 17 smallest EU countries combined.
But as Europe faces a potentially freezing winter, can heat pumps withstand the cold?
How do heat pumps work?
Heat pumps capture energy from air, water or the ground and turn it into heat or cold air – rather than burning fossil fuels on-site.
Think of it like a refrigerator but in reverse: heat pumps use a liquid chemical that turns into a hot gas through compression, which is then released into your central heating and hot water tank.
For every one kilowatt-hour (kWh) of electricity they consume, heat pumps typically deliver three to four kWh of heat. It is this efficiency that means they can run in the winter for a little as €2.20 per day.
Do heat pumps work in cold weather?
Contrary to popular myths, modern heat pumps can still extract heat from the air even in low temperatures.
“The key is the refrigerant: a special chemical that can boil even at very low temperatures,” explains UK energy firm Octopus Energy. “That means even when it feels cold outside to you and me (say -20°C), the air temperature is still hot enough to boil the refrigerant in your heat pump.
“That boiling action soaks up a bunch of heat energy. Then through the magic of valves and a compressor, the refrigerant temperature soars up to 65°C and gives up its heat to your radiator water. Then the cycle repeats.”
Of course, lower temperatures mean that the heat pump has to work harder, but experts say a modern heat pump can still perform at three times more efficiency than a traditional gas boiler during freezing conditions.
It’s therefore no surprise that Norway, Finland and Sweden, some of Europe’s coldest countries, have some of the highest heat pump installations in the continent.
According to EHPA, more than half the households in these countries already have a heat pump – while traditionally warmer countries like Spain and Portugal lag behind.
Can heat pumps work in old buildings?
Another common myth is that heat pumps are solely reserved for new build homes, with previous reports claiming the green technology would be impractical for more than half (54 per cent) of British households due to factors such as poor insulation and limited space.
However, The Fraunhofer Society, Europe’s largest application-oriented research organisation, states that heat pumps outperform gas boilers even in buildings more than 100 years old.
In a 2019 study, buildings between 15 and 150 years old that had been partially or fully refurbished with energy-saving measures, including a heat pump being installed, were analysed.
Researchers found that air-source heat pumps achieved an average seasonal performance rating of 3.1, meaning they’re more than three times more efficient than a gas boiler.

noticias.titulo: Christmas 2026 travel gift guide: Perfect presents for people who love travelling
noticias.resumen: If you’re making a list and checking it twice, then don’t forget to add in some of the travel gift options from our round-up.
noticias.texto:
If you’re making a list and checking it twice, then don’t forget to add in some of the travel gift options from our round-up.
From packing to itineraries, travellers just love a list. And at Christmas what better than making a list of all the nice things you’d like to receive as a present?
In our round-up below, we’ve picked out some great gift options for travellers. Though to be totally honest with you, the items are really what ***we’d*** like to receive rather than what we’d like to give.
Here are the travel gifts to add to the wish list this Christmas.
The Luxury Collection x Laila Gohar Advent Calendar
A gift for the Christmas countdown, The Luxury Collection has released a limited-edition advent calendar created in partnership with artist and designer Laila Gohar. Inspired by 24 locations across the Marriott brand’s global portfolio, the calendar pairs original illustrations by Joana Avillez with bespoke chocolates by Casa Bosques. Price: $218 (€199.15)
Little Worlds Alpine Ski Village Advent Calendar
We’re tempted to buy this ski-themed advent calendar for ourselves. It features 24 Alpine ski village ornaments, including skiers, chalets, and ski lifts, which can either be hung on a Christmas tree or used to create a mini winter village display. Price: £5.19 (€6.21)
Envami Scratch World Map
Forget ticking off the destinations from your bucket list, why not scratch them off instead? With this world map that’s exactly what you can do once you’ve been to a place. The map features icons and landmarks from around the world and comes in gold, rose gold, and silver. Price: £16.99 (€20.30)
Jastown Adventure Archive Box
If you’re anything like us, then you probably still have all your ticket stubs, postcards and general keepsakes from an unforgettable adventure. Now, instead of keeping them all in a forgotten drawer, display them in this archive box, which can sit on a table or hang on a wall. Price: £16.99 (€20.30)
Grupo Erik Travel Wall Calendar 2027
As readers of Euronews Travel you of course don’t need inspiration from elsewhere for where to go on holiday in 2027. But, if you actually do, then this calendar could also help you decide on your next travel adventure. Price: £8.99 (€10.74)
A&K Sanctuary x Globe-Trotter Sundowner Trunk
Crafting cases by hand in England since 1897, Globe-Trotter has a range of stylish carry-ons, totes, trunks and gifts on its website. One item that really took our fancy, however, is the Sundowner Trunk, created by Globe-Trotter to mark the opening of Abercrombie & Kent’s Kitirua Plains Lodge, an A&K Sanctuary in Kenya’s Amboseli region. Available to order by commission only, the bespoke portable bar gives a nod to a cherished safari tradition, “unwinding at sunset and soaking in memories of an incredible game drive with an ice-cold drink”. Price: £18,995 (€22,682)
The Little Shop by Raffles
Luxury hospitality brands don’t just offer a place to stay – you can also buy their fashion and design collections. The latest company to join the hotel-retail crossover is Raffles Hotels & Resorts, which recently launched The Little Shop by Raffles. Inspired by Raffles Singapore's 1940s boutique, the shop has a bespoke ready-to-wear collection and limited-edition partnerships. Items include Frette slippers, Christofle coffee cups, Globe-Trotter carry-on cases, Orlebar Brown swim trunks, Vanessa Sposi swimwear, Amambaih bags, Z Lab sleep masks, Smythson leather goods, and Ginori 1735 tableware.
Art of Travel - France: In the Footsteps of the Great Artists
The second volume in the “Art of Travel” series written by Nick Trend and illustrated by Cassandre Montoriol, “France: In the Footsteps of the Great Artists” invites readers to experience the cultural hot spots of France, with its best-loved artists as tour guides. With 12 chapters, each devoted to an artist or group of artists, the book has accompanying itineraries and bespoke illustrations. Price: £50 (€59.71)
Apple AirTag 2nd generation
Once you’ve bought your swanky new suitcase or carry-on, then you need to know of its whereabouts. The Apple AirTag makes it easy to keep tabs on your luggage as it makes its way through the airport or if it gets left behind. Either pop the tag into your suitcase as it is or buy the keyring case to clip it to something. Check your airline’s rules before putting an AirTag in checked luggage. Price: £29.00 (€34.65)
Airplane Pockets Tray Cover
If you like to keep all of your things to hand on a long journey to avoid disturbing other passengers by getting up and down for your bag, this gadget from Airplane Pockets is for you. It’s so simple, yet so ingenious. The polyester sleeve effortlessly slips onto your tray table, providing a clean surface to work and eat on and various pockets underneath to keep your magazines, phone, water, chargers and snacks organised. Price: £34.41 (€41.09)
The Big Blue 28W Solar Charger
One for the adventurers, this solar charger is essential for keeping in touch after hours hiking on the hills. When your gadgets need a boost, this panel will deliver a substantial charge in a variety of conditions. The panel is simple, with two USB ports and a classic fold-out design. Price: £89.99 (€107.40)
Language courses with Gymglish
If you’re travelling to a new destination then there’s nothing better than learning a bit of the lingo before you go. Gymglish offers a range of courses which are made to explore a language and its culture – and there’s “humour included”. Every lesson is made for the user: It goes back over your past mistakes, helps you memorise new vocabulary, continues your series and tests what you've learned. Two months of courses offers up to 43 lessons. Price: from €57
Perilogics universal phone mount
Whether you’re in a car, bus, train or plane, this little gadget enables you to watch a film on your phone hands-free. Simply clamp it to the back of a seat or tray table and relax. No more craning your neck staring down at your phone. Price: $13.99 (€12.79)
Charmast Mini Power Bank
Power banks can be clunky and eat into your hand luggage allowance. So when we saw Charmast’s mini pocket of power (which actually fits into your pocket), we just had to try it for ourselves. Being cordless, it’s easy and convenient to continue using your device as it charges. At just 90g, it won’t weigh you down if you’re taking a holiday selfie. Charmast offers three colours: black, pink and white and boasts speedy charging. Note, this model is only compatible with USB-C devices but there are other brands on the market which cater to different port sizes. Power banks must travel in cabin baggage. Price: £14.99 (€17.90)
Lonely Planet’s Where to Cheat on Your Cat
Described as the "ultimate travel guide for cat lovers", Lonely Planet’s new book highlights destinations where travellers can experience the charm, character and cultural significance of cats across the globe. Price: £13.99 (€16.70)
The Bon Voyage Traveler Kit
An easy choice for a stocking filler, the Bon Voyage Traveler Kit is ideal for anyone about to embark on a journey. The unique novelty kit is filled with handpicked items. Price: £3.99 (€4.76)

noticias.titulo: Inquiry into UK nuclear test veterans granted after 40 year campaign
noticias.resumen: Veterans say they were effectively used as test subjects, with some exposed to radioactive fallout without adequate protection.
noticias.texto:
Veterans say they were effectively used as test subjects, with some exposed to radioactive fallout without adequate protection.
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham has announced an independent inquiry into the impact of Britain’s Cold War nuclear weapons tests on military veterans and their families.
In a statement, the prime minister said: "Nuclear test veterans and their families have waited too long for the truth, and that’s exactly what the independent panel will establish."
Around 22,000 British service personnel witnessed nuclear tests in the Indian and Pacific oceans between 1952 and 1967. Many of those affected say they felt they were used as test subjects, with some exposed to radioactive fallout without adequate protection.
Veterans and their families have campaigned for recognition and compensation for around 40 years, linking the tests to illnesses affecting both participants and, in some cases, their children.
Campaigners met the prime minister at an event at 10 Downing Street. It came a day after the BBC aired a special edition of Newsnight on Tuesday, in which some surviving veterans shared their experiences.
Britain's nuclear tests
The UK's first atmospheric atomic test took place on 3 October 1952, when a plutonium implosion device was detonated near the Montebello Islands off Western Australia.
Dozens more nuclear explosions were carried out by the UK in Australia and Pacific territories, including Kiritimati, formerly known as Christmas Island.
Campaigners say many military personnel were exposed to nuclear fallout after being ordered to fly through mushroom clouds or witness explosions without protective equipment.
Unlike the United States and France, the UK has no dedicated compensation scheme for nuclear test veterans.
Britain's Ministry of Defence has said there was no evidence that Britain’s nuclear tests had caused increased health risks, citing four studies as well as research by Brunel University in 2022.
However, veterans and campaigners have accused the MoD of withholding complete medical records, including blood and urine test results, which they argue could help establish a link between radiation exposure and illness later in life.
The MoD released some official documents in July 2026, but said some records may have been inadvertently destroyed three years earlier.
An independent panel will take on the investigation
The British government says the panel will be modelled on the Hillsborough Independent Panel, rather than being a conventional statutory public inquiry. It says this should allow for a faster, more collaborative process, with veterans and their families closely involved.
The government says the panel's terms of reference are likely to include the conditions servicemen were exposed to, what the state knew and when, advice given to ministers and statements made to Parliament, as well as how veterans and their health concerns were handled.
The panel is expected to deliver an interim report by 3 October 2027, the 75th anniversary of Britain's first nuclear weapons test.
Andy Burnham said his government would also pursue memorialisation, education and research alongside the inquiry, rather than waiting for its final conclusions.
A national memorial service is being planned for 3 October 2027.

noticias.titulo: EU wants more data centres but won't force new green commitments, leaked draft reveals
noticias.resumen: The EU is preparing a voluntary agreement to accelerate data centre expansion as it seeks to triple capacity within five to seven years, despite growing concerns about electricity consumption and pressure on power grids.
noticias.texto:
The EU is preparing a voluntary agreement to accelerate data centre expansion as it seeks to triple capacity within five to seven years, despite growing concerns about electricity consumption and pressure on power grids.
A leaked European Commission draft accessed by Euronews reveals that the EU wants national governments, operators and energy companies to agree on measures to make new data centres easier to build and connect to electricity networks.
But rather than imposing binding sustainability requirements, the Commission is proposing a framework countries can adapt to their needs.
The document, "EU model for tripartite agreements on the sustainable integration of data centres into the energy system", describes the proposed commitments as a "toolbox rather than a single integrated package that needs to be adopted as such".
Countries could pick and choose measures covering grid access, renewable energy, storage, flexibility and the reuse of excess heat from data centres to warm buildings. Crucially, the draft states that "participation in local tripartite agreements is voluntary" and that the commitments "do not create any legal obligations for the signatory parties".
In parallel, Brussels is developing separate rules and standards to improve data centres' sustainability, raising questions about their compatibility with voluntary industry participation.
Europe's growing appetite for data centres
Data centres are facilities packed with servers that store, process and transmit digital information. They power everything from online banking and cloud services to AI, which demands huge computing capacity.
The leaked draft puts the EU's installed data centre capacity at approximately 12 gigawatts in 2025. According to International Energy Agency estimates, capacity stood at around 52 gigawatts in the US and 28 gigawatts in China that year.
The Commission sees expanding capacity as key to digital sovereignty. But MEP Benedetta Scuderi questioned whether this would strengthen Europe's autonomy, particularly if new infrastructure is developed by American technology companies.
"We know that we have very scarce resources for building data centres: energy, water and land. We need to be sure that what we build is what we need, that we don't go beyond that, that these data centres are not oversized or unnecessarily large-scale, and that they support our digital sovereignty. We cannot sell out our natural resources to American Big Tech because that would be of no benefit to us."
Data centres require huge supplies of electricity and cooling systems that can consume vast amounts of water. According to the Commission's draft, they already account for around 2.5% of EU electricity consumption, while their concentration near major hubs is increasing pressure on local grids.
That challenges Europe's energy transition, which also requires electricity for transport, buildings and industrial decarbonisation.
The draft's plans for centres and member states
The Commission is trying to balance these priorities through several energy and digital policy initiatives, including the Cloud and AI Development Act. Existing EU environmental and energy-efficiency rules already require data centres to report on sustainability, including energy efficiency and water use.
The leaked draft also mentions a common EU sustainability rating scheme to make facilities' environmental performance easier to compare. It proposes a collaborative approach through tripartite agreements, bringing together public authorities, data centre operators and energy companies to negotiate arrangements for individual projects or broader national and regional development plans.
According to the draft, the aim is to support "faster rollout of data centre projects, improve their visibility, improve local acceptance, and add value to the energy system and the community".
For member states, this could mean designating areas for new data centres based on grid capacity, environmental factors and opportunities to reuse excess heat. Authorities would also be encouraged to coordinate electricity, heating and digital infrastructure planning, streamline grid connections and prevent speculative projects from hogging scarce capacity. The draft suggests checking whether projects have permits, financing and sufficient technical readiness before granting grid access.
Data centre operators would share electricity demand forecasts and project updates with grid operators and consider flexible connection agreements. These could speed up grid access in exchange for limiting electricity consumption at certain times. Operators would also be encouraged to invest in clean power, sign long-term power purchase agreements and shift computing workloads to periods when electricity is more readily available.
Waste heat is another major focus, as heat generated by servers could be recovered to warm homes, schools and hospitals through district heating networks. The draft encourages operators to publish heat-reuse readiness plans, explore connections to local heating networks and negotiate long-term commercial deals where feasible. Governments could help through infrastructure planning, heat purchase agreements for public buildings and funding to cover upfront costs.
Voluntary commitments versus environmental ambitions
The proposed framework does not require every new facility to finance enough additional renewable energy to cover its consumption. Instead, it proposes that member states "explore options for pursuing the time matching of clean energy supply" with data centre demand, leaving the intervals, shares and implementation timelines to national authorities.
Scuderi warned of the consequences of increasing electricity demand in already strained energy systems.
"If you put a huge increase in electricity demand on an already pressured electricity system, what will happen is that we will have a collapse of the system. We will have a huge increase in prices, and we will not know where to get electricity for things that are strategic, such as industry and households.
"When you are asking for a certain number of megawatts for a data centre, we need to know where we're getting this electricity. This needs to come mostly from renewable energy.
"We need to require data centres to produce a certain amount of renewable energy, and the increase in the number of data centres needs to be sustainable in terms of electricity production, without an increase in emissions and without relying on fossil fuel-based electricity production."
While the EU's Energy Efficiency Directive already contains requirements for assessing waste-heat recovery opportunities, the draft's additional commitments would remain voluntary.
It also allows for commercial and technical constraints: where no heat recovery agreement is reached, operators could proceed with facilities designed to accommodate future heat exports. The framework would encourage earlier planning and cooperation without guaranteeing that recoverable heat will reach nearby communities.
While the document presents sustainability as a central objective, it also explicitly seeks to make data centre development faster and more predictable.
The Commission's role
Despite the voluntary nature of the agreements, the Commission plans to retain a central coordinating role, having developed the model with input from authorities in 18 member states and 14 industry associations representing data centres, electricity networks, renewables and storage.
The first local agreements could begin in 2027, potentially alongside data centre acceleration zones under the proposed Cloud and AI Development Act. Brussels would monitor progress annually until at least 2035, share best practices and regularly update the Energy Council and, where appropriate, the European Parliament.

noticias.titulo: Duran Duran pays tribute to guitarist Andy Taylor, dead at 65 after battle with prostate cancer
noticias.resumen: Taylor died "following a long and courageous battle with prostate cancer", the band announced.
noticias.texto:
Taylor died "following a long and courageous battle with prostate cancer", the band announced.
British synth pop-rockers Duran Duran have paid tribute to their guitarist Andy Taylor, who has died at the age of 65.
In a joint statement the band and Taylor’s family announced that Taylor had died “following a long and courageous battle with prostate cancer”. The statement added that he “passed away peacefully at home, surrounded by his family, on Monday November 23, 2026”.
“To the world, Andy was a brilliant guitarist, but to us, he was the most wonderful husband, a loving dad and the proudest grandfather,” shared Taylor’s wife Tracey on behalf of the family. “He was the rock of our family. For all the incredible experiences music brought him, family always came first. Nothing made him happier than having us all together, and no matter how far music took him, his heart was always at home."
“Andy faced the last few years with so much courage and determination. He never gave up, fighting until the very end, never losing his love of life. The kindness and support shown to him by fans from all over the world throughout his illness brought him immense comfort and strength, and for that we will always be grateful."
She added: “Andy knew just how deeply he was loved, and we take great comfort in that. We will miss him every single day.”
Meanwhile, Taylor’s former Duran Duran bandmates honoured his work across hit songs such as ‘Hungry Like The Wolf’, ‘The Wild Boys’, ‘Rio’ and the James Bond theme 'A View To A Kill’.
“Andy was there at the very beginning of our story,” the band shared. “From the moment he arrived in Birmingham from the North East with a guitar and an unshakeable belief in what we could become, he brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music. His playing drove the songs that took us around the world, and with a dry wit that was matched only by his wonderfully unsentimental, no-nonsense outlook on life he kept us grounded and gave the band its edge through the extraordinary years that followed."
“It was great to make music with him again when the original five reunited in the early 2000s, and that time together, both on stage and in the studio, meant a tremendous amount to all of us. When we were inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 2022, Andy was too unwell to join us, but his words that night reminded everyone of his strength and the bond we shared.”
The band continued: “Andy faced his illness with remarkable courage, honesty and grace. Our thoughts are with his wife Tracey, his children Georgina, Isabella, Bethany and Andrew, and grandson Albie. They all loved him deeply and we ask that their privacy be respected at this very difficult time. In lieu of flowers, the family has asked that donations be made in Andy’s name to Prostate Cancer UK. With love from Simon, John, Nick and Roger.”
Duran Duran members also shared individual statements on their website, with frontman Simon Le Bon remembering “the blond bombshell, firebrand teenager I met in 1980″.
“He’s the kid from the Northeast who can really play guitar,” he recalled. “If you like, he can play it like Mick Ronson, or he can play it like Jimmy Page, he can even play rinky-dink rhythm like Nile Rodgers. But what he does most is play guitar like guitar-genius – Andy Taylor! He came fresh off touring Army bases in West Germany. Spikey hair and spikey personality. Andy didn’t mince his words; he didn’t suffer fools gladly. Andy never took the easy musical route. His overdrive, overdrove us into being the only funk/rock/punk band in the New Romantic movement, with songs that still survive, decades later when his own life is cut so short.”
Le Bon concluded: “There’s a massive Andy Taylor shaped hole in my heart. It’ll never close up; I won’t let it. I will miss him and love him for all my days.”
Born in Tynemouth in Northumberland in 1961, Taylor began playing guitar age 11 when he was tutored by Dave Black from Bowie’s Spiders From Mars. He would join Duran Duran in 1980 after they advertised for a guitarist in Melody Maker.
Taylor was also a member of The Power Station with Robert Palmer and worked as guitarist, songwriter, and record producer with the likes of Rod Stewart and Belinda Carlisle.
Taylor revealed that he had been battling stage 4 metastatic prostate cancer for several years on the night he was inducted in the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in November 2022. He was unable to attend the event and said: “I would like to thank each of my brothers in this great band. You can dream about what happened to us but to experience it, on one’s own terms, as mates, was beyond incredible.”
Taylor published his memoir "Wild Boy: My Life In Duran Duran" in 2008.
He is survived by his wife Tracey Wilson, and their four children Andrew, Georgina, Bethany and Isabella.

noticias.titulo: Kabul's balloon sellers turn hardship into moments of joy
noticias.resumen: Amid Kabul’s busy streets, Shamsuddin and Omran sell up to 700 colourful balloons a day, turning memories of war and poverty into moments of joy.
noticias.texto:
Clusters of brightly coloured balloons floated above the bustling streets of Kabul, Afghanistan, on 23 and 24 November 2026, as vendors carried them by hand or tied them to bicycles.
          
          ADVERTISEMENT
        
          
          ADVERTISEMENT
        
Among the sellers was 49-year-old Shamsuddin Alizadeh, who spends his days filling balloons with helium. Growing up amid war and poverty, he dreamt of having one to play with. Today, selling them is his livelihood.
For 19-year-old Omran Alizadeh, the trade is about more than making a living. His shop sells between 600 and 700 balloons a day, he says, before he heads out with another 100 to sell at busy intersections.
For him, one of the greatest rewards is seeing the smiles on children's faces when they buy a balloon.

noticias.titulo: UniCredit secures final Polish approval for Commerzbank takeover bid
noticias.resumen: KNF's approval completes the authorisation process for the Commerzbank deal. Governance, the German public stake and the next stages of the offer still need to be defined.
noticias.texto:
KNF's approval completes the authorisation process for the Commerzbank deal. Governance, the German public stake and the next stages of the offer still need to be defined.
UniCredit has also obtained the final regulatory clearance needed to press ahead with the public takeover and exchange offer for Commerzbank. On 26 November the Polish financial supervisory authority (KNF) approved the transaction, completing the approval process required for the acquisition of the German bank. The green light from Warsaw was the last missing piece after authorisations from the European Commission and the US Federal Reserve.
The Polish approval specifically concerns the indirect change of control of Commerzbank's operations in Poland, including mBank, in which the German group holds 69.1 per cent. It is one of the country's main banking institutions, with around 5.9 million customers, and is also active in mortgages, investment and payments.
KNF authorisation was necessary because the acquisition of Commerzbank also entails UniCredit taking control of its Polish subsidiaries. Banking rules stipulate that a change of control of the parent company must be reviewed by the supervisory authorities also with regard to qualified indirect holdings in its subsidiaries.
The approval process and the agreement with Berlin
The Polish green light comes after that of the European Commission, which on 16 November cleared the deal unconditionally from a competition standpoint. Brussels assessed the impact of integrating Commerzbank and HypoVereinsbank (HVB), UniCredit's German subsidiary, and ruled out negative effects on the market. Authorisation from the Federal Reserve was granted in the same period.
On the political front, a decisive step was the agreement reached in mid-November between UniCredit's chief executive, Andrea Orcel, and the German government. To overcome Berlin's resistance, the Italian group made eight binding commitments regarding the bank's industrial and employment prospects and the preservation of a strong presence in Germany.
The guarantees include the central role of Frankfurt as the base for German operations, the retention of Commerzbank's stock market listing and its legal form as a German joint-stock company. UniCredit has also pledged to ensure adequate representation of Commerzbank and HypoVereinsbank on the group's executive committee and to propose the appointment of German nationals to its own board of directors when it is renewed in 2027.
The other commitments concern support for German small and medium-sized enterprises, the so-called Mittelstand, through UniCredit's international network, the appropriate allocation of capital and decision-making autonomy for operations in Germany. Investment in Frankfurt is also planned in training, digital technologies and artificial intelligence, along with continued dialogue with trade unions and protection of existing agreements for employees.
The issue of the German state's stake
The question of the state's stake in Commerzbank remains open. The German government holds about 13.3 per cent of the share capital through the SoFFin stabilisation fund and had already announced in June that it would not take part in UniCredit's offer by tendering its shares.
Berlin has not so far announced an immediate sale of its stake. The state's presence in the shareholding structure is also a way to monitor developments in the transaction closely and to verify that UniCredit honours its commitments, particularly on governance, employment and Germany's role in the group's activities.
Next steps
With the completion of regulatory approvals, the deal can now move on to the next stages of implementation. The crediting of the new shares to the custodian banks is scheduled to take place by 7 December 2026.
UniCredit has also asked Commerzbank to call an extraordinary general meeting to elect a new board of directors. This step is part of the process of defining the future governance of the German bank.
For UniCredit, the transaction implies an estimated capital absorption of between 200 and 225 basis points of CET1, the main indicator of a bank's capital strength, in return for a significant expected contribution to the group's profits.

noticias.titulo: Greece creates 20 free day centres for dementia patients and caregivers
noticias.resumen: Greece is opening 20 new day centres for people with Alzheimer’s disease and other forms of dementia.
noticias.texto:
Greece is opening 20 new day centres for people with Alzheimer’s disease and other forms of dementia.
Greece's Ministry of Health is moving ahead with plans to launch specialised services for people with Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia.
It will create and operate 20 new day centres for comprehensive mental health care, which will be supported by mobile units and will provide free services to citizens across the country.
The new facilities are part of the plan to reform psychiatric services and implement Greece's national dementia strategy. Strengthening community care and ensuring equal access to specialised services are key goals.
"With the 20 new day centres, we are building a coherent care network for dementia across the country, with an emphasis on community care, continuity of therapeutic support and the active involvement of the family," said Dimitris Vartzopoulos, Greece's deputy minister of health.
The 20 new centres will provide comprehensive, personalised care, tailored to the needs and stage of the illness of each patient. The aim of these programmes is to preserve the cognitive and functional abilities of people with dementia, strengthen their autonomy and improve their daily functioning.
They also aim to prevent or delay the worsening of symptoms, reduce social isolation and avoid early institutionalisation. The extended opening hours of the facilities are expected to make it easier for patients and their families to access the services.
Meanwhile, the mobile units will provide home care, particularly in cases where it is difficult or impossible for patients to travel to the centres.
The new facilities will also offer support for family carers, who shoulder much of the day-to-day care of people with dementia. They can access counselling services, psychological support and training programmes to help them manage caregiving demands.
The development of these services is particularly important, as dementia affects not only those who are ill, but also their family and social environment. The growing need for care, combined with an ageing population, makes it necessary to create facilities that provide stable, specialised and accessible support.
"Dementia does not concern only the person who is ill, but also their family, their carers and society as a whole," Vartzopoulos said. "The state must stand by them, with high-quality and free services, with respect for the dignity and autonomy of every person".
The centres will also coordinate with local health and social care services.
The new centres will be launched across Greece, with particular emphasis on strengthening regional coverage and reducing inequalities in access to specialised mental health services.
A total of €28 million from ΕΣΠΑ 2021-2027 – Greece's main partnership agreement with the European Union – is planned for the creation and operation of the 20 new units. The budget amounts to €1.4 million per centre and covers the operation of both the day centre and the corresponding mobile unit for two years.

noticias.titulo: Ship transporting 7,000 tonnes of diesel sinks off Ibiza, one crewman dead
noticias.resumen: The other 16 crew members are reported to have survived. The authorities have activated emergency plans and are monitoring the risk of marine pollution.
noticias.texto:
The other 16 crew members are reported to have survived. The authorities have activated emergency plans and are monitoring the risk of marine pollution.
A sailor died in the early hours of Thursday after a vessel carrying around 7,000 metric tonnes of diesel fuel sank off the coast of Ibiza, according to emergency services in the Balearic Islands.
The ship sank between 25 and 30 nautical miles north of the island.
The other 16 crew members survived the sinking, which prompted emergency protocols to be activated because of the risk of a fuel spill.
The Balearic government's director general for Emergencies and Interior, Pablo Gárriz, told reporters that the alert was received at around 1:20 am from Ibiza's harbour master. He said the vessel had suffered a breach which eventually caused it to sink.
The accident prompted a response from Spain's maritime rescue service by sea and air, with support from several ships in the area.
Of the 17 crew members rescued, six were taken to Ibiza airport and another was taken directly to Can Misses Hospital, where he was later pronounced dead, Gárriz said.
Balearic Islands activate civil protection plan over spill risk
The authorities’ main concern now is the possible environmental consequences of the sinking, given the amount of fuel the vessel, named Med Emre, was carrying.
"We are monitoring the possible environmental consequences that this accident may have," Gárriz said.
The sinking led to the activation of the National Maritime Pollution Plan at level 2, while the Balearic government activated the Territorial Civil Protection Plan of the Balearic Islands (PLATERBAL) at level 0.
The full scale of any environmental impact is not yet known, and authorities are assessing whether additional measures will be needed.
"Right now we are waiting for the assessments that are being made and for the possible evolution of this episode," Gárriz said.

noticias.titulo: Europe’s €2 trillion punch-up: Welcome to the Brussels fight club
noticias.resumen: Good morning. Leo Cendrowicz here with your Thursday newsletter. We have almighty punch-up on our agenda today, as EU leaders gather in Brussels to brawl over their seven-year budget – a slugfest that almost certainly won’t be resolved by the end of the summit.
noticias.texto:
Good morning. Leo Cendrowicz here with your Thursday newsletter. We have almighty punch-up on our agenda today, as EU leaders gather in Brussels to brawl over their seven-year budget – a slugfest that almost certainly won’t be resolved by the end of the summit.
Brace yourselves. EU leaders gather in Brussels this morning for what promises to be one of the angriest summits in years. There is precious little goodwill in the room, no obvious broker capable of bridging the differences and virtually no expectation of a breakthrough. The meeting could spill into tomorrow, although it is hard to see what another night of haggling might achieve.
As Jorge Liboreiro reports, two of the EU’s most divisive issues are heading for a collision: the next seven-year budget and the financing of Ukraine’s war effort. Technically separate, they have become politically intertwined. And nothing brings out the worst in European solidarity quite like an argument about money.
Nobody’s happy. European Council President António Costa has lopped €204 billion off the Commission’s original €2 trillion budget proposal for 2028-2034. His reward? Complaints from virtually every corner of Europe.
The German-led frugals, who now prefer to call themselves the “modernisers”, want deeper cuts to agricultural subsidies and regional development funds, prioritising defence, technology and competitiveness instead. The 17 Friends of Cohesion, predominantly southern and eastern countries, think the cuts have already gone too far.
France, despite securing concessions on farming subsidies and a proposed digital tax, is also deeply unimpressed. Paris wants to preserve spending while avoiding an increase in its national contribution – a particularly tricky equation given the parlous state of French public finances.
The elephant in the room. Marine Le Pen is not attending the summit, but her presence will be felt. The far-right frontrunner in next spring’s French presidential election has threatened to slash France’s contribution to the EU budget. Emmanuel Macron insists negotiations cannot extend beyond December. Unfortunately, imposing a deadline is rather easier than meeting it.
Enter Ukraine. Russia’s relentless attacks have left Kyiv facing a €70 billion budget shortfall next year. The Commission is proposing another €45 billion loan, financed through joint borrowing, but Hungary, Slovakia, Bulgaria and the Czech Republic want no part in it.
An exasperated Friedrich Merz is threatening to veto the entire EU budget unless all 27 countries agree to support Ukraine. Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico calls it a “textbook case of blackmail”.
The Commission’s suggested escape route would allow reluctant countries to contribute to the €20 billion earmarked for Ukraine’s civilian needs without participating in the €25 billion military component.
Guns versus butter. One of the more alarming aspects of the budget wrangling is that, for all the grand rhetoric about European sovereignty and military readiness, defence spending is also taking a hit. EU Defence Commissioner Andrius Kubilius warns that the proposed €39 billion cut to defence and space funding – a reduction of 30% – would jeopardise crucial pan-European programmes.
Former Commission President José Manuel Barroso weighed in, pointing to the glaring contradiction between European leaders’ declarations on defence and their willingness to pay for it. With Russia still waging war in Ukraine and Donald Trump proving an increasingly unreliable ally, the timing could hardly be worse.
Something to agree on? Leaders will also discuss Christine Lagarde’s successor at the European Central Bank, with Spain’s Pablo Hernández de Cos emerging as the favourite.
But the real measure of success by tomorrow will be whether a budget deal in December looks remotely achievable. The danger is that everyone leaves Brussels even angrier than when they arrived.
Meanwhile, the European Parliament is up in arms over Costa's proposed 10% cut to the MFF, threatening to reject the deal if it is struck by EU leaders. Vincenzo Genovese has the story from Strasbourg.
For more on this, follow our live blog on the EU summit.
In other news
With friends like these. So much for transatlantic trade peace. Donald Trump is proposing another round of tariffs on 14 major trading partners, including the EU, ostensibly to combat industrial overcapacity. European goods could face duties of 15% on top of existing most-favoured-nation tariffs, potentially rising to 20%. Brussels strongly rejects Washington’s premise, pointing out that Europe is itself a victim of global overcapacity. For Europeans who thought last year’s painstakingly negotiated trade deal offered some protection against Trump’s tariff whims, it’s another rude awakening.
Who picks up the tab? As EU leaders haggle over the next seven-year budget, Luca Bertuzzi and Kamuran Samar have put together a brilliant explainer on who would actually pay the proposed new EU taxes, complete with illuminating charts. The package could raise €60 billion annually, with Germany shouldering the biggest bill. Electronic waste, rather than Big Tech or tobacco, is the biggest money-spinner. Essential reading for understanding the national interests behind the budget horse-trading.
New faces, old dilemmas. Serbia’s absence from yesterday’s EU-Western Balkans summit has postponed a crucial test of its new leadership. The student movement that ousted Aleksandar Vučić is making encouraging noises about democratic reforms but remains decidedly coy about aligning with EU foreign policy. Sanctioning Russia, a move opposed by 67% of Serbians, and normalising relations with Kosovo remain particularly thorny issues. Brussels is still waiting to see whether Belgrade’s geopolitical compass has shifted.
Trouble in the marriage. The European Parliament’s Socialists and Liberals have suspended coalition talks with the centre-right EPP after it once again teamed up with the far right, this time to water down environmental safeguards, Vincenzo Genovese reports. They want written guarantees that Manfred Weber’s group will stop flirting with parties further to its right. Among the potential casualties of the spat: Roberta Metsola’s re-election as European Parliament president in January.
Taxing times. Brussels could slap a windfall tax on oil and gas giants without giving national governments a veto. A new legal study suggests the EU could sidestep unanimity rules if the levy genuinely serves climate or energy policy rather than simply raising revenue. With fuel prices soaring, fossil fuel companies enjoying bumper profits and EU leaders squabbling over the next budget, the timing is particularly intriguing.
Quantum leap. Having largely missed the boat on AI, Brussels is determined not to lose the next technology race. The Commission unveiled its Quantum Act yesterday, alongside a new fund designed to mobilise €50 billion in investment across critical technologies. Europe has a strong scientific pedigree in quantum but struggles to turn research into commercial success. There’s also a looming headache: quantum computers could crack today’s encryption systems.
Membership with strings attached. Getting into the EU is hard enough, but Montenegro could find itself under special scrutiny even after joining. The Commission wants to extend its monitoring of reforms beyond accession, alongside a 10-year probation period during which serious breaches of EU values could trigger the suspension of voting rights. It’s all designed to prevent another Viktor Orbán, although some member states question whether Brussels really needs another policing mechanism.
Follow the powder. Brussels wants to establish whether Irish-made alumina is feeding Russia’s war machine. Rather than banning exports of the raw material used to make aluminium, the Commission is proposing a reporting mechanism to track shipments to their final destination. Kyiv is disappointed, while Dublin fears hundreds of jobs could be at stake. An Irish investigation over the summer failed to settle the matter.
Political ippon? French judo legend turned presidential hopeful Teddy Riner has questioned France’s military support for Ukraine, saying that he did "not understand" why France was sending troops there. The five-time Olympic gold medallist asked whether Ukraine was even in the EU. Riner is currently polling at a modest 4.5%.
We’re also keeping an eye on
- Europe Today this morning features interviews Polish EPP MEP Michał Szcerba, Portuguese Socialists & Democrats MEP Carla Tavares and Florence Duveiller from the Security Studies Center at the French Institute of International Relations (IFRI).
- The European Council meets today and (maybe) tomorrow, starting. It will start Euro Summit
That's it for today. Jorge Liboreiro, Marta Pacheco, Luca Bertuzzi, Angela Skujins and Vincenzo Genovese contributed to this newsletter.

noticias.titulo: Gaudí's dying wish: New documents reveal Spanish architect's final gift to Sagrada Família
noticias.resumen: The inventory of Antoni Gaudí's estate reveals that the legendary Spanish architect wished to devote all his assets, including his Parc Güell house and his savings, to financing the works of the iconic Sagrada Família.
noticias.texto:
The inventory of Antoni Gaudí's estate reveals that the legendary Spanish architect wished to devote all his assets, including his Parc Güell house and his savings, to financing the works of the iconic Sagrada Família.
The inventory of Antoni Gaudí's estate has been revealed a century after his death and it shows the architect's deep committment to the Sagrada Familia. His last wish was to dedicate all his assets, from his savings to his home in Parc Güell, to financing the construction of the temple.
The document, kept in the Arxiu Històric de Protocols de Barcelona, is a 1926 copy of the will that Gaudí signed in 1911 in Puigcerdà. The original disappeared in 1936, after the notary's office that held it burned down in the first months of the Civil War. Among the papers is also the certificate of last wills signed by Manuel Azaña, then a Justice official and future president of the Second Republic.
As the dean of the Col·legi Notarial de Catalunya, José Alberto Marín, has explained, notarial documents are subject to protocol secrecy, but they are considered historical records and become open to public consultation once 100 years have passed.
An inheritance in the service of the Sagrada Familia
The inventory makes it possible to identify the three trusted heirs appointed by Gaudí, a figure specific to Catalan succession law. They were the priest Gil Parés i Vilasau, chaplain custodian of the Sagrada Familia; the doctor Pere Santaló i Castellví, a close friend of the architect; and Domènec Sugrañes i Gras, an architect and Gaudí's disciple who would later take over the direction of the works on the temple.
The three appeared before notary Luis Rufasta and recorded that Gaudí's express wish was to sell all his assets and hand over the money raised to the construction of the basilica. Sugrañes acted in place of Francesc Berenguer i Mestres, a close collaborator of the architect who had died in 1914.
A modest fortune and a single property
The inventory shows the austerity with which Gaudí lived in his final years. His savings were split between two bank accounts: one with 1,870 pesetas at the Banco de España in Barcelona, and another with 1,121 pesetas in a savings book at Caixa de Pensions per a la Vellesa i d'Estalvis.
His only property was the house in Parc Güell, in the former municipality of Gràcia, which the executors valued at 45,000 pesetas for the purposes of a possible sale. According to estimates by the Col·legi Notarial de Catalunya, that sum would be equivalent today to around €150,000 and represented an ordinary level of wealth for the time.
The documents confirm Gaudí's limited attachment to material possessions and his determination to put all his resources at the service of the project to which he devoted much of his life.
A document of particular historical value
The significance of the inventory goes beyond its financial content. The destruction of the original will in 1936 made this copy a key piece for reconstructing the architect's last wishes. In addition, the presence of Manuel Azaña's signature gives the document an element of particular historical interest.
After the legal period of 100 years has elapsed, the inventory will be available for consultation at the premises of the Col·legi Notarial de Catalunya, which has so far kept it in the Arxiu Històric de Protocols de Barcelona.
The archive also holds other documents linked to Gaudí and the Sagrada Familia, including the record of the laying of the basilica's first stone, signed before the architect took over the direction of the works.
Among its most recent holdings is also the document signed in June this year by the Pope Leo XIV and the Archbishop of Barcelona, Joan Josep Omella, which records the completion of the Tower of Jesus and the state of the works on the temple.

noticias.titulo: King tides and powerful waves destroy pier and flood homes in California
noticias.resumen: King tides and powerful waves destroy part of Pacifica's pier and flood coastal homes in California, US, prompting warnings from authorities.
noticias.texto:
Powerful waves combined with king tides destroyed part of the municipal pier in Pacifica, California, US, on Wednesday, 25 November 2026.
Heavy surf battered beachfront homes and flooded stretches of the coastline. The 350-metre pier, located south of San Francisco, had been closed since the summer after cracks were discovered in its structure.
The National Weather Service issued coastal flood and high surf warnings, with breaking waves expected to reach six to nine metres.
In Marin County, authorities temporarily urged residents of beachfront properties in Stinson Beach to prepare to evacuate. King tides, the highest tides of the year, occur when the gravitational forces of the sun and moon align.
This year, their impact is being amplified by warmer ocean waters associated with El Niño.

noticias.titulo: Three Iberian cities in Europe's 2027 top 10 for property investors
noticias.resumen: According to global property consultancy Colliers' 2027 report, Madrid, Lisbon and Barcelona rank among the ten European cities most sought after by property investors, as people in Spain and Portugal protest over the cost of housing.
noticias.texto:
According to global property consultancy Colliers' 2027 report, Madrid, Lisbon and Barcelona rank among the ten European cities most sought after by property investors, as people in Spain and Portugal protest over the cost of housing.
According to the annual "Global Investor Outlook 2027" study by Colliers, three cities in Spain and Portugal are among the ten most sought-after by property investors in Europe. The company specialises in commercial real estate, engineering and investment management. Its report analyses the outlook and strategies of property investors worldwide.
Madrid ranks third, and Lisbon and Barcelona share ninth place among the most sought-after cities for international property investors in 2027. The ranking covers Europe, the Middle East and Africa (EMEA). Milan leads the ranking, followed by London and Paris, which share second place.
"Lisbon’s position highlights the attractiveness of the Portuguese capital in a European context in which investors continue to identify opportunities, although with an increasingly selective approach, favouring assets capable of generating income growth, with solid fundamentals and limited supply," says Pedro Valente, Colliers’ managing director in Portugal.
In the EMEA region, the industrial and logistics sector tops investor preferences, accounting for 17% of choices, followed by apartment buildings and offices, both at 15%, ahead of the hotel and retail sectors.
Taken together, apartment buildings and other types of residential property account for 26% of investor preferences. Colliers says this reflects the importance of housing in European markets, where supply is tight, construction and financing costs are high, and new projects are difficult to develop.
The report points to returns increasingly linked to rental growth, active management of property assets and greater selectivity in investment decisions. Luke Dawson, Colliers’ head of global and EMEA capital markets, says that "the next phase of the market will be more selective" and that "investors will need to focus on assets where income can grow, supply is genuinely constrained, and local and macroeconomic fundamentals justify the cost of capital".
Colliers says Lisbon is attracting interest from international investors for 2027. Whether that leads to deals will depend on the potential for rental income to grow, the quality of the properties, access to infrastructure and the prices investors are willing to pay.
High housing costs, against a backdrop of growing foreign investment in property portfolios, have prompted a wave of protests in several cities in Portugal and Spain in recent weeks.

noticias.titulo: Europe Today: EU leaders in Brussels for budget talks and Latvian PM Kulbergs on Euronews
noticias.resumen: The EU’s 27 heads of state are meeting in Brussels for a European Council summit, which some are forecasting to be a long-term budget bust-up like no other. We speak with the Latvian prime minister Andris Kulbergs.
noticias.texto:
The EU’s 27 heads of state are meeting in Brussels for a European Council summit, which some are forecasting to be a long-term budget bust-up like no other. We speak with the Latvian prime minister Andris Kulbergs.
On today’s show
EU leaders arrive in Brussels for what is expected to be a long discussion over the EU's seven year budget. They will have to decide the bloc's priorities for the next seven years, from defence and competitiveness to agriculture and regional funding.
But there is another urgent question hanging over the negotiations: how to keep Ukraine financially afloat in 2027, with Kyiv facing a massive funding shortfall and Russia showing no sign of backing down. We speak with Latvian prime minister Andris Kulbergs minutes before he sits with other leaders. MEP Michał Szczerba will also give us his take on how to fund Europe's own defence while keeping Ukraine in the fight against Russia.
When and where to watch Europe Today?
You can join Euronews’ Stefan Grobe live on TV and Euronews' website as well as digital platforms (YouTube, Facebook, X, and Instagram), every weekday at 8 am, 9 am and 10 am Brussels time.
In just 28 minutes, our new format brings you the day's key events plus crucial analysis of all the stories shaping the EU and beyond. It's also available as a newsletter.

noticias.titulo: UK discounter Poundland enters administration with 11,000 jobs at risk
noticias.resumen: The collapse of Poundland marks another major setback for Britain's struggling retail sector, which has been hit by weak consumer spending, rising costs and fierce competition.
noticias.texto:
The collapse of Poundland marks another major setback for Britain's struggling retail sector, which has been hit by weak consumer spending, rising costs and fierce competition.
Struggling UK discounter Poundland fell into administration on Wednesday, its American owner announced, putting at risk around 11,000 jobs and 600 stores.
"The news that it has gone into administration just weeks before Christmas will be deeply concerning for workers and their families," British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said in a statement.
Poundland's owner Gordon Brothers earlier announced it had appointed administrators AlixPartners to try and save parts of the business.
"Efforts to preserve as many jobs and stores as possible will continue, led by the administrators," the US investment firm said in a statement.
Business consultancy firm AlixPartners said its "priority... is to work with all stakeholders", including the UK government and unions, "as we identify the best possible route forward".
"We would encourage anybody interested in acquiring the business in part or as a whole... to contact the administrators," added an AlixPartners spokesperson.
Retail trade union Usdaw accused Gordon Brothers of failing to engage with the body, adding that the fall into administration was "devastating news" for its members in the runup to Christmas.
Gordon Brothers had taken control of Poundland only in June last year, providing £85 million (€97 million) in financing to help turn around its fortunes, while shutting shops and axing staff.
Previous owner, Polish discounter Pepco Group, had said that the already-struggling business faced added pressure from a business-tax rise in the UK.
It was sold to Gordon Brothers for £1, with a portfolio of more than 800 stores.
Poundland and other discounters came to the fore in Britain following the 2008 global financial crisis, providing consumers with everyday essentials at knockdown prices.
However, they have struggled to compete in recent years owing to high inflation and increased competition from supermarkets.
"Supported by Gordon Brothers, the management team and colleagues at Poundland worked hard over the past 12 months to improve the underlying performance and achieve £100 million of cost savings," the owner added in Wednesday's statement.
"Despite a reduced cost base, looking forward, the business is still vulnerable to inflationary pressures or any downturn in sales and margin," it added.
AlixPartners said Poundland will continue to trade as normal as it explores ways to keep at least part of the business running.

noticias.titulo: Doomsday fears are fuelling panic-buying. Could it worsen global food waste?
noticias.resumen: As fears of a global conflict drive consumers to stockpile supplies, experts warn that panic-buying could lead to food waste, shortages and price hikes.
noticias.texto:
As fears of a global conflict drive consumers to stockpile supplies, experts warn that panic-buying could lead to food waste, shortages and price hikes.
Photos of bottled water, canned foods and spare batteries have flooded social media as consumers around the world stockpile emergency supplies in response to a wave of doomsday theories about an impending world war.
To prepare for the intensifying strain of extreme weather and prolonged conflicts in Ukraine and Iran, countries such as the United Kingdom and Japan have recently advised households to check their cupboards to make sure they have at least three days’ worth of essentials, from non-perishable foods to baby formula and first-aid kits.
But the guidelines, which seek to prepare people for all kinds of hazards, have been embroiled in online rumour-mongering that has stoked public anxiety and panic-buying.
Experts warn that excessive stockpiling could create unnecessary food waste, a problem that already accounts for up to 10 per cent of global emissions.
Misinformation is causing a wave of panic-buying
Scores of social media users in the United States, Europe and Asia linked the government advice to a spate of tech outages that disrupted flights and banking apps, speculating that another global conflict was just around the corner.
Professional fact-checkers have debunked several claims spreading in multiple languages online – including in Australia, where social media users falsely cited a Red Cross interview as evidence that Canberra had issued a nationwide emergency order.
The claims gained traction in online “prepper” groups bracing for the apocalypse by stockpiling, building bunkers and learning survival skills. Some members showcased pantries stuffed with piles of oats and beans alongside dozens of stacked cans.
In late October, UK media reported that sales of tinned food at Iceland, a British supermarket chain, had briefly surged by 40 per cent.
“Misinformation prevails in an information vacuum,” said Yotam Ophir, an associate professor of communication at the University at Buffalo, adding that when information lacks detail or context, people will “fill the gap with their own alternative explanations”.
Why Europe is stepping up emergency preparedness efforts
The latest wave of false theories circulated shortly after the UK launched “Be Ready”, a public information campaign encouraging household self-sufficiency, in October.
The campaign followed similar moves across Europe, including the EU Preparedness Union Strategy adopted in March last year, and aligns with guidance issued in France, Ireland and the Netherlands.
Those policies aim to ensure people can “put their torch on” during the first 72 hours of a disaster, said Lucy Easthope, a disaster planning expert and visiting professor at the University of Bath.
“We’re asking people to step into a mindset that these things could happen,” she said, adding that some “don’t realise how interconnected international disaster management is”.
“The proximity of some preparedness announcements to military speeches or international conflicts has contributed to speculation online,” said Sojin Jang, an assistant professor of emergency management and disaster science at the University of Nebraska at Omaha.
However, Jang said the timing has practical explanations, pointing to the rising number of severe weather events and cyberattacks.
How to stock up on emergency supplies – without wasting food
The goal of emergency preparedness is not to hoard food and supplies but rather to “strengthen community resilience”, Jang said, adding that people who can meet their basic needs after a disaster allow first responders to prioritise vulnerable populations.
She drew a distinction between responsible preparation, which could entail replacing some stored items before they expire, and excessive stockpiling, which risks creating unnecessary waste, shortages and price hikes that “disproportionately affect older adults, low-income households and people with disabilities”.
It can also affect the environment.
Globally, food loss and waste generate nearly five times the emissions of the aviation industry – and much of it comes from homes. In the EU, for example, more than half of the nearly 58 million tonnes of food waste generated in 2024 came from households.
To minimise waste, Germany’s Federal Office of Civil Protection and Disaster Assistance recommends buying food that people regularly eat and using up older supplies first. It also recommends storing non-perishable food in airtight packaging in a cool, dry and dark place.
The UK’s Be Ready campaign advises building up emergency supplies over several shopping trips and checking your cupboards first to see what you already have. Then, once you have your reserves in place, remember to check expiry dates every six months, eat food before they go off and replace items as necessary.
According to the UK’s Food Standards Agency, food should not be eaten past its ‘use by’ date, but products that have passed their ‘best before’ date can still be safe to eat if stored correctly.
