noticias.titulo: Here are the 13 least-visited countries in the world – and how to get there from Europe
noticias.resumen: From Pacific island nations where flights come weekly to a little-visited part of Europe, here’s where to head when you’re looking to visit a place none of your friends have been.
noticias.texto:
From Pacific island nations where flights come weekly to a little-visited part of Europe, here’s where to head when you’re looking to visit a place none of your friends have been.
As destinations battle overtourism, more and more of us are seeking out alternatives or “hidden gems”.
Some 102 million tourists made it to France, the world’s most-visited country, in 2025, so your odds of finding some unknown spot there are pretty unlikely.
But what about a country where the number of tourists doesn’t even hit 3,500 annually, or a European nation where tourist arrivals aren’t yet six figures?
Here, we’ve rounded up 13 of the least-visited countries around the world, and detailed how to get there from Europe.
NB: For obvious reasons, we’ve excluded countries that have travel advisories in place, like Sudan or Somalia, so this might not be the definitive list of least-visited countries.
Tuvalu
Officially the least visited country in the world, just 3,136 tourists made it to Tuvalu’s shores in 2023, according to the country’s Central Statistics Division.
If you want to count yourself among them, you’ll need to act fast, as the low-lying Pacific island nation is predicted to be 95% submerged as a result of rising sea levels by 2100.
As for what to do here, there are no real surprises: It’s mostly relaxing by the beach, or snorkelling and diving in the Funafuti Conservation Area. You should also catch a game of “te ano”, which is commonly played on the airstrip (only when there’s no scheduled flights, of course).
There’s only one airport on the archipelago – Funafuti International – and that is only served by one airline, Fiji Airways, from Suva and Nadi in Fiji.
As for getting to Fiji, there are direct flights from Asian cities including Tokyo, Hong Kong, and Singapore, which in turn have connections from European hubs including London Heathrow, Frankfurt, Amsterdam, Brussels and Rome.
Practically speaking, you’re probably better off having Tuvalu as an add-on to a travel itinerary around Australia or New Zealand, both of which have plenty of direct flights to Fiji (then onwards to Tuvalu).
Equatorial Guinea
Located on the west coast of Africa between Cameroon and Gabon, Equatorial Guinea is the only Spanish-speaking country on the continent, having gained its independence from Spain in 1968.
As one of the largest oil producers in sub-Saharan Africa, the country hasn’t put much emphasis on tourism – according to the World Bank, international visitor arrivals are around 6,000 annually.
Those who do venture here will be rewarded with volcanic peaks and stunning waterfalls on Bioko Island, as well as an abundance of wildlife, including 16 species of primates as well as the goliath frog, the world’s largest, at Monte Alén National Park. Equatorial Guinea is also known for its nesting leatherback turtles.
The country introduced a new e-visa in 2023. It costs $75 (€68), and you’ll need to show this at the border alongside a certificate proving you have had your yellow fever vaccination.
You should also be aware that visiting many tourist sites requires permits, so it may be easier to organise your visit through a tour guide who can sort these things out for you.
The capital moved from Malabo, which is on Bioko Island, to the purpose-built Ciudad de la Paz on the mainland in January 2026.
You’ll still need to fly into Malabo, which Air France serves from Paris Charles de Gaulle. You can also fly from Frankfurt with Lufthansa, although this flight makes a stop in the Nigerian city of Lagos first.
Marshall Islands
Back to the Pacific, the Marshall Islands is perhaps more associated with its depressing nuclear history than its tourism sites, having been used by the US for testing weapons in the 40s and 50s.
In fact, the country’s only UNESCO World Heritage Site is the Bikini Atoll nuclear site, where today experienced divers can explore various wrecks including the USS Saratoga, an aircraft carrier that was sunk during testing.
Aside from diving, you can learn about traditional canoe building at Waan Aelõñ in Majel, explore World War II ruins (this time on land) in the capital Majuro or on Wotje Atoll, and relax after a day of sight-seeing by sipping on “whiskey” made from pandanus fruit.
In 2024, some 7,312 international air visitors made it to the Marshall Islands, but there are definitely efforts to attract more. In August, the tourism office launched a new pocket guide covering all the main things to do.
You can fly to the Marshall Islands on the Island Hopper route which runs from Honolulu in Hawaii to Guam, which stops off at Majuro and then Bucholz Army Airfield in the Kwajalein Atoll, before heading to Kosrae International Airport, then Pohnpei International Airport, then Chuuk International Airport, all of which are in Micronesia.
Honolulu is connected to several US cities which have direct flights from Europe, including New York, Atlanta, Dallas, San Francisco and Las Vegas.
Turkmenistan
The ‘stans of Central Asia have been getting a lot of attention in recent years, with Uzbekistan named among the fastest-growing tourism destinations for the first quarter of 2026.
One nation that perhaps isn’t getting as much love is Turkmenistan, no doubt thanks to the difficulty in obtaining a visa. The country no longer publishes its tourism numbers, but international arrivals amounted to just 8,200 people in 2007.
While a new e-visa system was rolled out at the start of October, meaning you no longer need to apply through the embassy, you still need to organise your trip through a tour agency for your permit to be approved.
Once a key part of the Silk Road, tourists can head to the UNESCO-listed oasis city of Merv, which dates back 4,000 years, as well as the Dayahatyn caravanserai near the border with Uzbekistan, which is among the best preserved throughout the region.
The capital city Ashgabat made it into the Guinness World Records book in 2013 for having the highest density of white marble-clad buildings, having been rebuilt by Turkmenistan’s first president Saparmurat Niyazov. You’ll only see white cars being driven around, too.
One thing you must not miss while visiting Turkmenistan is the Darvaza gas crater, aka the “Gates of Hell”. Continuously burning for decades, the details around how it came to be are under wraps, although there are plenty of theories.
You can fly direct to Ashgabat International Airport with Turkmenistan Airlines from Frankfurt, London Gatwick, Milan and Istanbul, as well as with Turkish Airlines from the latter.
Kiribati
Those among us who are chronically online will no doubt have heard of Kiribati thanks to the hilarious postings of @KiribatiGov on X (which, sadly, are not actually the official musings of the government), but probably won’t know anything about it.
Located in the Pacific Ocean, the archipelago of Kiribati (pronounced Kiri-bass) spans some 3,441,810 square kilometres of ocean, yet has just 811 square kilometres of land.
If you look at a map of the world, you’ll note that the International Date Line makes a major detour around Kiribati, and its furthest islands to the east are actually in the most advanced time zone, GMT+14.
Like many of the other Pacific island destinations on this list, Kiribati is known for its water-based activities, including snorkelling, diving, and saltwater fly fishing, but you can also explore World War II remnants here.
Just 9,876 people visited in 2025. If you’re ticking off the Marshall Islands on the same trip, good news, as the two are connected by Nauru Airlines.
Alternatively, you can fly here from Nadi International Airport in Fiji. We’ve already covered how to get to Fiji from Europe when writing about Tuvalu, so scroll up for that.
Niue
Another Pacific island nation (are you sensing a pattern here?), Niue is located between Tonga, Samoa and the Cook Islands, and saw just 10,210 visitors in 2019.
One for stargazers, Niue became the world’s first whole country to become an International Dark Sky Place in 2020, and you can book guided astro-tours with members of the local community who have been navigating by the stars for generations.
Again, there’s plenty of diving, snorkelling and fishing, and you can also go whale watching, either from a boat or on shore as these beautiful creatures have been known to swim incredibly close to the islands. There are also numerous hiking routes taking you to swimming spots.
The only way to reach Niue is to fly from Auckland, with Air New Zealand operating flights twice a week.
To get to Auckland, you can fly via Middle Eastern hubs like Dubai or Doha, or Asian cities like Tokyo, Seoul, Singapore, Kuala Lumpur or Bali, plus numerous Chinese cities.
Micronesia
The Federated States of Micronesia (FSM), or Micronesia for short, is made up of around 600 islands to the west of the Marshall Islands and northeast of Papua New Guinea.
It’s split into four states – Yap, Chuuk, Pohnpei, and Kosrae – each of which has something different to offer tourists.
Yap, the westernmost state, is best known for its stone money, with large carved disks found throughout the island group, while Chuuk is famed for its wreck diving.
On Pohnpei, you’ll be able to see the UNESCO-listed Nan Madol, a city built more than 1,000 years ago atop around 100 islets that once served as the capital of the Saudeleur dynasty. Earlier this year, the site was named among the top 10 UNESCO World Heritage Sites by the world’s Most Travelled People.
Finally, Kosrae is also known for its ruins – both Lelu and Menke – as well as its hiking trails and diving sites.
In 2019, around 18,000 people visited Micronesia. The previously-mentioned island hopper stops at Kosrae, Pohnpei and Chuuk; there are also flights from Yap to Guam.
Solomon Islands
Emphasis on the islandS element of this country, which has more than 1,000 of them spread across Melanesia to the north east of Australia, with Fiji to the east and Micronesia to the north, although there are only six main ones.
Given its location, the Solomon Islands has much of the same things to do as some of the other spots on this list, although there are unique highlights including Kavachi, a submarine volcano nicknamed “sharkcano” for the wildlife living in its crater, and Marovo Lagoon, the largest saltwater lagoon in the world.
It’s also a great place to immerse yourself in the local culture, with many of the villages in the outer islands going without modern conveniences like electricity or internet.
You can also visit Skull Island, which is home to remains from between 300 and 1,000 years ago that were collected when headhunting was still practiced.
Official figures put the number of international visitors in 2025 at 27,329.
There are two international airports in the Solomon Islands: Honiara, which serves the capital, and Munda, in the Western Province.
The former has flights from Brisbane in Australia, as well as Nadi in Fiji, Papua New Guinea’s capital Port Moresby, and Vanuatu’s capital Port Vila; while the latter’s only international connection is Brisbane.
To get to Brisbane, you can fly via Doha or Dubai in the Middle East; or through Asian hubs like Seoul, Tokyo, Bangkok, Manila, Singapore, Kuala Lumpur, Hong Kong and Shanghai.
São Tomé and Príncipe
Leaving the Pacific Ocean behind (albeit temporarily), São Tomé and Príncipe is made up of two main islands off the northwestern coast of Gabon in central Africa.
Formed by the Cameroon volcanic line, which also created Bioko Island in Equatorial Guinea, the islands were uninhabited until being colonised by the Portuguese in the 15th century, with São Tomé and Príncipe gaining its independence in 1975.
On São Tomé, the larger of the two, you can visit the UNESCO-listed roças, aka Portuguese plantations for coffee and cocoa, or take on a two-day hike to the top of the country’s highest mountain for a view of the surrounding rainforest.
Príncipe, meanwhile, is known for the Baía das Agulhas, aka Bay of Spires, with its stunning volcanic rock towers, as well as its beaches.
A record-breaking 42,000 tourists made it to the country in 2025, according to the Portuguese news agency Lusa.
Both TAP Air Portugal and STP Airways offer direct flights from Lisbon to São Tomé, and you can fly to Príncipe on Afrijet or STP Airways.
Timor-Leste
Occupying part of the island of Timor (no points for guessing which part), as well as the exclave of Oecusse and the islands of Atauro and Jaco, Timor-Leste shares a border with Indonesia. The country’s name comes from the Malay word for east, making it the state equivalent of ordering a chai tea or paying a visit to the sahara desert.
One of the youngest countries in the world, having been occupied by Indonesia for nearly a quarter of a century, and Portugal for four centuries before that, Timor-Leste became a sovereign state in 2002.
Located in the Coral Triangle, divers headed to Ataúro Island will be able to see the greatest number of reef fish species anywhere in the world, while if you head out into the Wetar Strait and Ombai Strait between October and December, you’ll be able to go whale watching.
On land, you can hike the peak of Mount Ramelau, visit coffee plantations and support local artisans by buying tais, a traditional handwoven textile.
In 2025, 48,927 tourists visited Timor-Leste.
There are direct flights to the capital Dili from Kuala Lumpur, Bali and Xiamen, which in turn will have connections to Europe, as well as from Darwin in Australia.
Tonga
Found to the west of Niue and southeast of Fiji, Tonga is made up of more than 170 islands.
One of the best places in the world to swim with whales, the waters around the Vava’u island group are visited by the same population of humpbacks annually to mate and give birth.
Other things to do here include hiking in 'Eua National Park and paying a visit to Haʻamonga ʻa Maui, which is known as the Stonehenge of the Pacific.
In 2025, 64,183 tourists made it to Tonga.
You can fly here via Fiji’s Suva and Nadi, or from Sydney or Auckland.
Palau
The definition of small but mighty, Palau is made up of 340 islands covering some 466 square kilometres, making it the 16th smallest country in the world – yet its underwater offering is world-famous among divers.
Nicknamed the “underwater Serengeti”, popular dive sites include the UNESCO-listed Rock Islands Southern Lagoon, which has more than 385 species of coral and marine life including dugongs and 13 different types of shark, plus the Blue Corner, known for its abundance of reef sharks.
The country has put a big emphasis on protecting its natural habitats, and passports are stamped with the Palau Pledge on arrival, which visitors will need to sign, stating they promise to preserve and protect the islands.
On land, attractions include Ngardmau Waterfall, the Badrulchau Stone Monoliths, and World War II sites such as the Japanese lighthouse.
While tourism peaked in 2015 with some 168,000 visitors, a downturn in arrivals from China has meant that just 65,558 people got to experience Palau in 2025.
You can fly to Palau International Airport from Asian cities including Manila, Tokyo, Taiwan, Hong Kong and Macau, or from Brisbane.
Moldova
One of the least visited countries in the world can be found in our own backyard: Moldova.
In 2024, arrivals hit 67,631 – which was up 55% on the previous year, when tourist numbers were just 43,597.
Wine is the main reason to visit, with more than 200 wineries, many of which are open to the public. This includes Cricova, which has an underground wine cellar spanning some 120 kilometres, and Mileștii Mici, which has the largest wine collection in the world.
Tourists can also head to the cave monastery of Orheiul Vechi or visit Bender Fortress. Many also visit Pridnestrovian Moldovian Republic, aka Transnistria, an unrecognised breakaway state, but it should be noted that your travel insurance may be invalidated because many countries advise against visiting, including the UK’s FCDO.
There are direct flights to Chișinău Eugen Doga International Airport from all over Europe, including Amsterdam, Frankfurt, Brussels, Athens, Istanbul, London and more.
Alternatively, you can take a sleeper train from Bucharest that takes around 13 to 14 hours.

noticias.titulo: ADHD drugs in pregnancy do not raise risk of child development issues, study finds
noticias.resumen: The findings should reassure pregnant women with ADHD, researchers said.
noticias.texto:
The findings should reassure pregnant women with ADHD, researchers said.
Taking ADHD medication during pregnancy does not appear to raise children's risk of autism, ADHD or other developmental issues, a major new study has found.
Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) affects an estimated 3% of adults worldwide. Most people experience a mix of inattentive, hyperactive and impulsive symptoms, which can return if they stop treatment. Even so, many pregnant women stop taking medication amid uncertainty over how the drugs may affect their developing foetuses.
The new study, published in The BMJ, set out to answer that question. It included more than 3.6 million children born from 2000 to 2021 in Sweden, Norway and Denmark. About 7,600 of these children’s mothers took ADHD medication while pregnant, including nearly 2,400 in the second or third trimester.
There was no increased risk of neurodevelopmental conditions such as ADHD, autism, intellectual disability, epilepsy or learning disorders among children with prenatal exposure to ADHD medications, the study found.
The researchers also found no increased risk tied to specific drugs, including amphetamines, methylphenidate — sold as Ritalin — and atomoxetine, sold as Strattera.
The findings should reassure women who are considering whether to keep taking their ADHD medication during pregnancy, according to the Scandinavian research team.
“Concerns about children’s future risk of neurodevelopmental disorders do not justify discontinuation of ADHD drugs in pregnancy as the results are largely reassuring,” the researchers wrote.
Children who were exposed to ADHD drugs in utero were more likely to have a neurodevelopmental disorder than children who were not exposed. However, this relationship disappeared when the researchers accounted for other factors that could play a role, such as mothers’ education, smoking habits and ADHD diagnoses.
The study has some limitations. The researchers could not account for mothers’ ADHD severity or genetics, and they tracked whether pregnant women filled their ADHD drug prescriptions, not whether they actually took their medication.
The number of children with prenatal exposure to ADHD drugs was also low, making it difficult to draw firm conclusions about every medication and condition.
Still, the findings are in line with previous research that found prenatal exposure to ADHD drugs does not raise the risk of neurodevelopmental issues.
“In light of increasing use of ADHD drugs among women, our findings can aid patients and providers in their shared decisions about drug treatment of ADHD symptoms during and when planning for pregnancy,” the researchers wrote.

noticias.titulo: North Korea’s Kim vows to build more nuclear weapons after ignoring Trump’s overture
noticias.resumen: Kim accused Washington of encouraging its regional allies to acquire nuclear-powered submarines and of pledging to share its own nuclear weapons with them.
noticias.texto:
Kim accused Washington of encouraging its regional allies to acquire nuclear-powered submarines and of pledging to share its own nuclear weapons with them.
North Korea's leader has toured facilities that produce fissile material and demanded a bigger nuclear arsenal, days after Pyongyang left Donald Trump's offer of a meeting unanswered.
The message, carried by state news agency KCNA on Thursday, is a fresh sign that Kim has no intention of giving up the weapons programme on which his authoritarian rule rests.
According to the state media, Kim visited two nuclear material production plants on Wednesday, one newly opened and the other being expanded. He also toured a nuclear-powered equipment production base and a nuclear research institute.
Photos showed him and senior military officers walking past dense rows of what appear to be centrifuges used to make weapons-grade uranium and viewing halls with what were believed to be warheads. Some images were blurred.
Pyongyang did not say where the plants are. It has revealed enrichment sites several times since showing one at Yongbyon to visiting American scholars in 2010.
When it disclosed parts of another site in June, outside experts concluded it was probably a second enrichment facility at Yongbyon.
Pyongyang: drive to expand arsenal, "irreversible reality"
Kim presented the visit as a response to growing nuclear threats around the Korean Peninsula accusing Washington of encouraging its regional allies to acquire nuclear-powered submarines and of pledging to share its own nuclear weapons with them.
He described North Korea's status as a nuclear power and its drive to expand the arsenal in both quality and quantity as an "irreversible reality."
He also called for the urgent deployment of low-yield battlefield nuclear weapons across multiple domains, citing the danger on the border with South Korea.
Pyongyang has focused on tactical weapons in recent years as hostility with Seoul has deepened.
South Korea's Defense Ministry said it takes the remarks on battlefield weapons seriously and remains militarily ready, backed by its alliance with the US.
The Joint Chiefs of Staff declined to analyse the facilities, saying the information is confidential and shared with Washington.
Trump says meeting with Kim 'not really the right time'
Kim has accelerated the build-up of his nuclear forces since his high-stakes diplomacy with Trump collapsed in 2019 and has turned towards Cold War-era allies Moscow and Beijing.
Trump again voiced his wish to resume talks while in China last week for the APEC summit, but no meeting took place and Pyongyang did not respond publicly.
Speaking to the New York Post this week, Trump rejected the idea that Kim had ignored him, saying it was "not really the right time" during a busy two days.
He added that he could restart their exchange of letters at any moment, though he admitted they had not written to each other recently.
Kim has previously said he could return to the table if Washington abandons its "hostile policy" and accepts North Korea as a nuclear state. Experts say he is seeking recognition as a nuclear power so that he can demand an end to international sanctions.
Last week, International Atomic Energy Agency chief Rafael Grossi said North Korea has been expanding its original enrichment facility at Yongbyon, calling it a "serious concern."

noticias.titulo: Greece now borrows more cheaply than Italy and France
noticias.resumen: Greek 10-year yields have fallen below Italy's and France's as KBRA upgrades Athens and its debt ratio nears Italy's. Low household savings remain the weak spot.
noticias.texto:
Greek 10-year yields have fallen below Italy's and France's as KBRA upgrades Athens and its debt ratio nears Italy's. Low household savings remain the weak spot.
In early 2012, Greece was the country nobody wanted to lend to.
As Athens prepared the largest sovereign debt restructuring in history, the yield on its 10-year bonds climbed above 35%. Italy, then seen as the next domino, had paid more than 7% at the peak of its own scare a few months earlier.
Fourteen years later, the order has been turned upside down.
On Wednesday, Greece's 10-year yield stood at 4.15%, below Italy's 4.37% and well below France's 4.73%.
Greek borrowing costs first dipped below Italy's in November 2019 and have stayed beneath them without a break since 20 April. They slipped under France's for the first time in January 2025, and have held there every day since 15 June.
"Its debt is largely fixed-rate, with very long maturities, and markets view the sovereign far more favourably than in the past, as you can see in bond spreads," Ken Egan, senior director and head of sovereign credit at KBRA, said in exclusive comments to Euronews.
On 20 November, KBRA, a US-based credit rating agency, upgraded Greece to BBB+ from BBB, two notches above the lowest investment-grade rating, with a stable outlook.
"Credit ratings should be forward looking, and not backward looking, and recognize when credit risks have receded," Joan Feldbaum-Vidra, senior managing director for sovereigns at KBRA, said.
The surplus that changed the story
Greece ran a primary surplus of 5.1% of GDP in 2025, meaning its revenues exceeded its spending by that margin before interest payments. According to KBRA, that is the strongest in Europe.
Tax collection has improved sharply.
The VAT compliance gap, the share of value added tax that should be paid but never reaches the state, narrowed from 24% in 2019 to around 9% in 2024, roughly in line with the EU average.
"It's a very different picture from the sovereign debt crisis years," Egan said.
The economy has followed. Real growth averaged 4.1% a year between 2021 and 2025, well above the euro area. Unemployment fell to 7.6% in September from 8.8% a year earlier.
Greek banks, once the weakest link, are healthier too: their share of bad loans fell from 6.9% in June 2024 to 3.4% in June this year.
Greece is closing in on Italy's debt
According to Eurostat, Greek public debt fell to 140.8% of GDP in the second quarter of 2026, from 152% a year earlier.
Over the same period, Italy's debt rose to 139.9% from 137.6%, while France's climbed to 119.1% from 115.4%.
A gap of more than 14 percentage points between Athens and Rome has shrunk to less than one. KBRA expects Greek debt to fall to around 129% by 2027.
Athens is also repaying its bailout-era loans well ahead of schedule, which Egan described as "one of the clearest signs of Greece's turnaround."
Greece's debt is easier to carry precisely because of its default. The bailout loans were restructured several times, with lower interest rates and longer repayment periods.
The average maturity of central government debt is 18 years, and 32 years for loans from the European Stability Mechanism, the euro area's rescue fund.
With most of that debt at fixed rates, refinancing is not KBRA's biggest concern in the near term, Egan said.
Athens stocks are pricing in the turnaround
Investors in Greek shares appear to have reached a similar conclusion.
The ATHEX Composite, the main index of the Athens Stock Exchange, has gained 15.8% since the start of the year, even after falling 2.8% on Wednesday.
That is far ahead of the Euro Stoxx 50, the benchmark of the euro area's largest companies, which is up 1.8%. Italy's FTSE MIB has gained 7.1% and Germany's DAX 0.9%, while France's CAC 40 is down 2.1%.
The contrast with France is telling.
Paris has spent much of the year dealing with political turmoil and a rising debt burden, and its stock market has gone nowhere.
In Greece, a state that runs surpluses and pays down its debt has lowered the risk investors attach to the whole country, from its government bonds to its banks.
What still stands between Greece and an A rating
Greece has made "remarkable progress" on its public finances, Egan said, but strong budget surpluses alone would not be enough to lift it into the A range.
KBRA would need to see debt fall further and the recent improvements sustained over time.
"The bigger challenge is the broader economy," he said.
Income and productivity levels still lag European peers, he added, while competitiveness and external vulnerabilities remain structural weaknesses that will take longer to address.
Prices are another concern. Greek inflation reached 5.7% in October, against 4.0% in the euro area, driven by energy costs linked to the conflict in the Middle East. The country relies heavily on imported fuels, and energy inflation hit 25.4% in September.
For now, Egan sees the inflation gap mainly as a domestic problem, squeezing household incomes and raising costs for businesses. He does not expect it to last long enough to undermine the country's competitiveness, and tourism demand, which accounts for around 13% of GDP, remains strong.
KBRA is, however, watching services inflation closely. It stood at 6.3% in October, almost double the euro area rate.
"The concern would be if higher services inflation became more entrenched, gradually eroding the country's relative affordability," Egan said.
Wage and price cuts after the crisis made Greece cheaper and more competitive. Losing that edge, he said, "would interfere with its still nascent diversification away from tourism."
A weakness that has moved
The biggest risk, according to KBRA, no longer sits with the state.
"The bigger vulnerability is Greece's exceptionally low level of household savings," Egan told Euronews.
Investment has picked up, with productive investment reaching a 30-year high as a share of GDP in 2025.
But Greeks are not saving enough to pay for it, so the gap is filled by money from abroad. KBRA expects the current account deficit, which measures how much more a country spends abroad than it earns, to reach 6.6% of GDP this year.
That reliance is manageable while investor confidence is strong, Egan said, but it leaves Greece exposed to external shocks, and Europe has faced "quite a few of those recently."
He was careful to draw a line with the past. The shortfall in savings now comes from the private sector, partly covered by foreign direct investment, rather than from the government, which he described as being "in sharp contrast" to the dynamics behind the debt crisis.
Building domestic savings will require stronger incomes and productivity, he said. "This takes time."
In 2012, investors feared the Greek state could not pay its bills.
In 2026, the state pays less to borrow than Italy or France, and the question has moved to whether Greek households can earn and save enough to keep it that way.

noticias.titulo: EU budget and Ukraine aid headed for collision at turbulent summit
noticias.resumen: EU leaders will have their hands full as they wrangle over the next budget and future support for Ukraine. Both issues make for a potentially unpredictable mix.
noticias.texto:
EU leaders will have their hands full as they wrangle over the next budget and future support for Ukraine. Both issues make for a potentially unpredictable mix.
Two of the EU's most contentious issues are set to collide at a turbulent summit in Brussels: the bloc's next long-term budget and continued support for Ukraine.
The talks on Thursday, which might stretch into Friday, aim to pave the way for a final deal at a pivotal meeting in December.
On the one hand, the 27 leaders will spar over the bloc's new long-term budget, which will determine the level of spending for critical areas like farming subsidies, infrastructure, border control and green energy for the next seven years.
António Costa, the president of the European Council, has offered a compromise that cuts the original proposal by €204 billion.
"The time has come to reach an agreement," Costa told leaders ahead of the summit.
On the other hand, they will scramble to plug Ukraine's soaring deficit and maintain a steady flow of financial and military assistance as Russia's brutal war rages on.
The European Commission has tabled a €45 billion support loan backed by joint debt to keep the country's economy afloat and its armed forces in the fight.
On paper, the two issues are separate. Politically, however, they are increasingly intertwined, creating a combustible mix that could descend into a bitter dispute.
"You can't avoid the discussions being mixed up," a diplomat said.
Stuck on red lines
The battle lines are starkly drawn.
The so-called "frugals" – Austria, Belgium, Denmark, Finland, the Netherlands, Sweden and Germany – are displeased with Costa's compromise and demand deeper cuts to traditional envelopes, namely agriculture and cohesion, to channel more cash into modern-day priorities such as defence, climate and technology. (Hence why they have rebranded themselves as "modernisers".)
This has met with pushback from the 17 "Friends of Cohesion", a group encompassing Southern and Eastern European countries, who want to preserve high expenditure on both traditional and modern priorities. This camp is unhappy with Costa's proposal because, they say, it cuts excessively across the board.
"I think it would have been more useful to put forward a relatively good proposal rather than playing out a bazaar scene reminiscent of Cairo, Tunis, or Marrakesh," Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar said ahead of the summit.
France has adopted a hardline stance, slamming Costa's compromise as "highly disappointing", despite including the digital services tax that Paris has long advocated.
France, mired in a financial crunch at home, is keen to boost EU-wide taxes to maintain spending without increasing its national contribution.
The chasm between the competing sides has proven irreconcilable and left member states stuck on their red lines. Diplomats admit that discussions over the past few months have gone round in circles, with little meaningful progress to show for them.
The impasse puts Costa, the moderator-in-chief, in the hot seat to deliver a unanimous deal by the end of the year. The Council president intends to steer the two-day summit through bilateral and multilateral meetings to coax leaders face-to-face.
The budget is widely seen as a defining test of Costa’s presidency, with the outcome potentially weighing heavily on whether he secures a second 2.5-year term.
If negotiations spill over into 2027, they will become dangerously entangled with the French presidential election. Marine Le Pen, the frontrunner, has vowed to upend the deal and cap France's contribution at €5 billion per year.
Paris has upped the ante to avoid such a scenario.
"Several other member states will also be holding elections, beyond the French presidential election, throughout the first and even the second half of 2027," the Élysée said. "Therefore, our position has been, and remains, very clear: the negotiations cannot go beyond December."
A divisive ultimatum
Ukraine further muddles the equation.
Russia's non-stop attacks, deliberately aimed at devastating the Ukrainian economy, have drilled a €70 billion hole in Kyiv's 2027 budget.
The Commission's €45 billion loan is meant to cover two-thirds of this gap. Other allies, such as the UK, Norway, Canada and Japan, are expected to cover the remaining third.
Four member states – Slovakia, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Bulgaria – have already said they do not want to participate in this new loan, which will come on top of the ongoing €90 billion credit line and add to annual interest payments.
Their request has enraged German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who has threatened to veto the budget if support for Ukraine is not agreed by all 27 member states. Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico has denounced this as a "textbook case of blackmail".
Brussels is split on whether Merz's ultimatum will succeed or backfire.
Some believe his forceful attempt to link the two files is well-founded because Russia's aggression poses a threat to the bloc as a whole.
"Security is a public good. Security is, by definition, indivisible," another senior diplomat said. "It's very difficult to understand that four countries that are getting so much cohesion funding from the EU are being so egoistic not to support the common good of security. That doesn't make sense (and) is unacceptable."
Others, however, say it is a risky manoeuvre that could alienate leaders and exacerbate mistrust. The "Friends of Cohesion" believe the optics of a deal that cuts funding for poorer regions but boosts it for Ukraine would send a politically damaging message.
The Commission has offered a way out of the showdown by allowing countries to opt in to the loan's budget strand (€20 billion) and out of its military strand (€25 billion).
Costa wants leaders to look beyond 2027 and start a serious debate on how to finance Ukraine in the longer term, whether it is a longer war or a costly recovery.
The conversation will unfold against a backdrop of a sourer, darker mood. A new poll has found 53% of Germans oppose continuing military aid for Kyiv.
Thursday's summit comes amid intense efforts to bring the peace negotiations into a multilateral format with Ukrainian, European, US and Russian officials at the same table. The Kremlin has refused to commit and instead invited the European delegation to Moscow to discuss their possible participation in the next round of talks.
Brussels thinks Russia is not yet serious about peace and has already proposed fresh economic sanctions.

noticias.titulo: Indonesia: rescuers race to find 13 miners trapped in flooded illegal gold mine
noticias.resumen: The disaster began late on Monday, when heavy rain made the Ciseureuh River burst its banks and pour into a mine shaft, which is estimated to be around 100 metres deep.
noticias.texto:
The disaster began late on Monday, when heavy rain made the Ciseureuh River burst its banks and pour into a mine shaft, which is estimated to be around 100 metres deep.
Rescuers in Indonesia on Thursday were contending with rising water, darkness and steep, slippery ground as they combed the site in Bogor regency, a mountainous area south of the capital Jakarta.
Rescuers say they are searching for 13 more miners believed trapped by flooding in an illegal gold mine where 13 bodies were recovered earlier.
The disaster began late on Monday, when heavy rain made the Ciseureuh River burst its banks and pour into a mine shaft, which is estimated to be around 100 metres deep. Miners were digging for gold at the time.
Some escaped from one section of the excavation before the shaft filled with water.
Authorities said the illegal nature of the operation meant they were not alerted straight away. Local miners and residents first tried to pump out the water themselves until the situation spiralled out of control.
Police received the first reports of trapped miners some 16 hours after the flooding. The nearby state-owned mining company PT Antam passed a formal report to the Jakarta Search and Rescue Agency shortly after midnight on Wednesday, which set a full-scale operation in motion.
Search focuses on two shafts
Teams have been using submersible pumps to drain the shaft and working to seal openings where groundwater is seeping in.
On Thursday, 325 personnel concentrated on two adjacent shafts, using rope-access techniques to reach victims, said agency chief Desiana Kartika Bahari.
The flooded shaft lies close to facilities run by PT Antam's Pongkor gold mining unit. The company said the incident had nothing to do with its operations.
Informal mining is widespread in Indonesia, where thousands of people work in hazardous conditions.
Miners risk landslides, flooding and tunnel collapses, while gold processing often exposes them to toxic mercury and cyanide with little or no protective equipment.

noticias.titulo: EU could bypass national vetoes on fossil fuel windfall tax, lawyers say
noticias.resumen: A new legal study suggests Brussels could circumvent the EU’s unanimity requirement by designing a levy on oil and gas companies’ excess profits around climate or energy policy objectives rather than revenue raising.
noticias.texto:
A new legal study suggests Brussels could circumvent the EU’s unanimity requirement by designing a levy on oil and gas companies’ excess profits around climate or energy policy objectives rather than revenue raising.
The EU could introduce a new windfall profit tax on oil and gas companies without requiring unanimous backing from all EU countries, as long as the measure is designed primarily to advance climate or energy policy and not to raise public revenue, according to a new legal study.
The findings could potentially reopen a politically sensitive debate over who should pay for the EU's energy crises just as EU leaders gather at a summit in Brussels on Thursday and Friday to discuss the bloc's multi-annual budget for 2028-2034.
The closure of the Strait of Hormuz, renewed fuel price increases and record profits for energy companies have revived calls for an EU windfall tax. The European Commission has rejected such an EU-wide tax, citing legal challenges. It ultimately reverts the matter for capitals to decide on their own.
In the study commissioned by German environmental organisations Germanwatch and Klima-Allianz Deutschland and conducted by Baldon Avocats, several possible legal routes for Brussels to impose a levy on fossil fuel companies were identified.
The legal study examines how the EU could require EU countries to introduce, collect and administer such a levy, with revenues potentially flowing either to national treasuries or the EU budget.
Avoiding unanimity
A striking finding that could pave the way for a windfall profit tax is that the Commission could potentially avoid the unanimity requirement normally associated with EU taxation by using existing treaty provisions covering environmental protection or energy policy, according to the study.
However, the tax must genuinely pursue an environmental or energy goal as its main purpose. If its main intention is to raise and redistribute money, it would be classified as a fiscal measure, triggering the unanimity requirement.
The lawyers argue that the design of the levy would be crucial.
“The label given to the instrument (‘excess profits’ or ‘windfall profits tax’, ‘solidarity contribution’) carries limited weight for the characterisation of a measure as primarily fiscal. What matters most are the aim and content of the measure,” reads the legal study.
A question of framing
A climate-focused mechanism could target profits generated specifically by fossil fuel activities, discourage further investment in polluting operations and direct revenues towards climate mitigation or adaptation.
An energy-focused version could finance energy efficiency, security of supply and measures to reduce bills for consumers.
However, framing the measure solely as a climate or energy levy would not be sufficient to bypass national vetoes. Its actual goals, tax base and allocation of revenues would determine its legal classification.
Another possibility would be to introduce the tax as part of a broader package of environmental or energy measures, with the overall purpose of the law determining its legal basis.
The 2022 precedent
The study also identifies a more immediate route akin to that used by the EU in 2022 following Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
That mechanism required EU countries to impose a temporary contribution of at least 33% on exceptional profits made by companies in the crude oil, natural gas, coal and refining sectors. It applied to profits exceeding by more than 20% the average profits recorded over the previous four financial years.
Under EU law, the Council can adopt emergency economic measures by qualified majority, avoiding the need for unanimous agreement, the study noted.
The lawyers argued that a new temporary contribution could follow the same model, provided they can demonstrate exceptional circumstances and the need for emergency intervention.
The study also sees as plausible establishing a permanent EU crisis framework that could be activated temporarily whenever exceptional economic or energy circumstances arise.
However, the legal precedent is not yet settled. Energy companies have challenged the 2022 contribution before EU and national courts, questioning its legal basis and compatibility with fundamental rights.
EU Court of Justice's Advocate General, Athanasios Rantos, backed on 22 October the validity of the contribution under EU law. The Court of Justice is expected to deliver its ruling in 2027.
Who gets the money?
Beyond whether the tax can be introduced, who gets the money could become another major political battleground.
The study proposes allowing revenues to remain in national budgets while restricting their use through EU legislation, using the revenues to create a new EU budget own resource, or assigning the proceeds to a dedicated European fund.
The first option would broadly replicate the 2022 arrangement, giving national governments control over collection while requiring spending to follow goals established by EU law.
The second would be more complicated, according to the lawyers. Establishing a new EU own resource requires unanimous approval by EU countries and ratification at the national level, potentially bringing back the very veto problem that supporters of the tax would seek to avoid.
But the third option could provide an alternative. The lawyers argued that revenues could be assigned to a dedicated EU fund through secondary legislation without creating a new own resource.
Spain's proposal for a European Climate Resilience Levy on fossil fuel profits, with revenues directed towards a dedicated Climate Adaptation Fund, is one example flagged in the study.
The lawyers stress that the mechanism would require national authorities to levy and collect the tax. Direct collection by the EU itself would be difficult under the existing treaties.

noticias.titulo: Moment fuel truck fire engulfs traffic on Cairo highway
noticias.resumen: At least 31 people have been killed and 21 injured after a crash involving a fuel tanker triggered a massive fire on a major highway near Cairo. The blaze engulfed more than two dozen cars and motorcycles on the Ring Road in Giza on Wednesday night.
noticias.texto:
At least 31 people have been killed and 21 injured after a crash involving a fuel tanker sparked a massive fire on a major highway surrounding Cairo on Wednesday night, Egyptian authorities said.
          
          ADVERTISEMENT
        
          
          ADVERTISEMENT
        
The fire broke out on the Ring Road in Waraq, a densely populated neighbourhood in Giza, part of the Greater Cairo area. Huge flames rose into the night sky as vehicles and people passed the burning area.
According to the Health Ministry, more than two dozen cars and motorcycles were destroyed in the blaze.
The incident is the latest deadly road accident in Egypt, where thousands of people lose their lives in traffic crashes every year.

noticias.titulo: Global markets rebound as tech shares recover and tariff fears ease
noticias.resumen: Asian stocks staged a rebound on Thursday from another hard day of selling as trading in the tech sector stabilised, while investors took in their stride a fresh round of proposed US tariffs.
noticias.texto:
Asian stocks staged a rebound on Thursday from another hard day of selling as trading in the tech sector stabilised, while investors took in their stride a fresh round of proposed US tariffs.
The gains came after a dip-buying afternoon rally helped US markets finish well off their initial lows as Wall Street headed into the Thanksgiving holiday on an only slightly negative note.
Beaten-down Asian tech firms led the gains Thursday, with Seoul, Tokyo and Taipei again at the centre of the action, having seen wild swings this week amid concerns about the AI boom, while the euphoria over Jensen Huang's reinstatement at Nvidia has worn off.
Japanese chipmaker Kioxia and investment giant SoftBank were the standouts, surging by double figures, while South Korean titans SK hynix and Samsung were also comfortably up.
Tokyo's Nikkei 225, the Kospi in Seoul and the Taipei Taiex all climbed more than 1%, as did the Hang Seng in Hong Kong. There were also gains in Sydney, Shanghai and Singapore. Wellington and Manila dipped.
Global markets have whipsawed this week, with news of Huang's return lighting up Asian screens Tuesday before a crushing drop Wednesday.
After a stellar start to the year, selling in the past five months has been fanned by fears over vast capital expenditure and when that will pay off, as well as rising interest rate expectations and talk of tighter AI regulation under a new Democrat-led Congress.
Some observers have said there were signs the pain could be nearing its end.
But Michael Boutros at Forex.com warned that "buyers still need to demonstrate that renewed demand extends beyond short-lived relief rallies".
"The focus heading into December is on whether semiconductor shares can regain traction and support a broader recovery or whether the recent deterioration signals further downside."
Expectations for a Federal Reserve rate hike next month were given a fresh boost Wednesday by data showing US inflation last month at a three-year high, while economic growth for the third quarter was revised up.
There was little movement in reaction to the unveiling of proposed US tariffs on 14 economies following a months-long probe into alleged excess production.
The duties of up to 20% face a period of public comment before taking effect, with an official adding that the proposals take existing trade deals into account.
The new levies target some of the largest US trading partners, including the European Union, India, Japan and South Korea.
China faces a 20% toll, the joint-highest for any economy, but US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the new levies were within the bounds of existing trade negotiations with Beijing.
Beijing warned Washington not to engage in "tariff wars and trade wars".

noticias.titulo: Why Jean-Luc Mélenchon has it in for Germany
noticias.resumen: France's far-left leader is tapping into a growing unease with Berlin across the political spectrum.
noticias.texto: PARIS — It’s an unusual way to prepare for a trip to Berlin: suggesting Germany might pose a military threat to your country. But that’s exactly what French presidential contender Jean-Luc Mélenchon did ahead of his visit this week. “I’m not ok with Germany’s pledge to build the largest conventional army in Europe,” the far-left leader said earlier this month, on Armistice Day, a holiday that in France commemorates the end of the intense fighting between France and Germany in World War I. “Because if it does, I have to ask: Who does it want to go to war against?” The comments up the ante on Mélenchon’s long-standing defiance toward France’s neighbor, which he accuses of acting as a hegemon in Europe. His hostility toward Berlin — part longtime obsession, part political positioning — is one of the many ways the far-left leader clashes with his country’s establishment, which has traditionally worked closely with Berlin to shape the continent. Unsurprisingly, his comments have riled many in Germany, given that the rearmament effort was a response to Russia’s 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine. “Mélenchon paints a distorted picture of Germany and Franco-German relations,” said Roland Theis, a German lawmaker from the conservative Christian Democratic Union who chairs the Bundestag’s Franco-German Parliamentary Group and sits on its Defense Committee. U.S. President Donald Trump speaks with Germany’s Chancellor Friedrich Merz during a work lunch as part of the G7 summit, in Evian on June 16, 2026. | Pool photo by Christian Hartmann/AFP via Getty Images The leftist veteran is polling in second place ahead of next year’s presidential election, putting him within reach of a runoff against the far-right front-runner, Marine Le Pen. For some in Berlin, neither prospect is particularly reassuring. “On security and European affairs, his political positions are at least as dangerous as Le Pen’s,” Theis said. A critic of Berlin’s traditional positions on fiscal and European affairs, Mélenchon is the author of a 2015 book subtitled “The German Poison.” His France Unbowed party has long criticized joint Franco-German defense projects, arguing they favor German interests at the expense of French defense companies. The party also mistrusts the United States — Mélenchon has pledged to leave NATO — and his lieutenants have described Berlin as Washington’s “Trojan Horse” in Europe. He intends to double down on his criticisms at an event in Berlin on Friday night, where he will present a German translation of another book: “Now, the People! — Revolution in the 21st Century,” which lays out his vision for France, Europe and the world. In his presidential platform, Mélenchon pledged to radically overhaul the EU , disobeying its rules if necessary. “We are being honest,” said Hadrien Clouet, a lawmaker from Mélenchon’s France Unbowed who will accompany him to Germany. “We have to say what we think: Chancellor [Friedrich] Merz is a problem for Europe.” The event is being organized with the support of the Rosa Luxemburg Foundation, which is affiliated with Germany’s far-left Left Party. Mélenchon is expected to meet privately with party representatives Saturday. Aurélien Taché, the party’s point person on the French National Assembly’s foreign affairs committee, said Mélenchon’s problem wasn’t with the German people. “We think there is a very strong German influence [in Europe], with an ordoliberal vision that we strongly reject,” Taché said. Concerns about hybrid warfare by Russia “don’t justify recreating a Wehrmacht as Europe’s leading military power,” Taché said, using the German word for Nazis’ armed forces. Germany jitters While Mélenchon has taken his antipathy toward Berlin further than any other leading French politician, doubts around the Franco-German relationship aren’t limited to the far end of the political spectrum. In a November poll conducted by the French branch of the European think tank More in Common, 71% of respondents described Germany as an ally. While that was more than any other international partner, it was down 6 percentage points from last year, led by a sharp drop among conservatives, traditionally among the most pro-German part of the electorate. Even mainstream French politicians have begun to temper their enthusiasm for Franco-German industrial cooperation after Germany decided unilaterally to pull the plug on a joint effort to design and build a next-generation fighter jet and in the face of cooled support by Berlin for a similar project for tanks. Leading center-right candidates such as Edouard Philippe, a German speaker, have said that Paris should look beyond Berlin to form new partnerships and beef up its security. Le Pen, who has long shared Mélenchon’s defiance, said on Thursday she wanted to end the era of “German Europe.” “German rearmament strikes a chord historically for many voters,” said Paul Maurice, an expert on Franco-German relations at the French Institute of International Relations. “It speaks to the collective psyche.” Beyond security fears, German defense spending also plays on French insecurities as the country grapples with a prolonged public finances crisis. “When [voters] look at Germany today, they see what France is not capable of doing any more,” Maurice said. Tellingly, he added, “Mélenchon is the first candidate to go to Berlin” during the campaign. And, so far, the only one.

noticias.titulo: 5 budget battles to watch at the EU summit
noticias.resumen: From farmers' subsidies to tech taxes, leaders are expected to disagree over almost everything at the European Council.
noticias.texto: 5 budget battles to watch at the EU summit From farmers’ subsidies to tech taxes, leaders are expected to disagree over almost everything at the European Council. By GREGORIO SORGI in Brussels Illustration by Natália Delgado/POLITICO EU leaders are bracing for a huge fight over the bloc’s next seven-year budget as they gather in Brussels on Thursday for a summit that none of the rival governments expect to conclude with an agreement. European Council President António Costa is trying to muster support for his budget proposal that was presented on Saturday and envisages €44 billion in additional cuts from a previous plan. All leaders will discuss the EU budget and a €45 billion loan to Ukraine at lunchtime on Thursday, after which they will hold several hours of meetings in smaller groups or one-on-one later in the day. They’ll reconvene Thursday night to see whether the discussions helped them make progress — but no deal is expected before the final summit of the year starting Dec. 17. “Europe cannot demand more of itself while at the same time choosing to invest less,” Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis said in a statement from his office on Wednesday evening. “There can be no strong Europe with a weak European budget.” Over a dozen diplomats preparing for the summit said they expect flare-ups and tensions among leaders, who have signaled they are unwilling to make compromises at this stage of the negotiations. European Council President António Costa and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz address a press conference at the Chancellery in Berlin on Sept. 9, 2026. | John Macdougall/AFP via Getty Images “It is not the summit for convergence. It is not the time to climb down,” said an EU diplomat who, like others quoted in this story, was granted anonymity to discuss confidential negotiations. “Costa knows he probably needs a bad EUCO [European Council] before he can have a good one” in December, said a second senior EU diplomat. Here’s what’s going to be on the leaders’ minds: 1. The actual size of the thing This is the mother of all battles. A bloc of northern states, including Germany and the Netherlands, is pushing for a smaller budget geared toward what they consider “modern” priorities like defense and competitiveness. They are challenged by a rival camp of governments from Europe’s south and east, including Italy and Poland, demanding the EU spend more and maintain its focus on what the bloc has traditionally spent money on, like farming and its poorer regions. Tensions are so high that EU governments can’t even agree on how much larger the proposed budget is than the current one. While German Chancellor Friedrich Merz claimed that Costa’s proposal is 40% higher than the last seven-year budget agreed in 2020, rival governments said this ignores the rise in inflation and the repayments of the EU’s post-Covid debt, which eats up roughly 10% of the total. “Some keep pretending that the budget still increases as compared to the current MFF [Multiannual Financial Framework],” EU budget commissioner Piotr Serafin told the European Parliament Wednesday. “But that is only because they do not factor in inflation — and that is simply not convincing.” Expect more flashpoints during the summit. 2. Protecting the farmers So far, farmers have been among the few stakeholders sheltered from efforts to shrink the budget. But that’s still not enough for France, home to a powerful farmers’ lobby and facing elections in April and May, with far-right candidate Marine Le Pen leading the polls . The latest budget proposal comprises up to €297 billion in direct payments for farmers from 2028 to 2034. President Emmanuel Macron is pushing to increase ringfencing of this figure from 80% to 90% — to the annoyance of several other countries. French President Emmanuel Macron and Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico arrive for a working session during the informal EU leaders’ retreat at the Alden Biesen Castle, in Rijkhoven, on Feb. 12, 2026. | Nicolas Tucat/AFP via Getty Images “France also has to be able to make compromises,” said a third EU diplomat. “They feel like they are doing everyone a favour if they agree so they want all their priorities addressed.” 3. New taxes Costa faces an uphill battle to convince the EU’s 27 leaders to support new EU-wide taxes to bolster the budget and reduce contributions to Brussels directly from national governments. The latest proposal would see five new taxes, to generate €60 billion per year. But given the sensitivity of the EU acquiring new taxing powers, leaders won’t give any approval until the whole budget deal is finalized. Each government wants to get rid of the tax that would disproportionately affect it. Poland opposes using revenues from the emissions trading scheme to target polluting firms. Luxembourg objects to funneling tobacco tax proceeds. Ireland is skeptical about a levy on tech giants over fears it will ignite U.S. retaliation. 4. Link to Ukraine Germany’s Merz is using the budget as leverage to pressure four countries — Hungary, Slovakia, Czechia and Bulgaria — to help repay the borrowing costs associated with a €45 billion loan to Ukraine. Berlin, which pays around one quarter of the total EU budget, has threatened to slash its contributions if they hold out. But behind closed doors, Hungary and Bulgaria are open to contributing to the loan while Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico is more reluctant, said two EU diplomats with knowledge of proceedings. Czechia remains sceptical towards the loan to Ukraine, a Czech official told POLITICO. A potential solution could involve paying the borrowing costs of the Ukraine funding that doesn’t finance military spending, a Bulgarian official said. But most countries reject this idea. “There isn’t a menu in Europe where you decide what to pay and what you don’t,” a fourth senior EU diplomat said. 5. European preference Macron is leading a rearguard push to lock non-EU firms out of defense funding under the new budget. Costa proposed giving access to companies from allied countries including the U.K., Canada, Norway and Ukraine — but left out the U.S. While this compromise is acceptable to most governments, it’s still not enough for Macron, who wants to raise the issue during the summit, an EU diplomat said. On the other hand, Romania is pushing in the opposite direction. It insists that U.S. arms companies gain more access to the European market. “We need the American technology in Europe, and from my perspective we should identify ways to collaborate and to have the American presence,” Romanian Defense Minister Ștefan-Radu Oprea told POLITICO . Camille Gijs contributed to this article. CORRECTION: This article was updated on Nov. 26 to correct Czechia’s position.

noticias.titulo: How to watch the Spanish election like a pro
noticias.resumen: High turnout is expected for Sunday's election, which is widely seen as major potential turning point.
noticias.texto:
An electoral campaign billboard for Spanish Prime Minister and Spanish Socialist Paty (PSOE) leader Pedro Sánchez is pictured near the Sagrada Familia Basilica in Barcelona on November 25, 2026. | Manaure Quintero/AFP via Getty Images
Almost 39 million Spaniards are eligible to vote in Sunday’s election, which is tipped to shift the country’s political trajectory to the right and end Pedro Sánchez’s eight-year Socialist premiership.
Turnout is projected to be high, with many voters seeing the contest as a potential turning point — not least because the conservative People’s Party is expected to form a governing coalition with the nationalist Vox party, ushering the far right into power for the first time since democracy was restored in the 1970s.
Alberto Núñez Feijóo, leader of the PP, has vowed to bring “the necessary change” to Spain, telling POLITICO that his party and Vox agree that “sanchismo [Sánchez’s rule] is going to end in our country.”
Advertisement
Sánchez himself is framing his long-shot bid for reelection as an existential choice between joining a “far-right wave that drives regression wherever it governs” or having Spain “remain a bastion of openness, social justice, and environmental responsibility.”
Here is everything you need to know about how the election will work and what to expect after the result and coalition haggling begins.
What are people voting for?
Spaniards are voting to fill the two chambers of the Spanish parliament, or the Cortes Generales: the Congress of Deputies and the Senate.
Spain’s Congress of Deputies wields significant political power: it examines all proposed bills, has the final say on which laws are passed, and can bring down governments.
The Congress will ultimately decide who governs Spain, and the next prime minister needs the votes of 176 of its 350 members to win.
In Spain’s last general election, the PP won the most seats in Congress, but Sánchez retained power by striking a deal with a key regional party.
Advertisement
When will we know who wins?
On election day, polls open at 9 a.m. and close at 8 p.m. The Interior Ministry will publish turnout updates at 2 p.m. and 6 p.m.
When polls close at 8 p.m., counting begins, with congressional ballots counted first.
At 9 p.m. (8 p.m. in the Canary Islands), official results will start to come in. National media will publish the most recent polling data they have, instead of a traditional exit poll. The results come in quickly on election night, with the winner clear within a matter of hours.
The final count is conducted by provincial electoral boards starting from three days after the election and the official results are those published in the Official State Gazette.
How are the lawmakers chosen?
The 350 MPs are elected across 50 provinces and the two autonomous cities of Ceuta and Melilla in North Africa. Each city elects one representative, using a first-past-the-post system. Every other province elects a minimum of two lawmakers, with the rest of the seats allocated based on the size of the population.
Madrid and Barcelona elect 38 and 32 lawmakers, respectively, while provinces that appear large but are not densely populated, often described as España vaciada (“Emptied Spain”), can account for just a handful of seats.
Advertisement
Voters select a party on their ballots, and candidates are then assigned to seats based on their position on a closed list drawn up by each party.
Seats are given to each party in proportion to the share of votes it receives in each province. Specifically, this calculation uses the D’Hondt system to allocate seats among parties that have received more than 3% of the valid votes (which include blank votes in Spain.)
Which regions matter most?
The most important battlegrounds vary across elections, depending on prospective coalition alliances — for instance, this year Andalusia and Catalonia will be key places to watch — but the structure of Spain’s electoral system means that winning over rural voters is particularly advantageous.
This is because the two-seat minimum requirement means that rural areas are actually over-represented in the legislature, while voters in the capital have less relative power.
If all of Spain’s eligible voters voted for the 350 MPs in the upcoming national election, each lawmaker would represent about 110,000 people. But in reality, the number of voters a deputy represents can vary massively across provinces.
Spain’s two main nationwide parties tend to win a larger share of seats than their actual national voter share. This is, in part, because in the majority of constituencies that only have a handful of seats available, smaller parties would need to get a significant share of the vote — well above the formal 3% threshold — to be in contention to win seats.
Advertisement
What about the Senate?
Some 209 senators will also be elected directly by voters, with four coming from every province on the mainland and additional representatives elected on Spain’s islands and North African exclaves. Regional parliaments appoint the remaining senators.
The Senate is less powerful than the Congress, providing second readings of proposed legislation and territorial representation. The body has a reputation for being a dumping ground for sidelined party grandees and a refuge for politicians whom Spain’s political groups seek to shield from judicial investigations through parliamentary immunity.
However, its support is vital for constitutional reform, and the chamber has the power to appoint magistrates to the Constitutional Court. Although the Senate doesn’t normally get much attention during elections, right-wing parties are hoping to secure three-fifths of the seats this year, enough to push through appointments that could shift the Constitutional Court’s ideological balance without consulting the left.
In the hopes of gaining control of the chamber, the Socialists and the PP have both struck deals with like-minded parties to withdraw candidates from constituencies where they would run against each other.
What happens after election day?
Once all the votes are counted and seats in Congress are assigned, coalition negotiations and vote-whipping for investiture debates formally begin. This can take months and has become increasingly long-winded in recent years as Spanish politics has become more fragmented.
The process is, in theory, simple: The candidate who wishes to become prime minister meets with the king, who tasks them with forming a government. This candidate then presents themselves to the Congress for an investiture debate and vote, in which they need at least 176 votes from their peers to be elected.
Advertisement
If they fail to win support in the first investiture vote, another one is held with a lower bar: a candidate only needs more votes in favor of their leadership than against. If they fail at the second vote and no other prospective leader can get enough support to become prime minister, another election is called.
Assuming the PP wins the largest share of the national vote and, combined with Vox’s seats, a working majority in Congress, Feijóo is expected to become prime minister relatively quickly — perhaps in January. The key question will be whether the two parties enter a formal coalition agreement together, or whether they agree to more limited cooperation supporting each other in congressional votes.
If Sánchez manages to win the largest share of the national vote, things could become more complicated. He would have a mandate to go to the king to ask to form a government, and could try his luck at negotiating with smaller parties to govern together. Assuming PP and Vox still end up controlling a majority of seats in Congress, it is expected Sánchez would fail to win the investiture votes, at which point Feijóo would have his opportunity to put himself forward as leader and repeat the process.
This would be similar to the scenario after the last general election, in which Feijóo’s PP won the largest share of the public vote but failed to win support to form a government in Congress.
If neither the PP and Vox nor Sánchez and his left-wing allies are able to form a majority, the situation could become extremely complex, with a possible repeat of the failed attempts to form governments after the 2015 and April 2019 elections.
Aitor Hernández-Morales and Ángel Villarino Pérez contributed reporting.

noticias.titulo: This Riviera mayor wants to bring Javier Milei’s chainsaw politics to France
noticias.resumen: The right-wing challenger wants sweeping spending cuts, looser business rules and tougher immigration controls.
noticias.texto: PARIS — When he presented his plan to slash French public spending in April, David Lisnard brought a paper shredder. It was a more safety-conscious take on uber-libertarian Argentine leader Javier Milei’s chainsaw. The right-wing mayor of Cannes fed it sheets representing France’s labor, environmental and urban planning laws. He vowed to shred large chunks of French legislation, cut 400,000 civil service jobs and reduce public spending by at least €200 billion. The proposals are an unusual pitch for a country deeply attached to a strong centralized state. And yet Lisnard’s popularity ratings have shot up, shaking up a presidential race in which the far right’s Marine Le Pen and the far left’s Jean-Luc Mélenchon have made the early running. “Lisnard is very different, very free,” said Geoffroy Boulard, a mayor and vice president of Lisnard’s New Energy party. “Some say he’s nothing but an online bubble, but there’s a surge of popular enthusiasm around him.” Partly thanks to his stunts, the plain-speaking, athletic 57-year-old has become a social media phenomenon, with supporters posting AI-generated videos that portray him as a Marvel superhero, a World War I soldier or even a member of the Ghostbusters team. Lisnard, a former member of the conservative Les Républicains party, openly praises Milei’s methods in Argentina. He argues that France needs its own “radical and cultural break” with the “infernal spiral” of debt, tax hikes and deteriorating public services. POLITICO’s Poll of Polls puts Lisnard at 11% in the first round, neck and neck with the center-right Edouard Philippe and the center-left Raphaël Glucksmann. Even Le Pen is under pressure to react to the emergence of a fresh face in the race, attacking him for failing to defend workers . The Lisnard buzz is “a bubble,” said one of President Emmanuel Macron’s ministers who, like others quoted here, was granted anonymity to speak candidly. “But like Emmanuel Macron was at the beginning. We all laughed at him when he would lose his voice at his first political rallies.” “Maybe the bubble will burst,” the minister added. “But it could also be the beginning of something.” Crowning moment Lisnard has never been elected to parliament or held a ministerial post. But he is not exactly an outsider, either. As mayor of a world-famous conference resort, he has plenty of networking opportunities, and since 2021 he has led the powerful French mayors’ lobby. On Wednesday, Lisnard was re-elected president of the Association des maires de France with 72% of the vote. The question on everyone’s mind is whether his re-election will be a springboard to the Elysée Palace. At the AMF’s annual gathering, the mayor of Cannes was in his element. Lisnard is “energetic, outspoken,” said Olivier Maurin, the mayor of a village in southern France who joined the New Energy party last month. “He’s got a positive attitude,” said David Pommier, a conservative mayor from near Lyon. Argentinian President Javier Milei gestures while delivering a speech at an economic forum in Madrid on Oct. 21, 2026. | Thomas Coex/AFP via Getty Images But others are fed up with what they see as his use of the organization — which is supposed to be a pluralistic forum for more than 34,000 mayors — to boost his presidential bid. “It’s starting to get awkward,” said Françoise Gonnet-Tabardel, the mayor of a small rural town. Before his re-election, Lisnard said on the sidelines of the conference that “not that many people are bothered” by his bid for the Elysée. “It’s being weaponized by my opponents,” he said. He refused to take questions about his presidential bid. The newcomer Lisnard’s big advantage in the campaign is that he is not in any way associated with Macron’s decade in power. “Lisnard’s strength is that he is new,” said the minister quoted above. “People like the fact that he embodies order … But they don’t buy the libertarian politics.” The son of small-business owners in Cannes, Lisnard has spent most of his life in local politics. He ran the city’s Palais des Festivals before becoming mayor in 2014. That role gave him the chance to rub shoulders with Hollywood stars and with leaders in the advertising and real estate industries, who spend lavishly at marquee trade events each year in the Mediterranean resort. Lisnard is also capable of rubbing people the wrong way. He recently clashed with a journalist who chided him live on TV for arriving late for his morning interview. He also said that he didn’t “give a damn” when a student questioned him about the Oct. 17, 1961 massacre in Paris, when French police turned on Algerian demonstrators, and dozens were thrown in the Seine and drowned. “I wasn’t born then,” he said. A long-distance runner and a fan of Nina Hagen and The Clash, Lisnard claims political inspiration ranging from Argentina’s Milei to British Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher, arguing that she “liberated the creative energy of her country.” Targeted As the newcomer in the presidential race, Lisnard is taking hits from across the political spectrum. National Rally President Jordan Bardella called him a “masked Macronist” who would bring the centrists back to power. Meanwhile, Lisnard’s rivals accuse him of preparing an alliance with the far right in France. Candidates are often asked who they would vote for if they fail to qualify for the second-round runoff, and while Lisnard said in a television interview Sunday that he would vote for Philippe against Mélenchon, he did not say whether he would pick his center-right rival against Le Pen. Lisnard “finds it difficult to say whether he will vote for Le Pen or myself,” the center-right Philippe told reporters on the sidelines of the AMF conference. “It shows that you can like chainsaws, but don’t know where to draw a line,” he said. Philippe’s allies say that once the public finds out about Lisnard’s policy ambitions — which, in addition to radical spending cuts, include eliminating regional health agencies and pushing back the retirement age — voters will come back to earth. On immigration, the mayor of Cannes also wants to hold a referendum and introduce strict immigration quotas. For now, the Lisnard bubble shows no sign of bursting. He says he already has enough endorsements from elected officials to run in the presidential election and this week the New Energy party said its membership had crossed the 150,000 mark. He is the fourth most influential politician online at the moment, behind Le Pen, Mélenchon and far-right leader Éric Zemmour, according to Visibrain, a social media monitoring platform. Over the past three months, Lisnard has drawn 2.2 million likes and mentions across social networks, 14 times more than Philippe. A centrist former minister said the emergence of France’s version of Milei shows that candidates who are former members of Macron’s governments are now seen as tainted: “Voters don’t want a baby Macron.”

noticias.titulo: [Interview] Europe’s next budget risks ‘making the strong stronger’ by diverting funds from poorer areas, EU regions chief warns
noticias.resumen: As 2026 draws to a close, EU institutions and capitals are finalising the bloc's 2028 to 2034 budget, with catch-up funding for poor regions likely to face deep cuts, even is its top advocate in Brussels is fighting back.
noticias.texto: As the first Hungarian citizen to head an EU institution, Kata Tüttő was predisposed to sympathise with marginalised communities. A former deputy mayor of Budapest, the socialist politician and economist has been heading the European Committee of the Regions since 2025, and now faces the biggest task so far in her role. Ahead of a crunch summit at which EU leaders will discuss cuts to the EU budget on Thursday and Friday (26 and 27 November), Tüttő spoke to EUobserver about the difficulty of getting Brussels to prioritise investment in Europe’s underdeveloped communities. What are the risks to the regions under the existing proposals for the 2028-2034 EU budget? In the cities and regions, the expectations are big, because we have a lot of challenges. There was a feeling in the air that if we have new strategies, if we have new ambitions to become climate neutral, to become strategically independent, to invest in housing. There was a sense that money will follow. One of the most important policies in the European Union is called cohesion policy. Historically, one-third of the budget has gone into food security and common agricultural policy. Now it’s seen as being really justified that we invested, so European farmers don’t stop producing food. The other one-third is the so-called cohesion policy. It’s the most important investment policy of the EU.
